title: The 2027 Coachella lineup is here: Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA to headline
summary: The 2027 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival lineup is finally here
story: The 2027 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival lineup is finally here
INDIO, Calif. -- Three acts who are no strangers to Coachella will headline the annual festival in the California desert next April, the organizers announced Wednesday.

Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA, who have all previously performed at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, will each headline one of the evenings of the event, which is held on consecutive three-day weekends.
Tame Impala, the musical project of Kevin Parker, claimed one of the top spots back in 2019, when he became the festival's first Australian headliner.

Both Lipa and SZA have Coachella experience, too. SZA joined Justin Bieber on stage as a surprise guest during his headlining set earlier this year. And Lipa joined Martin Garrix on stage back in 2017.

And Daddy Yankee, who will become the first Latin urbano artist named artist of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammys Thursday night, is a featured act making his Coachella debut. Last month, he released “La Postal,” his first concept album.

Also in next spring's Coachella lineup: Madonna, Phoebe Bridgers, Weezer, Dom Dolla, Don Toliver, Robyn, Zara Larsson, Steve Lacy, Kelela, Kehlani, Jisoo, Diljit Dosanjh, Tiësto, Kygo, Adéla, Måneskin, Four Tet, Underworld, Giorgio Moroder, Peggy Gou, Angine de Poitrine, Social Distortion and many other acts.
The festival will be held at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California, on April 9-11 and April 16-18, 2027.
Tickets go on sale Friday at 3 p.m. EST.

title: Rapper Yella Beezy convicted of hiring gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in Dallas
summary: A Dallas County jury has unanimously convicted rapper Yella Beezy of capital murder in a brazen daylight attack on rapper MO3 on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020
story: A Dallas County jury has unanimously convicted rapper Yella Beezy of capital murder in a brazen daylight attack on rapper MO3 on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020
DALLAS -- Rapper Yella Beezy was found guilty on Wednesday of hiring the gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in a brazen daylight attack on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020.

Yella Beezy, 35, whose real name is Markies Conway, was unanimously convicted of capital murder by a Dallas County jury in the death of MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In September, a jury found Kewon White guilty of capital murder for fatally shooting Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Prosecutors said the killing was the result of an escalating feud between Conway and Noble that had lasted years. Both men lived in Dallas.
Prosecutors said Conway paid White $40,000 for the shooting.

Noble, 28, was driving on Interstate 35 in south Dallas around noon on Nov. 11, 2020, when White pulled alongside him, authorities said. White stepped out of his vehicle holding a gun. Noble got out of his own vehicle and began running on the freeway as White shot at him, authorities said.
Prosecutor Tommy Adams said White wore a mask and fired over 40 rounds from an AK-47-style pistol while chasing Noble.
White shot Noble and a bystander who was inside a car, police said. The bystander survived, but Noble died at a hospital.

During closing arguments, prosecutors showed jurors a video clip of Conway talking about revenge in an interview, saying he would “get his lick back.” Prosecutor Krystal Biggins drew a comparison between Noble’s killing and a roadway shooting that injured Conway in 2018.
In October 2018, Conway survived being shot while driving on a tollway in the Dallas suburb of Lewisville when someone pulled up next to him and opened fire, hitting him three times.
“This was for the world to see,” Biggins said. “Over a rap beef, we are here for capital murder.”
The defense argued prosecutors hadn’t proven their case. “This is capital murder and the state has brought you a lot of speculation," defense attorney John Gussio said.
Noble had more than 800,000 Instagram followers and was best known for a 2019 remix of “Errybody,” with Baton Rouge, Louisiana, rapper Boosie Badazz.
Conway is best known for his 2017 single, “That’s On Me,” and the 2019 song “Bacc At It Again” with Quavo and Gucci Mane.

title: Irma P. Hall, 'Soul Food' and 'The Ladykillers' actor, dies at 91
summary: Irma P
story: Irma P

Irma P. Hall, the veteran actor who brought warmth and authority to matriarchal roles in “Soul Food” and “The Ladykillers,” and whose acting career took off after decades as a teacher, died Tuesday in Dallas. She was 91.
Her family announced her death Wednesday. No cause was given.

Hall was best known to many viewers as Big Mama, the family’s steadying force in the 1997 film “Soul Food.” The role earned her an NAACP Image Award and led to a return as the character in the television series based on the film.

She received a Cannes Film Festival Jury Prize for her performance as Marva Munson, a Bible-reading landlady opposite Tom Hanks in the Coen brothers’ 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers.” Hall also appeared in “A Family Thing,” “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil,” “Beloved,” “Patch Adams,” “Collateral” and Tyler Perry’s “Meet the Browns.”

Hall was 60 when “A Family Thing” brought her a major film role. She played Aunt T., a blind woman whose counsel helps guide two half brothers, played by James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall. The part drew attention to an actor who had spent years developing her craft onstage and in smaller screen roles.

“I was just concentrating on developing this craft,” Hall said in a 1996 interview with The Associated Press. “I guess you really never know where you are, you probably think you are on a lower rung than you really are.”

Hall had not set out to become an actor. Born Irma Dolores Player on June 3, 1935, in Beaumont, Texas, she was raised in Chicago and later returned to Texas for college. She taught English and foreign languages in Dallas public schools for more than two decades.

Her path to the screen began when actor and director Raymond St. Jacques heard her recite poetry in Dallas and cast her in his 1973 film “Book of Numbers.” Hall continued teaching as she took acting roles, then made performance her full-time work in the 1980s. She also helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre and remained involved in developing young artists.

Hall’s career included theater, television and film. Her credits ranged from the 1997 Clint Eastwood drama “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” to the 1998 films “Beloved” and “Patch Adams.” She also voiced Great Aunt T. in the 2001 “Rugrats” Kwanzaa special.

In 2004, Hall was recovering from serious injuries suffered in a car crash, including open-heart surgery, a broken arm and a crushed ankle, when she traveled from a Chicago convalescent center to attend a private screening of “The Ladykillers.”
“I loved the whole thing,” she told The Associated Press. “You never really know until you see it on the screen.”
Hall said she had heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers while recuperating. They had signed her pillow, she said. “Whenever I miss them, I hug it.”

In Dallas, Hall was also a longtime member and Church Mother at Inspiring Body of Christ Church. Her family remembered her as a woman of faith who read to children at the church’s school and stayed active in its theater ministry.
“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said in the family’s announcement.

title: Actor Stacy Keach, star of stage and ‘Mike Hammer’ series, dies at 85
summary: Stacy Keach, known for his role as Mike Hammer on TV and work onstage, has died at 85
story: Stacy Keach, known for his role as Mike Hammer on TV and work onstage, has died at 85

Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.

Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure,” his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.

Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.

Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating “World's Most Amazing Videos” on TV. He played a deranged colonel in “The Ninth Configuration” (also known as “Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane”), led the TV show “Titus," had a role in Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama “Nebraska,” and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama “Blue Bloods.” Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in “Jay Kelly.”

“My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career,” he told New York magazine in 2012. “My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I’ve gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.”

Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie “Lone Rider,” said in a post on X that Keach was a “consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him.”

He played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries “Mistral's Daughter,” a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz's novel “Princess Daisy,” Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli's “Jesus of Nazareth” and Maj. Jonas Steele in “The Blue and the Gray.” He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds (16 kilograms).

Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play “Indians,” played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in “King Lear” on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in “The Kentucky Cycle” in 1993, “The Country Wife” in 1965 and “Other Desert Cities” in 2011.

He also headed the national touring company cast of “Frost/Nixon,” portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with “Sleuth” with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of “King Lear” at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for “Pamplona,” a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run's cancellation.

While he was still doing “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer” (later titled “The New Mike Hammer”), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.

“As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats,” he wrote in his 2013 book, “All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage.” He added: “It was the lowest moment of my life.”

He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book “The Blue and the Gray.”

The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.

In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, “The Long Riders.” He said the experience was “very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity.”

After prison, he narrated the TV documentary “High on the Job,” and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. “There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one's existence,” he testified.

Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centers. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the “Hammer” series. He said he treasured her photos and letters behind bars.
Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.

His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, “Intimate Strangers” with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, “The Return of Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer,” also played well, and then the “Mike Hammer” series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS' 1986-87 schedule.

Many years later, in the TV series “Prison Break” that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.
Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.

In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne. He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New York’s Public Theater in “Hamlet” with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles.

Keach made his film debut in 1968 in “The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter” and played stoner cop Sergeant Stedenko from the Cheech and Chong movies. He worked for director John Huston twice, in “Fat City” and “The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean” and had roles in “American History X” with Edward Norton and “The Bourne Legacy.” He played a tough trucker in “Roadgames,” was electrocuted in “Children of the Corn” and a robot removed his heart in “Class of 1999.”
His biggest break, though, came with the role of Hammer, whom he played as a modern-day knight, a champion of the underdog.

“Keach makes a dashing, dapper Hammer. He looks almost jaunty in his tilted gray fedora,” said Fred Rothenberg, a TV writer for The Associated Press, in 1983. “He knows how to speak lust with his eyes, and talk dirty with his fists.”
AP Entertainment Writer Andrew Dalton contributed reporting from Los Angeles.

title: Huge crowds, low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as pope visits South America
summary: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
story: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles.
Cases are already surging in the region this year and mass gatherings provide an opportunity for one of the world's most contagious viruses to spread further.

The Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, and officials in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru have been preparing for potential problems to different degrees for months, including mounting vaccination campaigns and increasing surveillance to try to limit spread.

Uruguay, where thousands of people attended a prayer vigil and a Mass celebrated by Leo, implemented a nationwide intensified surveillance monitoring period until Nov. 29, three weeks after Leo’s departure from the country, according to Nataly Rodriguez, director of epidemiology at Uruguay’s health ministry. Uruguay has also taken steps to boost its vaccination rate to among the highest in the region.
“As a preventive strategy, the ministry has been emphasizing the importance of keeping vaccination schedules up to date,” Rodriguez said.

The Nov. 6-17 trip to the continent where around 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics live marks a return home for Leo, who spent two decades ministering in Peru as a missionary priest and then bishop.

Ahead of the visit, PAHO assessed the public health risk of measles in the context of the religious mass gatherings in South America as “very high.” That's in part because there has been a nearly five-fold increase in cases between January and October compared with the same period last year.
“We’re seeing children not going to school, children being hospitalized,” said Daniel Salas Peraza, the head of immunization at PAHO. “It’s a very complex situation.”

Measles spreads easily through the air when an infected person breathes, sneezes or coughs. A person can be contagious even before they show symptoms. The virus first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes and a rash. It most commonly affects children and while it usually isn’t fatal, it can be.

The vaccine for measles is extremely effective, but the first of two doses is not usually recommended for babies until their first birthday. In order to stop the disease from spreading in a community, to protect infants and others who can't get the vaccine, at least 95% of the population must be fully vaccinated with two doses.

As of 2025, only Uruguay had achieved that number, according to data from the World Health Organization. Peru has reached 90% with one dose and 82% with two doses while Argentina has reached only 84% with one dose and 55% with both doses.

PAHO reported 57,666 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories in the Americas between January and the end of October, nearly five times the number recorded during the same period in 2025. At least 81 people have died so far this year due to the disease.
With nearly 3,000 cases, Peru has seen the fourth highest number of cases in the Americas after Guatemala, Mexico and the United States.
In the five Peruvian cities Leo will be visiting including Lima, Chiclayo, Cajamarca, Cusco and Pucallpa, a total of 170 measles cases have been identified so far in 2026.

Ahead of the Pope’s visit, Salas Peraza said PAHO had supported efforts to encourage vaccination in Peru, including initiatives targeting adolescents, deploying equipment to strengthen vaccine storage and delivery capacity, and intensifying vaccination along the border with Brazil.

In late October, authorities carried out measles vaccination campaigns in areas with the highest rates of transmission. These included a dose for babies aged six to eleven months, as well as vaccination for people up to 29 years old.
By the end of September, 1.2 million vaccine doses had been administered since April in Peru, with more than two million additional doses available.
Still, with vaccination rates so far below the threshold needed for community protection in parts of the region, experts say conditions are ripe for further spread.

In Argentina, authorities issued a warning in late October about the high risk associated with the pope’s visit, after estimating that they expected up to 4 million people in the province of Buenos Aires.

But Argentina President Javier Milei has slashed Argentina’s healthcare budget, eviscerating agencies tasked with planning, financing and tracking immunization campaigns. The cuts coincided with a measles outbreak that in April 2025 led to Argentina’s first measles death in two decades and some are concerned that efforts are falling short.

Marcela Lopez Yunes, a doctor and pediatric infectious disease specialist, said she hadn’t seen what she considered sufficient public communication to encourage vaccination. “We need to do a little more to give diseases such as measles the attention and importance they deserve,” she said.

A spokesperson for Argentina's health ministry said that while the federal government is in charge of purchasing and distributing vaccines, provinces are in charge of administering them to their populations. They also said that there is an ongoing public service announcement speaking to the importance of vaccination in general.
Leo took aim at Milei’s austerity measures as he arrived in Argentina Sunday, insisting that political leaders must put people, not the economy, first.
Associated Press journalists Ramiro Barreiro in Montevideo, Uruguay, and Franklin Briceño in Lima, Peru, contributed to this report.

title: US, Mexico are on the verge of forfeiting a major health victory. Here's what to know
summary: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
story: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
NEW YORK -- International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the United States and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories — the elimination of measles.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past two years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths.

Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico — that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations' borders.
“It’s a big deal. The decision represents us moving backwards,” said Dr. David Margolius, director of Cleveland’s health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments.
Here's a look at the meeting's deliberations and why it's important.

In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for one year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024.
“It’s solely based on genetics,” said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have “eliminated” measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998.

The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said.
A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said this week.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks,” she said in the statement.

But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation's health agencies.

Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule, reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and lauded Trump’s executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups’ recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say.

Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30.

The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak.

But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine — which is credited with saving millions of lives globally — is possibly “quite lethal.” Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities.

Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah and South Carolina. And the more than 5,100 confirmed cases this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year — more than any year in more than three decades — and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.

A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed — in 1963, in the U.S. — and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016.

Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected.
As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old.

The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan lost their status.
Associated Press writer Megan Janetsky contributed to this story from Mexico City.

title: Preliminary study finds a clue in the quest to help diagnose CTE in the living
summary: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head
story: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head

WASHINGTON -- Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.

Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death.

The new clue involves a protein called tau that normally supports neurons but becomes abnormal in Alzheimer’s, tangling inside those nerve cells. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis were using autopsy samples to study a tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243 that may help track those tangles when they found something unusual: a patient with high levels of that biomarker even though records showed the person didn’t have Alzheimer’s but advanced CTE instead.
The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and other samples, and eventually tested blood stored from 11 people who had been classified as having CTE.

Compared to healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study coauthor Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn’t reliably identify early-stage CTE.

It is an interesting but very preliminary finding, requiring far larger studies to see if there is a real connection, cautioned Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who wasn’t involved with the research.

Abnormal tau is found in several brain diseases, many of which can overlap in older adults, adding to the difficulty in teasing apart its role in any one disease, including CTE. Sato, who studies such tauopathies, also stressed much more research is needed.
The findings were published late Friday by the medical journal JAMA and presented at a scientific meeting in Japan.

title: Trump administration will fund new research on controversial psychedelic drug ibogaine
summary: Federal officials say there's new funding to study the medical potential of a powerful psychedelic
story: Federal officials say there's new funding to study the medical potential of a powerful psychedelic

WASHINGTON -- Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder, a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans.
The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose and design studies of the drug.

Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy and most other psychedelic drugs.

Veterans organizations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status.

Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal.
“That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to have, I think, a record drug approval process.”
Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said.
Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and “best-in-class research.”
“For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce,” Collins said.

Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances.

Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions.

Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the Food and Drug Administration. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months.
Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly.

The little data currently available mostly comes from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby.

Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: “Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let’s do it.”

title: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
summary: Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, highlighting the severity of the situation
story: Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, highlighting the severity of the situation

BUNIA, Congo -- Congo’s Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the spread of the disease.

According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.

The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces.

The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.
While Ituri accounts for nearly 70% of total cases, North Kivu has emerged as the main site of new transmission, according to Congolese Health Minister Roger Kamba.
Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.

The outbreak has affected some schools in Ituri, with more teachers contracting the disease. Two head teachers in Bunia, the provincial capital of Ituri, told The Associated Press they are worried about their teachers and students after losing members of staff.

"Our students and the entire staff have been left traumatized. At this stage, we need psychologists to support us, as the situation is extremely difficult,” Isaac Singoma, one of the headteachers, said.
Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the outbreak in Congo. The disease has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

title: Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes, deep in Amazon
summary: Pope Leo XIV is demanding justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon
story: Pope Leo XIV is demanding justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon

PUCALLPA, Peru -- PUCALLPA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Sunday demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging, illegal mining and the “insatiable thirst for domination.”

On the penultimate day of his South American odyssey, Leo traveled into the Peruvian Amazon and channeled one of Pope Francis ’ core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the northeastern city of Pucallpa.
He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010-2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

In addition to the decades-long problem of deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Miners use makeshift suction dredges and mercury, a toxic metal, to extract gold.

Raphael Hoetmer, Western Amazon program director at Amazon Watch, said wars and conflicts around the world have driven up the price of gold, increasing demand that in turn is resulting in more extraction from the Amazon.
“It’s causing pollution, health issues, and environmental degradation,” he said.
Illegal mining and coca production also drive deforestation and encroach on Indigenous territories, threatening ancestral lands and exposing communities to violence and organized crime.

Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’ constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.

During the encounter and a subsequent Mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous who care for it rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.

“Very little has been done — and very slowly at that — while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at Mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”

In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions. In 2025, the Peruvian courts upheld a 28-year prison sentence for four timber merchants for the murder of four Indigenous people who opposed logging, following a trial that lasted a decade.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.

In August, a court sentenced four people to up to 35 years in prison. The court found that Inuma had filed a complaint against the defendants to prevent deforestation and other crimes such as drug trafficking, and that those convicted plotted his death because he had spoken out against the crimes.

Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in Condorcanqui province in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “complicity,” “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council, or Comuawuy, has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the province between January and July alone.

Following the women’s persistent demands for justice, specialized prosecutors’ offices were created, and the government launched a prevention plan. In January, the Ministry of Women and Vulnerable Populations announced a 32-year prison sentence for a man accused of sexual violence against a 14-year-old girl.
Leo said the church was “deeply concerned” by the suffering endured by the victims and called for healing, consolation and reparation.
“Such abuse leaves deep wounds, often compounded by complicity and impunity,” he said. “Corruption and arbitrary practices undermine the trust in the basic goodness of others.”
Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, criss-crossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains before he arrived in Pucallpa in the rainforest.

His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire. There, Leo praised the traditional expression of popular piety, such as processions and religious festivals, as effective ways of forging community and transmitting the faith, especially to young people.

Huge crowds lined Cusco’s cobblestoned streets and packed its central Plaza de Armas, an imposing square decorated with a blend of Inca and Spanish colonial buildings. Many people wore the traditional Andean hats and colorful wool vests typical of the region, while others wore plastic ponchos to guard against a drizzling morning rain.

“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus, sleep in a tent and eat Peruvian food from stalls. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”

The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.

In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate. While others traveling on the papal plane have fallen ill, Leo has shown no sign of weakness or fatigue since the trip began Nov. 6, and in fact seemed energized, especially from the days spent in his former diocese of Chiclayo seeing old friends.
The Rev. Peter Hughes, an 84-year-old Irish priest who has lived in Peru for more than six decades, said Leo’s itinerary reflected the church’s concern for the poor.

“In Latin American terms, the Indigenous peoples, or what is left of them, are the most important collective representing the truly poor,” he said. “That is what makes leaders like Pope Francis and Pope Leo speak the language of the Gospel in very human terms, putting a premium on justice and peace."
"In the Christian sense of justice, the most important people are the poor, the marginalized, and those who have no voice,” he said.
Suarez reported from Lima, Peru; Savarese from Cusco, Peru.

title: Thousands run Cuba’s Marabana marathon as many protest US sanctions
summary: Thousands of people have run in Cuba’s Marabana marathon, using the event to protest U.S. economic sanctions
story: Thousands of people have run in Cuba’s Marabana marathon, using the event to protest U.S. economic sanctions
HAVANA -- Thousands of people ran Sunday in Cuba’s most important international marathon, with some using the race to protest U.S. economic sanctions against the island.

The Marabana marathon, held every November to commemorate the founding of Havana, took runners along city's iconic streets and landmarks, such as the Paseo del Prado and the Capitol building. Many wore signs expressing solidarity with Cuba.
“Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is,” read the signs that many of the 3,000 participants wore on their backs.

The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960, after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations. As a result, the Caribbean country has endured decades of economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba.
The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that disrupt water supplies and internet and telephone services.
“The blockade is suffocating the Cuban people," Yuraldi Cava, a 58-year-old state employee, said while running. “We are going to win this fight.”

Mayté Vigoa, Havana’s provincial government coordinator for sports, said the city had to make a major effort to hold the international race because of the island’s precarious economic conditions. She confirmed that the sportswear brand Adidas, a longtime sponsor of the competition, did not provide support this year.
Other companies with longstanding ties to Cuba, including Meliá Hotels International, said they were withdrawing from the island because of the tightening of sanctions.
Participants included families with children and people with disabilities dressed in sportswear and carrying water bottles as enthusiastic onlookers cheered them on from the sidewalks.
Those protesting the sanctions included foreigners who wore red-and-white sweatshirts with the message “Cuba is not alone.”

The marathon is recognized by the Association of International Marathons and Distance Races, and runners can use their times as official qualifying marks. The event also features a half-marathon, as well as the more popular 10-kilometer and 5-kilometer races.

title: Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as 'role models' on surprise Ukraine visit
summary: Prince Harry has hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as role models, emphasizing the need for continued support from Kyiv
story: Prince Harry has hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as role models, emphasizing the need for continued support from Kyiv

LVIV, Ukraine -- LVIV, Ukraine (AP) — Britain's Prince Harry hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as society's role models Sunday and said they need to continue receiving support from Kyiv as he wrapped up an unannounced weekend visit to the war-torn country.

It was Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the war started and his second time in the western city of Lviv to meet with patients and staff at Superhumans Center, an orthopedic clinic that treats wounded military personnel and civilians.

"We’ve invested in them before they put the uniform on and we must invest with them once the uniform comes off,” Harry said during trials for the Invictus Games, a Paralympic-style event he founded to inspire military veterans around the world to overcome battlefield injuries.

Harry, a British Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, watched wheelchair rugby players clash on Saturday and pickleball players — many with prosthetic limbs — compete to represent Ukraine at next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham, England.
The Duke of Sussex grabbed a paddle and teamed up with a player with an amputated arm as they competed against two men who had each lost a leg.

“I asked him to play and he didn’t refuse," said Oleksandr, a 49-year-old veteran from Odesa with an amputated leg. “He talks to people, he isn’t like a royal personage. He loves ordinary people. He is completely different.”
Harry hailed the resilience of Ukrainians and hoped the war would soon end.
“The rest of the world will continue to support you," he said. “In my mind you’ve already won.”
Harry met Kostiantyn Vlasenko, who was the first Ukrainian airlifted by drone from the front lines near the village of Synkivka in the Kharkiv region.
Harry called Vlasenko “impressive” to which the soldier replied, “stubborn.”

Vlasenko was seriously wounded in combat in February with injuries that eventually forced the amputation of both his feet — one that he performed himself, according to the office of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who awarded him the Hero of Ukraine honor, the nation's highest honor.
Vlasenko maintained his position for 232 days hiding from the Russians and relaying important observations to his fellow troops until he was flown out in early October.
“I have a huge amount of admiration and respect for you," Harry told him.

title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters
story: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters

PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.
The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.

The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.
“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.”

Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.

Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.”

The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings.

Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others.
“We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading.

Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.”
Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom.

He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves.
Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion.

His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry.

"While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said.
Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report.

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

title: Cape Verde election could deliver first woman president since independence in 1975
summary: Cape Verde has held a presidential election in which former Justice Minister Joana Rosa is challenging incumbent José Maria Neves
story: Cape Verde has held a presidential election in which former Justice Minister Joana Rosa is challenging incumbent José Maria Neves

PRAIA, Cape Verde -- PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Cape Verde residents voted Sunday in a presidential election that could make Joana Rosa the country’s first woman head of state since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Polls closed Sunday evening in the vote in which the former justice minister is challenging President José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term. Six candidates are competing. If none wins more than half the votes, a runoff will be held Nov. 29.

Rosa has the backing of the opposition Movement for Democracy, which governed for a decade before losing May’s parliamentary election. Women have held senior Cabinet positions, but the Atlantic island nation off West Africa has never had a woman president or prime minister.
The archipelagic country in the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of West Africa, is battling with challenges such as a high unemployment rate and costs of living.
“I see many promises that are not fulfilled. I am tired, but I am still voting,” Aderito Cardoso, a 44-year-old resident of Villa Nova in the capital city Praia, said after casting her vote.

Under Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs policy and holds most executive power. The directly elected president’s role is largely ceremonial, although the office carries the power to veto legislation.

The country of about half a million people has a record of competitive elections and peaceful transfers of power that stands out in the region. Nearly 77,000 citizens living abroad are registered to vote, accounting for almost a fifth of the electorate.

Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde, said limited economic opportunities were pushing young people to leave. Many voters also feel disconnected from political leaders and want a president who understands their daily struggles, she said.
Neves, who won the presidency in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has promised to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.

His incumbency has given him greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said. Rosa’s candidacy, meanwhile, challenges traditional expectations of women in a society that remains “very patriarchal.”

Rosa has focused her campaign on the balance of power, arguing that the presidency should serve as a counterweight to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, which backs Neves and controls the government and most municipalities.

The party, known as PAICV, won a parliamentary majority in May, ending a decade of rule by the Movement for Democracy. A Rosa victory would again place the presidency and government in opposing political camps.
For Cape Verde-based writer Rosário Luz, party loyalties matter more than Rosa’s gender.
“We have a lot of women in politics, but we don’t have the policies for women that we should have,” she said.
Women shoulder much of the financial responsibility for their households, but government policies have failed to address that burden, Luz said.

title: Africa is charting a different road to electric mobility with motorbikes and versatile 3-wheelers
summary: In Africa, the electric vehicle transition is taking a different route from wealthier markets, with motorcycles and three-wheelers emerging as practical alternatives to passenger cars
story: In Africa, the electric vehicle transition is taking a different route from wealthier markets, with motorcycles and three-wheelers emerging as practical alternatives to passenger cars

HARARE, Zimbabwe -- The electric vehicle revolution in Zimbabwe began on rural dirt paths. Three-wheeled vehicles carried cabbages to markets, women farmers to their fields and patients to clinics in communities where transport has long been scarce.
For farmer Agefi Mutambo, the owner of an electric three-wheeler since 2021, it has transformed her business and family.
Before, she walked seven to 10 kilometers (4.3 to 6.2 miles) balancing a 20-kilogram (44-pound) bucket of tomatoes on her head that she sold for $6.
“The money wasn't even enough for food. I would do a single trip a day, arrive at the market late and the produce would no longer be as fresh,” the 56-year-old said.

Now she makes two to three deliveries a week transporting 300 kilograms (661 pounds) of produce on each trip, grossing roughly $80 a trip supplying schools and clinics. She also ferries neighbors to hospital, sometimes at midnight for a woman in labor.
“When my battery is low, I simply swap it for $4, and I am back on the road,” she said.
Mutambo is among dozens of rural women entrepreneurs in Zimbabwe whose lives have been transformed by electric tricycles introduced by local social enterprise Mobility for Africa in 2019.

The company introduced the solar-charged tricycles, powered by lithium-ion batteries, mainly for rural women, under a lease-to-own scheme costing about $30 a week. Called “Hamba,” meaning “go” in the local Ndebele language, the vehicles can carry loads of over 400 kilograms (880 pounds) and travel about 100 kilometers (62 miles) on a single charge. Solar-powered charging stations and swappable batteries allow drivers to exchange depleted batteries rather than wait for them to recharge.

Across parts of Africa, motorcycles and three-wheelers are emerging as a route to electric mobility, particularly in rural communities long overlooked by conventional mobility businesses. While electric cars gain ground in wealthier markets, these smaller vehicles can operate with less extensive and expensive charging infrastructure, offering a potentially cheaper leapfrog to electrification for the continent of 1.5 billion people.
Despite holding vast reserves of critical minerals used in electric vehicle batteries, Africa remains a minor player in the global EV market.

Africa sold about 25,000 electric cars in 2025, concentrated in Egypt, Morocco and South Africa, compared with more than 20 million worldwide, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook 2026.
In 2026, the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa identified unreliable electricity infrastructure, limited technical capacity and weak regulation as barriers to adoption.

But the market for small electric vehicles that are relevant to everyday transport, deliveries and commerce is growing, said Hezbon Mose, an e-mobility expert. Africa’s transition is largely centered on income-earning motorcycles and three-wheelers, with Ethiopia an exception because of its car-focused policies, he said.

While two-wheelers remain dominant, a three-wheeler market is emerging. In Kenya, annual electric three-wheeler registrations rose from 39 in 2023 to 517 in 2025, reaching 1,965 by June this year, said Mose, co-founder of non-profit, E-Mobility Africa.

The shift also has potential public health benefits. Electric motorcycles and three-wheelers produce no exhaust fumes, offering an opportunity to reduce roadside pollution. In Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, where motorcycles are part of public transport culture, road transport alone is responsible for 40% of fine particle air pollution, according to the Clean Air Fund.

A 2025 study published in the World Electric Vehicle Journal also found that electrifying Nairobi’s motorcycle fleet would eliminate tailpipe particulate emissions from those vehicles, while cutting daily automotive carbon dioxide emissions by about 85%.
For entrepreneurs, the appeal lies in the economics of income-generating vehicles rather than luxury, said Mose, the expert.
“Electric three-wheelers already pay for themselves for working drivers,” he said.

A taxi electric three-wheeler in the Kenyan coastal city of Mombasa can save roughly $4 to $10 a day in running costs compared with a petrol-powered vehicle, with the higher purchase price recouped in five to 21 months, said Mose.

“They suit Africa because they are income assets, not consumer goods. The same chassis serves as taxi, last-mile delivery, waste collection, and produce haulage, widening the market well beyond public transport,” he said.

Citing industry figures, Mose said roughly 30 million Africans earn a living on two- and three-wheelers, yet fewer than 200,000 are electric. “An owner buys on daily cash flow, which is exactly where electric wins,” said Mose.
Investors are backing businesses developing electric motorcycles, three-wheelers, charging infrastructure and battery-swapping systems, especially in East Africa.
Shantha Bloemen, the Mobility for Africa founder, reckons lasting growth requires financing models that can survive beyond donor-funded projects.

“We have seen what happens with aid, how temporary it is when countries look at other priorities,” she said. “They cut Africa, their projects go to the ground. We need humanitarian assistance, but we need development finance more.”
For Bloemen, the idea was to address basic obstacles to rural economic activity: the lack of reliable, affordable transport and funding.
“When transport is scarce, produce rots in fields, children miss school and families cannot access healthcare,” Bloemen said. “Transport becomes the difference between subsistence and commerce.”
Bloemen argues that improving access to transport can help unlock the potential of rural economies often overlooked by conventional lenders.

“The rural informal economy is where most people live,” Bloemen said. “And if you look at my market, rural small-scale farmers... none of the banks will lend to them because they are deemed not creditworthy.”
Rural women, Bloemen said, are often most affected.
“We have a gender bias. We don’t take women small-scale farmers seriously, which is really not a clever thing to do because women are so entrepreneurial and the backbone of every economy,” she said.
Mutambo, the farmer, sees herself as an example. Her improved earnings have paid for one child’s teaching diploma, high school fees for another and primary schooling for five grandchildren.
“We were looked down upon,” she said. “Now we are the pride of the village.”

title: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
summary: Southeast Asian leaders have opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila for three days of talks
story: Southeast Asian leaders have opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila for three days of talks

MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections.

The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.

Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said.

The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They also are expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says.

The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”
Marcos said it’s crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc’s diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds.

“That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats,” Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay.
Marcos warned problems across the world “are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone.”
But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China.
ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region’s conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea.

Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials.

Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila’s presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries’ decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren’t being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi,” U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said.
He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia.

“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” Poling said. “With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises.”
China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said.
Associated Press journalist Haruka Nuga in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: Spain says nearly 2,200 migrants reached Canary Islands in 2 days
summary: Spain's maritime rescue service says nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived in the Canary Islands over the past two days
story: Spain's maritime rescue service says nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived in the Canary Islands over the past two days
MADRID -- Nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived by boat in Spain’s Canary Islands over the past two days, Spain’s maritime rescue service said Sunday.

The Spanish archipelago off northwest Africa is one of the main entry points for migrants into the country, as people mainly from West Africa attempt the dangerous Atlantic crossing in ramshackle boats. Of the just over 28,000 people who arrived in Spain by sea between January and the end of October, more than 13,000 arrived in the Canary Islands, according to the Interior Ministry.

The Maritime Rescue Service said it had assisted 1,324 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom arrived on the island of El Hierro. The figure was close to the daily record for this route — 1,461 people rescued on Nov. 7, 2020.

The strip of the Atlantic Ocean between West Africa and the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. The islands are roughly 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the closest point in Africa, but to avoid security forces, many migrants attempt longer journeys that can take days or weeks. The majority depart from Mauritania.
