The president posted his message calling on Vance to steer away from Iran negotiations the morning after The Wall Street Journal reported Vance was thinking about resuming talks. Trump — who had been aware of Vance's deliberations — believed the Iranians weren't acting in good faith, the person added.
Trump is also increasingly confident that he can credibly declare that he's achieved his military objectives in the war.
But traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains treacherous. The United Nations reports October had the highest number of incidents against commercial ships in the contested waters since February.

Still, Trump believes with oil shipments through the strait reaching near-prewar levels, he could potentially leave it to Gulf countries to negotiate a deal with the Iranians on governing the critical waterway, the person said.
The other regional diplomat described the push for peace as falling into a holding pattern as people await clarification from the White House on Trump’s intentions.

That diplomat added it was not entirely clear to mediators or the Iranians if Trump’s comments meant he was abandoning a negotiated agreement or was just posturing after the congressional midterm elections that cost his Republican Party control of Congress.
Iran remains unwilling to engage in negotiations over its nuclear program until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement.
Differences with Iran over its nuclear activities remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

Tehran's rhetoric has hardly cooled. Iran’s deputy U.N. ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi told the United Nations Security Council on Friday that Iran “has never closed the door to diplomacy.” But he warned that should the U.S. or Israel return to bombing, his country would offer “an immediate and decisive response.”
Rubio earlier this week stressed that the U.S. is not opposed to mediators continuing their efforts.
“If there’s a deal to be done, the president will be the first one to be in favor of it," Rubio said. "But it’s not going to be a stupid deal. It’s not going to be a bad deal.”

Michael Singh, managing director at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said he expects the status quo to persist for some time, with the U.S. and Iran locked in a stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. continuing its monthslong naval blockade that's curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Singh said the American strategy of squeezing Iran economically is a far more attractive option for Trump than military escalation or making concessions to Tehran.
He also suggested Trump could always reverse his position on Vance engaging with Iranians if the president finds the Iranians are ready to seriously negotiate.

“It’s probably the most sensible path as well to sort of be patient, keep the pressure on, allow the mediators to keep doing their work,” said Singh, who worked on Middle East issues in former President George W. Bush's White House. “And when the time is right, but not before then, is when you want to engage senior officials like the vice president and so forth.”
Associated Press writers Nicholas Riccardi in Denver and Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations contributed reporting.

title: The Nvidia scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of Trump's visit
summary: The scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia is threatening to intensify the rivalry between the U.S. and China on artificial intelligence
story: The scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia is threatening to intensify the rivalry between the U.S. and China on artificial intelligence

HONG KONG -- Well before reports emerged that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the advanced chips made by his company were at the center of the race between the U.S. and China to dominate artificial intelligence.
The scandal now threatens to intensify that rivalry.

As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week in China, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Congress are seizing on the affair to press for tighter restrictions on technology exports to protect America's edge.

“The scandal, in many ways, encapsulates the rivalry, where concerns around national security, export control, and foreign policy get intertwined,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at London-based technology research and advisory group Omdia.

At the heart of the competition to build the most advanced artificial intelligence is the race to access the most powerful AI chips. U.S.-led restrictions have barred China from getting the world’s most advanced AI chips, a strategy that has led Beijing to accuse the U.S. of pursuing an AI monopoly.

Once commanding some 95% of market share in China, Nvidia’s sales to China have plummeted due to the export restrictions, first applied during the Biden administration. After Huang lobbied Washington to loosen the limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Trump earlier this year greenlighted the export of its highly-advanced, though not the most powerful, H200 chips.

Trump has spoken admiringly of Huang — a man at the center of the AI boom Trump has been keen to promote — and the two have talked regularly during his second term, including at least twice this week as the scandal grew around the tech executive.

The strategy in Washington has been largely focused on hardware, with officials believing if they controlled where California-based Nvidia’s best chips go, they’d be in control of the race for the most capable AI, said Shaoyu Yuan, an assistant professor at New York University’s Center for Global Affairs.
That strategy was effective in slowing down Chinese companies, Yuan said, but it assumed the primary threat was the physical hardware, not access to leaders like Huang.

Yuan said what he called “China hawks” in Congress — who have been bullish on oversight and stronger export controls long before this incident — will now have “a story with a name and a face” to support their argument.
“I don’t think anybody in Washington wants to be seen as loosening the controls on chip exports to China right now,” he added.

This week several congressional Democrats wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to ask what officials knew of Huang's affair with a reported Chinese spy — and to demand an immediate halt to exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.

Lawmakers from both parties have become more outspoken in their calls for tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. The Senate version of a defense policy bill includes authorizing Congress to review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, authorizing the Commerce Department to track AI chips to ensure they aren't diverted to unauthorized regions, and compelling U.S. allies to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.

Beijing has warned the U.S. against using the episode as a reason to impose new restrictions, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning telling reporters on Thursday: “The U.S. should stop fabricating the ‘Chinese spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions.”

The woman in the relationship with the Nvidia chief is reported to be Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to reporting by The New York Times, U.S. officials suspect she was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its cutting-edge chips more available to China.
Beijing has refuted claims she was a Chinese spy and called the allegation “unsubstantiated.”

Trump doe s not plan to confront Xi on the Nvidia issue, according to senior U.S. officials who briefed reporters Friday on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House. The officials also said they do not expect Chinese retaliation if they close loopholes to existing measures that prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips.

Huang has been a frequent visitor to the White House, and in May, he jumped onto Air Force One in Alaska, joining Trump at the last minute for a state visit to Beijing, where he captivated locals by sampling street food. He and his wife, Lori, were seated at the head table with the two leaders when Trump hosted Xi in September in Washington. At a tech summit that month, Huang took a phone call from the president while he was in a live appearance.
Meanwhile, the U.S. and China have committed to the idea of a hotline for AI national security-related incidents.

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Washington-based think tank Brookings Institution, said the Nvidia scandal — and the possibility of new U.S. export control measures — could throw a wrench in the AI talks. “The question is whether Beijing can separate export controls from the AI safety discussion or will view them as connected issues,” Chan said.

The U.S. and China have been moving AI technology forward in different ways. U.S. companies are chasing AI frontiers supported by cutting-edge chips and the country’s rapidly expanding data center infrastructure. China is pursuing wider global adoption of its open-source, more affordable models.

Increasingly, experts say, China is emerging as an AI counterweight to the U.S. and closing the gap in its lead on the technology. But advanced chips and other technology from Nvidia are still crucial for many Chinese AI companies and research, analysts say.

Chinese chipmakers, including Huawei, have been making rapid progress to narrow the gap by finding ways to work around the U.S. restrictions, including by clustering large numbers of less advanced domestic chips. But Nvidia's cutting-edge chips still lead in single-chip capability and outperform Chinese alternatives in training advanced AI models, analysts say.

China's push for technological self-reliance may have contributed to a reluctance to buy larger amounts of American chips. Despite the U.S. approval to sell some H200 chips to China, Nvidia said earlier this year it had shipped only a small amount to China.
The Huang episode could ultimately add momentum to China's domestic chip industry, said Rui Ma, founder of Tech Buzz China and a China tech expert.

“For Beijing, the fallout only adds urgency to its efforts to build a domestic semiconductor supply chain. That was already a strategic priority, but if access to Nvidia computing power becomes even more restricted, Chinese companies will have increasingly few alternatives,” Ma said.
AP journalists Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles, and Didi Tang, Seung Min Kim and Kevin Freking in Washington contributed.

title: Democrats try out a strange new emotion at post-midterms What's Next conference — hope
summary: Democrats met for two days in Denver to pore over the results of the midterm elections and emerged feeling pretty good about themselves
story: Democrats met for two days in Denver to pore over the results of the midterm elections and emerged feeling pretty good about themselves

DENVER -- When Democrats started planning a post-midterms conference in Denver months ago, political consultant Stephanie Valencia figured it would be more of the same — a bunch of strategists poring over the latest results and plotting a path forward in a country dominated by President Donald Trump.

She never expected that her party would still be celebrating what they consider a dream election, where they won virtually every contested race, flipped U.S. Senate seats in Mississippi and South Carolina, turned Texas blue and won big majorities in Congress.
"I did not expect to be coming here with so much hope,” said Valencia, the co-founder of Equis, which researches Latino voters. “For the first time we can see the outlines of a post-Trump era.”

Democrats spent two days chewing over their future at the What's Next conference and trying to deal with the fact that it looks, for a moment at least, quite bright. Suddenly, anything seemed possible for a party that's become more accustomed to hand-wringing than fist-pumping. Speakers tossed around the word “supermajority.” One data analyst casually discussed pushing for 60 seats in the Senate and displayed a slide suggesting there were winnable races in places like Missouri and Utah.

“Everybody's happy about the results, but everybody's looking over their shoulder saying, ‘Can we really be happy about this?’” quipped former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, one of several potential presidential candidates who attended. He urged the party to celebrate while not taking future wins for granted.

Some warned that voters hadn't fallen back in love with Democrats, they were just turning to them out of frustration over high prices, the Iran war and concerns about government corruption. No clear recipe emerged from the conference to address widespread dismay about affordability and the economy. But there was hope among attendees that they had the power to figure it out.
Jason Delattre and several friends came to Denver from the Rio Grande Valley after working on Democratic campaigns in Texas. They were still stunned at the opportunities now open to them.
“We have to figure out what we're going to do next,” said Delattre, wearing a cowboy hat and pin for winning U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico.
“We have so much power we didn't have before,” said his friend, Jose Robbie Juarez.
Some even had hope that statehood for Puerto Rico was finally possible.
“It finally feels we're going to get it done,” said Luis Davila, the Democratic chair on the island.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a possible White House contender, suggested that his party should aim for a landslide win in the next presidential race. Instead of “going out and scrapping for 270,” the minimum electoral votes for victory, they should be "fighting hard to swing for 370.”
That would be five more Electoral College votes than Barack Obama won in his historic 2008 presidential campaign, which was Democrats’ previous high-water mark this century.

The setting was tailor-made for good vibes — a well-known music venue in one of Denver’s hippest neighborhoods, with concert-style posters of politicians and operatives plastered on the walls. Distant snow-capped peaks framed the horizon outside.

Some old divisions reared their heads. A handful of protesters from the leftist Sunrise Movement protested outside the gathering Friday, complaining that it was sponsored by a group, Majority Democrats, that's more centrist and funded by wealthy businesspeople.

A couple of protesters interrupted what was supposed to be a triumphant appearance by the likely new House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries. They demanded a Green New Deal and an arms embargo against Israel. One man shouted profanities at Jeffries and called him a “traitor” while being led from the auditorium.
Jeffries brushed it off.
“I’m from Brooklyn," he said. "This is light work.”

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for caucus leadership, appeared at the conference Friday. He's allied himself with Democrats' liberal wing, and he argued that voters have demanded change.
But many were not worried about those signs of discord.
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, who may run for president again, said the leadership fight was a “family conversation” the party would have in Washington, and he welcomed signs of dissent.

“I think this is a wonderful thing that we have right now, that we're having a real discussion,” Booker said in an interview. “At a conference like this you're seeing the future," he added, returning to the party's optimism. "A new day is dawning in America.”
Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado said Democrats were “the big tent party.”
“We have an ideological spectrum that covers virtually every element of Democratic thought," he said in an interview. "And I think that’s exciting.”

title: Trump is taking Elon Musk on his Asia trip, but he plans to avoid talking about Nvidia scandal
summary: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
story: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump plans to take the world's wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China.

As the head of SpaceX and Tesla, Musk has economic and national security interests that make him a valuable adviser to Trump, according to administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president's plans on a Friday call with reporters.

The journey comes as the fallout spreads from Jensen Huang being ousted as the CEO of Nvidia for having an extramarital affair with an alleged agent of the Chinese government. Beijing denies that Alice Huang is a spy. Her company Megaspeed was accused last year of shipping Nvidia's advanced computer chips into China.

But Trump does not plan to confront Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the matter and administration officials do not expect Chinese retaliation for any follow-up actions to prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips, officials told reporters.

The administration believes the situation with Nvidia should not have any bearing on the trip, as the U.S. does not make its use of export controls subject to negotiations with foreign countries. Trump's aides are discussing the possibility of closing loopholes in existing trade measures, including the use of export licensing and preventing the ability of Chinese firms to use advanced chips over the internet through remote access.

The trip will be capped with a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, where efforts to limit nuclear weapons will be a chief topic. Still, there are no plans for Trump to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose nuclear arsenal has been a source of consternation to the U.S. and its allies.

Trump is set to arrive Tuesday in the Philippines to meet with his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. While in Manila, he intends to sign a trade deal with Thailand and meet with the Quad, an alliance composed of the U.S., India, Australia and Japan.

On Wednesday, Trump will leave for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he’ll have his third in-person meeting this year with Xi. Afterward, Trump and Xi will hold their joint meeting with Putin.

The leaders are expected to talk about the Iran war, but Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be part of the agenda, officials said — and Musk, whose Starlink system has been integral to Ukraine's ability to fight back against Russia's invasion, will not be part of the trilateral meeting.

title: Savannah Guthrie, popular and enduring face of morning TV, renews NBC contract after 15 years
summary: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, ensuring she continues as co-anchor on "Today."
story: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, ensuring she continues as co-anchor on "Today."
NEW YORK -- Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract at NBC News, ensuring she will continue to greet viewers each morning on “Today” after more than 15 years at the network.

The move by one of morning television's most enduring and popular personalities was confirmed to The Associated Press by a person close to the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity because the news has not been made public. It was not clear for how long the contract was extended.

The extension also came during a year of personal pain and turmoil for Guthrie. Her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84, was last seen at her home just outside Tucson on Jan. 31 and was reported missing the following day. Authorities believe she was kidnapped, abducted or otherwise taken against her will. The case remains dogged by questions; no suspects have been arrested.

In July, authorities released two ransom notes initially sent to a Tucson television station days after Guthrie went missing. The first note, sent Feb. 2, said she was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $4 million in cryptocurrency. The second note, sent Feb. 6, said Guthrie died shortly after she was kidnapped.

Guthrie and her family have shared their pain and pleaded for information in videos posted to social media. Most recently, Guthrie addressed the tragic situation on Instagram, posting an old drawing from her daughter, Vale, which she said “says so much about how I feel.”
The drawing depicted an umbrella amid falling raindrops, with an accompanying message: "I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
“The world goes on, things appear 'normal,' ” Guthrie wrote in her post, “as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids — but it’s not and it never will be.”

“We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward,” she wrote in the post, to which she also attached a smiling photo of her mother. “We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.”

Guthrie, 54, became a main co-anchor of “Today” in 2012, after joining the show the previous year. She now co-hosts with Craig Melvin. She is also a primary anchor for NBC's election coverage, most recently for last week's midterm elections.

title: Rubio acknowledges 'people are struggling' economically in speech after GOP midterm wipeout
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy

WASHINGTON -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a sweeping speech to fellow conservatives on Friday evening acknowledging that Americans are struggling in the current economy, while also railing against what he called the “weaponization” of international law to constrain the U.S. from acting in its own interests.
His comments to the conservative Federalist Society touched on a core issue of the midterm elections — economic pain — that U.S. voters cited in delivering massive losses to Rubio's Republican Party.

“I think we have to recognize that people are struggling. There’s no doubt about it,” he said. “The health of our economy has nothing to do with the stock market. The health of their economy is whether they have enough money to be able to afford the things they need.”

President Donald Trump often points to the stock market as evidence that the economy is doing well. But voters angry over higher costs gave Democrats control of Congress after blaming Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.

Rubio's remarks had the overtones of campaign speech, though the former Florida senator has consistently refused to discuss whether he would seek the presidency in 2028 in a race that could pit him against Vice President JD Vance. Rubio gave another wide-ranging speech last month in Greece that focused on Western values and also appeared to reflect his political aspirations beyond being America’s top diplomat.

Rubio on Friday defended the Iran war, arguing that it was necessary to stop the threat of the Islamic Republic obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he acknowledged that the unpopular conflict has driven up gasoline prices for Americans and other connected costs.

“It’s not easy to address these things because it’s not popular to address them," Rubio said. “It’s difficult. And oftentimes it inflicts, you know, pain, economic pain and otherwise. So we recognize that.”

He also pointed to the need for American leaders to continue a tradition of ensuring the next generation is better off than those before them. Economic prosperity is “not self-perpetuating,” he said, but an enormous undertaking that requires years and decades and is not accomplished “election cycle to election cycle."

“That’s the challenge before us now, because I do think there’s a legitimate fear that we will be the first generation to leave the next worse off, and that can’t happen. That’s un-American,” he said.

Rubio also hit back hard on critics of Trump administration policies such as deadly strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America, the January capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and strict immigration policies.
He accused other countries and international organizations of trying to stymie the U.S. from acting in its own best interests by accusing the Trump administration of violations of international law.

“We’ve heard the concept international law invoked against nearly every major foreign policy decision or action of this administration,” he said, describing it as “the weaponization of international law.”

Rubio also condemned the United Nations, the International Criminal Court, the “global elite” and organizations staffed by “international activists and bureaucrats,” all of which he said want to weaken the United States.

“They lecture us on the importance of sovereignty, even as they demand that nations surrender control of their borders and outsource their immigration laws to unelected international courts,” Rubio said. "They oppose, they say, all forms of imperialism, of conquest, of domination, but they seek to exercise authority over every country and every government on earth.”
AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee in Washington contributed.

title: Investigation says understaffing and unexpected fire behavior led to firefighter deaths
summary: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June
story: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June

Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of highly trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June, according to a report released by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The firefighters, working for the U.S. Forest Service and the newly created U.S. Wildland Fire Service, were part of an interagency response to the Knowles fire that merged with others to form the Snyder Fire on the Colorado/Utah border. The Rifle Helitack crew had been dropped in a remote area to work on a fire line, but became trapped when strong winds blew the fires in their direction and overtook them.

Their deaths came after the Trump administration revived a previously discredited policy to stomp out all wildfires quickly. Decisions on how to fight the Knowles fire were driven by the desire to prevent the spread of cheatgrass and protect sage-grouse habitat and a downwind community, the report said.

These factors “established an organizational posture to aggressively suppress new starts while small,” the report said. “This policy framing drove the decision to insert helitack firefighters onto small wilderness starts on a day with extreme fire weather conditions forecast.”

Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson, and Sydney Watson were killed at the scene while Nathan Matthews sustained burn injuries and died on July 24. A fifth firefighter on the team sustained burn injuries but survived.

Ron and Lisa Hutcherson, Nick's parents, said the crew should not have been sent out ahead of the fire because dangerous winds were in the forecast. After meeting with investigators and visiting the site, they said they believe the deaths were preventable and were caused by a failure of leadership and oversight.

“Telling us how the fire reached our son does not answer why he was still there,” Ron Hutcherson said in an email to The Associated Press. “Who was watching the bigger picture? Who was responsible for bringing those firefighters home while there was still time?”
Lisa Hutcherson added: "My son depended on the people responsible for tracking the fire threatening him and making the decisions needed to keep him safe. We want answers, and we want accountability.”
The Serious Accident Investigation report detailed the circumstances that led to the decision to send out the helitack team and the many problems that led to their deaths.
Multiple lightning fires ignited on June 27 in Colorado's Black Ridge Canyon Wilderness. The region was experiencing extreme drought conditions, and the winds were picking up.

An incident team orchestrated coverage of the various fires by calling in aircraft and crews. At one point, the official in charge ordered all aircraft to the Jones fire, but constant high winds challenged all pilots that day, with many saying it was the most difficult flying of their careers, the report said.
By the early afternoon, communication systems broke down, with many trainee dispatchers trying to coordinate operations. There was also confusion over who would track aircraft.

“Dispatchers simultaneously tracked up to 16 active aircraft, three emerging incidents, multiple new starts, county river evacuations, and non-stop media inquiries, leading to severe cognitive task saturation,” the report said. “Due to constant radio congestion and workload strain, dispatchers felt they were unable to transmit the mandatory scheduled 1000 Fire Weather Forecast broadcast across the zone.”
The incident commanders on the Snyder and Jones fires did not have clear information about the location of the firefighters on the Knowles and Gore fires to the east, the report said.

“Because no operational role was assigned to continuously map personnel location against the emerging fires’ trajectories, overhead did not recognize that firefighters were positioned directly in the fire’s line of advance,” the report said.

A large fire about eight miles to the west of the helitack crew was observed three and a half hours before the entrapment, the report said. In less than three hours, the fire ran over complex terrain and reached the five firefighters, who were forced to deploy fire shelters, because a helicopter was unable to reach them in time.

The Hutcherson family met with fire investigators in Grand Junction on Oct. 26 for a three-hour official readout of the report, they said. The review described a failure of lookouts, communications, escape routes and safety zones, they said.

An aging mobile radio system and software crashes compromised official channels during critical operations, the family was told. Overlapping transmissions and confused radio traffic forced firefighters to use cellphones to communicate.

The Knowles fire was in a remote location, the family said, so the central question remains: “What justified keeping this crew exposed as communications, observation, and extraction options deteriorated?”

Timothy Ingalsbee, executive director of the nonprofit Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics and Ecology, said the problem can be traced back to the Trump administration's full-suppression policy, which has prompted crews across the country to take unreasonable risks.

“It was outrageous to have a full-suppression policy on a lightning-caused fire in the wilderness to prevent the spread of cheatgrass,” Ingalsbee said. “The policy driving this aggressive attack of all fires is an obsolete paradigm that is just humanly or ecologically unsustainable. And unfortunately this crew paid the ultimate price, ultimate sacrifice.”

title: Trump administration cancels mandatory pay hike for Head Start teachers
summary: The Trump administration said it would cancel a rule mandating pay increases for teachers in the Head Start preschool program
story: The Trump administration said it would cancel a rule mandating pay increases for teachers in the Head Start preschool program

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Friday said it would cancel a rule mandating pay increases for teachers in Head Start, the federally funded early education program that serves more than 700,000 of the nation's neediest preschoolers every year.

The move will undo a requirement that large Head Start programs gradually increase pay for teachers, so they would reach parity with their local public preschool teachers. The rule, created under Democratic President Joe Biden, also called for expanding employee benefits and would have cost around $2.1 billion annually by 2031.
The Trump administration announced Friday that it was finalizing the repeal of the pay-hike mandate. The new rule will take effect in January.

The money saved could allow Head Start programs to serve more children with the same amount of federal funding, President Donald Trump's administration said. The administration has pushed to scrap many of Head Start's quality regulations, saying programs can enroll more kids if they have more flexibility on spending.

“The Trump Administration is working hard to ensure that the promise of Head Start reaches as many children as possible with the funds Congress has appropriated,” said Alex J. Adams, an assistant secretary at Health and Human Services who oversees Head Start.

Advocates for Head Start educators say eliminating pay hikes could actually hurt enrollment. Some programs have been unable to recruit enough staff to operate at capacity and have had to shutter classrooms and preschool centers. Teacher turnover was particularly acute during the pandemic. More than 20% of Head Start teachers left in 2022, some fleeing for higher-paying jobs in public schools or in other sectors, such as retail or food service.

A majority of Head Start teachers hold bachelor’s degrees. But according to data reported by programs in 2026, Head Start teachers with master’s degrees earned less than $60,000 a year on average, while those with only a bachelor’s degree earned less than $50,000. Meanwhile, public schoolteachers earn an average of $75,000 a year, according to the National Education Association union.

The Trump administration “asks Head Start educators to keep doing more for less,” the National Association for the Education of Young Children said in a statement. If teachers move on to other jobs, kids cannot enroll, the group said. “A funded slot without a qualified teacher serves no one.”

The change had also been condemned by congressional Democrats, who take control of Congress in the new year. This past June, they authored a letter urging the Trump administration to change course and leave the Biden-era pay requirements in place.

Head Start was started in the 1960s as an antipoverty initiative. It targets children in low-income households, plus those who are homeless or in foster care or have disabilities. The program, which provides training and job opportunities for parents along with education for preschoolers, has long had bipartisan support.

But it has faced threats under the Trump administration. A White House budget draft last year proposed scrapping the program altogether. More recently, Adams proposed scrapping many of Head Start's regulations, which form the basis for many of its signature offerings, such as medical screenings and family supports. His proposal would also do away with federal student-to-teacher ratios, deferring to state childcare regulations, which tend to be looser.
AP Education Writer Alia Wong contributed to this story.

title: US gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
summary: President Donald Trump's administration is giving states another six months before they must remove beneficiaries from Medicaid rolls for failing to meet new work requirements
story: President Donald Trump's administration is giving states another six months before they must remove beneficiaries from Medicaid rolls for failing to meet new work requirements
President Donald Trump’s administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requirement.

The requirement is scheduled to take effect nationally on Jan. 1, and states have been scrambling to put in place the staffing, training and technology to implement it by then. The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won't have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.

Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for lower-income people. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told state Medicaid directors on Friday that they'll still need to determine whether many enrollees and applicants for benefits are meeting new requirements that they are working, in school or volunteering.

The move announced Friday gives state social service departments more time to make sure complicated changes are ready to run before there are consequences. CMS said that states are making progress but have implementation challenges.

“I think these extra six months are going to give states the ability to respond to the change, and there will be fewer people that lose their coverage due to administrative failures” resulting from states’ inability to prepare, Kathy Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told The Associated Press.
Still, she said it's not clear which states will opt to use the additional time.
Kate McEvoy, executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, said state Medicaid leaders “appreciate the additional flexibility that CMS is providing."

The decision also could give some breathing room to Congress to consider changes to the requirement. Democrats who are taking control of both chambers in January after their sweeping election victories last week have said they want to roll back the requirements.

The news comes after Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, of Oregon, and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, wrote to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz this week, asking to delay implementing the work reporting requirements. Their letter cites, in part, a recent decision out of a Boston federal court that determined medically frail people should not be bound by the work requirement qualification rules.

“The practical reality is that this significant implementation issue may not be definitively resolved for months, creating untenable uncertainty for states that need a final resolution of this issue before going live with work reporting requirements,” the letter states. “The court ruling is an important victory for the millions of medically frail people who rely on Medicaid for their health care coverage."

Under the policy, many Medicaid beneficiaries must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month or be in school at least half-time. The new policy applies only to people who receive Medicaid under a voluntary expansion that 40 states undertook and which was intended to get health coverage to more lower-income adults who don’t have kids at home. There are exceptions for those who are over 64, caring for kids under 14 or deemed too medically frail to work.
Critics say that most enrollees covered by the mandate are already working and that people are more likely to lose coverage because of the paperwork to prove it rather than failing to work.

The federal government is pushing states to use data from other government departments or elsewhere to verify whether beneficiaries are working as a way to reduce the burden on the beneficiaries to show proof.
A few states have launched the work requirements early.
The first of them was Nebraska, where they started in May.

Preliminary data presented to the state’s Medicaid Advisory Committee showed that more than 9 in 10 people subject to the work requirement and due to have their benefits renewed in July and August qualified.

But 533 people were denied continuing coverage. For most of them, it was over paperwork: They didn’t show that they were working or were exempt from the requirement. Of those denied, 43 lost coverage because they did not meet the new requirement.

Similarly, most of the new Medicaid applicants who were denied coverage due to work requirements from May through August did not get the coverage because they did not provide information to verify whether they were complying.
Among both groups, it’s not clear how many people didn’t provide information because they weren’t working — or how many might meet the requirements but failed to show it.
“There are likely people who are still eligible for coverage who lost it,” said Amy Behnke, the CEO of the Health Care Center Association of Nebraska.

title: A gathering of ‘Rocky’ fans in Philadelphia breaks a world record
summary: Fans celebrated the legacy of Rocky Balboa 50 years after the film with a record-breaking gathering in Philadelphia
story: Fans celebrated the legacy of Rocky Balboa 50 years after the film with a record-breaking gathering in Philadelphia
PHILADELPHIA -- The story of Rocky Balboa is one that audiences love and know well – of resilience, grit and persevering despite the odds.
Fans honored his legacy 50 years after the film with a Guinness World Record-breaking gathering of people dressed as Rocky on Friday at the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
The uniform? A black beanie, grey sweatpants and sweatshirt, and black high-top Converse sneakers.
A growing number of Rockys amassed in front of the museum steps Friday afternoon, cheering as stragglers showed up to aid the record-breaking attempt.
“What's your name?” the announcer asked one participant. “Rocky Balboa,” they replied.
A minimum of 250 people needed to be there for the occasion, according to Guinness. The official record was certified with 570 participants, an announcer said.

The city organized a host of events this month to honor its fictional underdog boxer, including a sprint up the stairs that Rocky stormed up in the film, a rededication marking the permanent installation of the Rocky statue, and a meat market challenge where fans can recreate a scene in the film where he trained by punching slabs of frozen meat.
After the world record was confirmed, the group ran up the stairs to pose for a picture in front of the museum.
On Saturday, tourism officials said 45,000 runners from all 50 states and 75 countries will participate in a “Rocky Run” throughout the city.

The 1976 film written by Sylvester Stallone tells the story of a small-time boxer from South Philly who gears up to take on the heavyweight champion of the world, Apollo Creed, fighting in the city to celebrate America’s bicentennial. Though he ultimately loses the fight, Rocky proves himself and wins the heart of Adrian, the neighborhood pet store clerk.
The movie was shot for less than $1 million, and Stallone was an unknown actor who had written the script in a desperate bid to land himself work.

The film won the best picture Oscar and became the highest-grossing sports movie at the time. Its numerous spinoffs and sequels has helped it hold the record for most successful sports movie franchise, according to Guinness World Records.

Philadelphia held its inaugural Rocky Day in 2023 with Stallone in attendance, expanding celebrations to a weeklong Rocky Fest the next year. The city kicked off this year’s festivities with the release of Stallone’s memoir, “The Steps,” on Sep. 29.

title: Family Dollar to pay $63M to settle allegations it routinely overcharged customers
summary: Family Dollar will pay $63 million to settle state and federal allegations that it routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on its shelves or on its website and mobile app
story: Family Dollar will pay $63 million to settle state and federal allegations that it routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on its shelves or on its website and mobile app
Family Dollar will pay $63 million to settle state and federal allegations that it routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on its shelves, website and mobile app.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 states filed federal charges against the company Thursday and announced the proposed settlement the same day. The settlement must still be approved by a judge.

According to the FTC’s complaint, consumers from across the country have been reporting price discrepancies at Family Dollar for years. In January 2025, for example, consumers from at least seven states reported that Family Dollar refused to honor a “2 for $20” sale on a package of diapers, even though the price was advertised on its mobile app and on shelf tags.

One Michigan consumer took a picture of the “2 for $20” shelf tag and brought it to the register, but reported that the store manager said the price was wrong and quickly removed the shelf tag, the complaint said.

Over the last five years, state and local regulators have cited Family Dollar for thousands of pricing violations, resulting in fines of more than $3 million, the complaint said. It has also entered into multiple settlements with state attorneys general and consumer protection agencies over inaccurate pricing.
Family Dollar said Friday it will work with the FTC and state agencies to meet the settlement's requirements and provide clear information to customers about how the settlement could impact them.

“We take our responsibility to deliver a positive shopping experience seriously,” Family Dollar spokeswoman Janella Escobar said in a statement. “We remain focused on strengthening pricing accuracy across our stores and maintaining our customers’ trust.”

Family Dollar, which is privately owned and based in Chesapeake, Virginia, has more than 8,000 U.S. discount stores. It reported revenue of $13 billion in its most recent fiscal year, according to a company statement.
The case is similar to one the FTC and 20 states filed last month against Dollar General, a rival bargain chain. That case is ongoing.

Under the proposed settlement, Family Dollar will be required to establish a $40 million consumer redress fund payable to eligible consumers. The company must notify customers about the fund through notices in stores and on its digital platforms.

The settlement requires Family Dollar to establish a $20 million discount program for its customers and pay $3 million to the states involved in the case. Those states are: Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
The settlement also requires Family Dollar to implement a pricing accuracy program that is independently assessed and annually certified.

title: Survivors of the deadly Brooklyn building collapse recall shock, terror and grief
summary: Survivors of a Brooklyn apartment building collapse are desperate to know what caused the catastrophe that killed relatives and neighbors and destroyed their homes
story: Survivors of a Brooklyn apartment building collapse are desperate to know what caused the catastrophe that killed relatives and neighbors and destroyed their homes

NEW YORK -- One man's pregnant wife was pulled alive from the rubble, while two of his roommates perished. A woman living next door woke from a nap to bright daylight flooding her bedroom because her apartment wall was suddenly gone.
Survivors of the Brooklyn apartment building collapse that killed eight people wept as they recounted their terror and grief during a news conference Friday.

New York officials, from building inspectors to prosecutors, say they're investigating what caused the three-story building to come crashing down as workers were digging at an adjacent construction site.
Those who lost family, neighbors and their homes demanded answers.

“As they’re taking me, evacuating me from the building, I could see my neighbors coming out on stretchers,” said Ciahola Lawrence, whose apartment building next to the one that collapsed had a shared wall ripped away, exposing an abyss of dust and debris below.
“We didn’t deserve this,” said Lawrence, who sobbed in her husband's arms as she spoke with reporters.
Among the dead were two children, ages 9 and 10, according to city officials. Another 18 people were injured, including four firefighters.

Mamadou Mouctar Balde stepped out to buy groceries Wednesday, leaving his pregnant wife and two roommates, 31-year-old Mamadou N’Diaye and 23-year-old Mamadou Barry, at home. Barry was cooking and N’Diaye was sleeping on the couch, he said.
He returned to find firefighters, police and neighbors gathering outside and assumed there had been a traffic accident. Then a woman told him a building had collapsed.
“I didn’t see my wife. I didn’t see my friends,” Balde recalled, a tear streaking his cheek. “I no longer knew where I am.”
First responders found the bodies of N’Diaye and Barry while combing the wreckage. Balde's wife, Fatoumata Bah, was pulled alive from the rubble. He said she and their unborn child were doing OK.
N’Diaye and Barry were Guinean nationals who came to the U.S. about five years ago from Conakry, the capital of the West African nation. Their uncle said their family is heartbroken.
“We ask the city and the Guinean community to stand for us, to have a justice for this tragedy,” he said.
Other victims came from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador and Trinidad, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.

New York police identified the others who died as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Edgar Sapon, 26; and Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26.
Ahmed Tigani, commissioner of New York's Department of Buildings, said Friday that his office is conducting “an exhaustive investigation” of the Brooklyn collapse.

The city has ordered inspections at more than 160 sites in New York that are associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition site next to the fallen building, Mamdani said, significantly raising an earlier count of sites subject to renewed scrutiny.
“I think it is always an outrage when eight New Yorkers lose their lives, when 18 New Yorkers are hospitalized, and when families are shattered as a result of all of this,” Mamdani said.
If investigators uncover “any evidence of criminality,” Mamdani said, “it is one that we follow through to the fullest extent of the law.”

One witness who works across the street said he watched bricks fall minutes before the disaster. A woman in a neighboring building said she and fellow residents blamed vibrations from the construction for cracks that appeared in their apartment walls.
Lawrence said the construction work had been a source of constant disruption, producing noises so loud that “you would hear that thumping and movement in your soul.”

A security camera above Lawrence’s door recorded video of her apartment’s shared wall and the building next door collapsing in a clattering rumble and a thick cloud of dust. Inside her apartment, a closet filled with hanging clothes and bags was exposed to the outside.
The security video shows Lawrence leaving her damaged home with a firefighter, who held her hand as they descended a stairway overlooking mounds of wreckage below.
“This feeling is indescribable,” Lawrence said. “I was right there.”
Zariah Coleman, who lived in the building next to the one that collapsed, was concerned about her cat. She said Friday that she too had felt the building shake because of the construction.
“I just really hope they come and get our cat,” Coleman said in tears. “He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.”
Rescue operations ended Thursday after crews spent more than a day searching for victims beneath debris removed with power saws, pickaxes and an excavator.
Building records show there were four apartments on the upper two floors and a commercial unit on the ground floor of the collapsed building.

The surrounding blocks along Flatbush Avenue, a busy Brooklyn thoroughfare, are tightly packed with older brick buildings and a few newly built apartment complexes. A mix of Caribbean and Mexican restaurants reflects the diversity of the neighborhood.

A one-story building was demolished earlier this year on the construction site next to the collapsed building. Records show a contractor, Mordechai “Marty” Waisbrod, notified the city that excavation would begin in September and would include rock blasting. The contractor has not responded to phone messages left and emails sent to one of his Brooklyn-based businesses.
Permit applications indicated plans to dig below 15 feet (4.5 meters).

A stop work order was issued in March after inspectors concluded the demolition site lacked adequate overhead protection such as netting to protect neighboring buildings and pedestrians, according to the city's Department of Buildings.

In April, inspectors found that the demolition work had resumed in violation of the stop work order, the department said. Work was allowed to continue after the problems were corrected, Tigani, the city buildings commissioner said Friday.
“We’re looking at the entire history,” he said, “and if there are additional things we need to see, that will be part of the investigation.”

The Brooklyn collapse was the second high-profile structural problem with a building in New York in the past five months. In July, several buildings in Manhattan were evacuated after support columns buckled inside a skyscraper that once was the headquarters of Pfizer.

Fingerhut reported from Des Moines, Iowa, and Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. Associated Press journalists Jennifer Peltz in New York and Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed.

title: US declares three Guatemalan gangs to be terrorist groups, imposes sanctions
summary: The Trump administration has declared three Guatemalan gangs to be terrorist groups for financing violence and crime with proceeds from drug trafficking
story: The Trump administration has declared three Guatemalan gangs to be terrorist groups for financing violence and crime with proceeds from drug trafficking
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration has declared three Guatemalan gangs to be terrorist groups for financing violence and crime with proceeds from drug trafficking.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday imposed the terrorist designations on Los Lorenzanas, Los Huistas and Los Mendoza, all of which the U.S. says have deep ties to Mexican drug cartels.

Los Lorenzanas was designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization, while the other two were identified as Specially Designated Global Terrorists. Both labels subject the groups and their members to U.S. sanctions, including freezes on assets they may have in U.S. jurisdictions. The FTO designation goes further and allows criminal prosecution of people found to have provided those organizations with material support.

“The Trump administration will continue to use all available tools to protect our nation by keeping illicit drugs off our streets and disrupting the revenue streams funding violent narcoterrorists,” Rubio said in a statement. “We will not stand by while these foreign terrorist organizations corrupt Guatemala’s institutions.”
Los Huistas, which operates in western Guatemala along the Mexico border, is known to have support from local politicians and businesspeople who have helped it survive and operate with impunity.

Guatemalan authorities accuse the group of having ties with both the Sinaloa Cartel and Jalisco New Generation Cartel in Mexico. Last year, Guatemala’s government extradited one of its leaders — one of the 100 most wanted men by the U.S. government.

Los Lorenzana is a family clan accused of ties to drug trafficking in eastern and northern Guatemala along the border with Honduras. It’s accused of drug trafficking, and Guatemalan authorities say it is allied with the Sinaloa Cartel.

Los Mendoza is also a family clan accused of drug trafficking, with ties to Guatemalan politicians and government officials. Its operations are concentrated along Guatemala’s borders with Honduras and Belize. It’s known for violent land grabs in the region it dominates.
Sonia Perez in Guatemala City contributed.

title: Billy Evans tells his side of "You Can See Everything," Elizabeth Holmes' portrayal
summary: In his first TV interview, Billy Evans, partner of disgraced Theranos co-founder Elizabeth Holmes, talks about his characterization in the documentary "You Can See Everything," as well as threats he says have been made against his family's safety.
story: Billy Evans may be the most-talked-about person in the most-talked-about film of the year, the documentary "You Can See Everything." He sat down with "CBS Sunday Morning" for his first-ever TV interview.

Why now? "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life," he said. "And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, 'You can't lose your voice.'"

"You Can See Everything" is a film by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, who shot to fame as an absurdist comedian, and who (along with cameras) moved in with Evans and his partner Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison in 2023.

Evans, a 34-year-old MIT grad who'd also worked in high-tech, emerges as a shape-shifting central character. Asked if he is the person we saw in the film, or something else, Evans said, "I'm deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do. But no, I am not some controlling monster who's leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things."
It's easy to understand why the genre-bending film has become a cultural phenomenon … harder to understand why Evans agreed to do it.

"I think sometimes I take too big of risks," he said. Such as? "Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape or form that they so choose."

In the film, Evans is portrayed as a villain – controlling and manipulative. Yet, Evans doesn't seem angry about that: "It's super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn't help change it. Look, I'm going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. But if they don't, what I care about is the people that I know, people that love me."

In fact, of the documentary that has gotten rave reviews, Evans says, "I love the film," despite the fact that he is made out to be a villain. "I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment, you know, and I didn't get to control that edit."
His goal, he said, was "to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is."

In 2014 Forbes Magazine crowned Holmes the youngest self-made female billionaire. By 2017, the year she and Evans met, she was under investigation for defrauding investors for a diagnostic machine that she falsely claimed could test for hundreds of diseases with a single drop of blood.

Evans says when they first met, he did not know who she was. "I had been at her office earlier that week," he said. "I had, like, seen her the same week. But no, really, like, the first time I met her, I did not know."

"You Can See Everything" leaves us questioning what the truth is. There are also moments that are cringe-worthy, as when Evans is filmed in the shower completely naked. [You really can see everything.]

"I did not give consent to do that," said Evans. "Now, did I know they were filming me in the shower? Yes. But we would film 16 hours a day. Like, all sorts of things were filmed with assurances made. I was just as surprised as the rest of the country to have my whole body on camera for the world to see, and it's been an awkward experience in having, like, your kids' teachers see that. It's really uncomfortable."

Evans said there were "inappropriate" and "awkward" things that happened every single day, as well as requests to film things that, he said, "are not appropriate for television. All sorts of things that the details I'd rather spare the audience."
The film's production company, A24, said, "Everything that was filmed was filmed with their consent."

Some who see the film leave convinced the co-director, Nathan Fielder, had feelings for Holmes. "I think that there are bits that are played up to criticize his own bias," said Evans. "This is a film about, what can you trust? And at the end nothing is clear."

Evans says he has not spoken to Fielder since he's seen the film. "I think they're probably worried I'm gonna sue 'em," he said, adding he has no intention to do so. "Because maybe I'm a different person than most people think I am."

Evans lives with their two young children in Texas close to Holmes' prison, and carries a gun 24/7, he says, to keep his family safe. "We have threats of violence against us daily," he said. "I've got two kids. Threats of violence daily. And I would never forgive myself for having the tools, the skills, and the ability to protect my family and not doing it.

"I will give you an example: The other day, I was driving my kids to school. And a car came up behind us really, really quickly. And we stopped at the light. And the guy starts screaming next to me. And this isn't just road rage, okay? And his window is down. And he is screaming the most vile things you have ever heard about: 'I know where you live. I know who you are. I know where your kids sleep, and the things that I will do to you.' And it was terrifying."

Even given the fallout from the movie, he says he would do it all again: "With the same people, making the same film again, with everything that I know right now? 100%. Because I would also have a better understanding of what I was walking into."
Elizabeth Holmes could transfer to a halfway house next summer. Until then, Evans and their children visit her every week behind bars.

Having his children see their mother in prison, Evens said, has become "strangely normal. Like, I hate it. I absolutely hate that my daughter's first steps were in federal prison. I hate that. … But it doesn't mean that we can't find joy as we experience this. And our job, to them, is not to talk about how much it hurts and how painful it is, but to find the joy in seeing how many acorns we can collect in the prison yard and fit in a water bottle. It's finding, you know, the small, little games that we can play to make each time we go to the same place, every weekend, feel like you're going to Disneyland."

Evans said he used to count the days she was in prison, but that became too painful. "It's been since May 30th of 2023," he said. "I miss her so much. You know, I talked to her right before I came in here. And I told her, I said, 'I'm kinda nervous.' And she said, 'Just be zen. Enjoy it. Embody love. And I'll talk to you, when you're done.'"

title: The Reader: A new review source for book lovers
summary: With most newspapers and wire services closing the book on sections devoted to book reviews, Washington Monthly introduces its new online resource, offering reviews, essays, and recommendations by some of the world's top writers.
story: It's become an all-too-familiar story: Earlier this year, the Washington Post put an end to Book World, its weekly book review supplement.
"Books are expensive," said bestselling author Jonathan Alter. "Readers need help to know what's good out there."

Alter says Book World's closure created a void: "Thirty years ago, there were 30 American newspapers that, as part of their Sunday newspaper, had a book review section," he said. Today, only The New York Times still maintains a separate book review section.
"So, we stepped into the breach, and we're doing something about it," said Alter, who is co-founder of The Reader, a new, general interest, online book review, to be published every weekday.

Executive editor Haley Sweetland Edwards said, "We will have mostly book reviews, but also essays about books, columns about the literary book world, and top authors like Robert Caro and Margaret Atwood and Ann Patchett will be providing recommendations of books that have slipped below the cultural radar."

The Reader is part of Washington Monthly, a non-profit magazine. Edwards says authors lined up to be part of it: "We have 31 Pulitzer Prize-winners who have agreed to be contributors over the next year. These are the crème de la crème, and they will be reviewing for us."

Alter said, "We will review books that are going to become big bestsellers, but we're also going to review those books that sometimes fly under the radar, that are really good and that just aren't getting the recognition that they deserve."
And that's where "Sunday Morning" comes in. Each weekend, we'll offer two books for your consideration – one fiction, one non-fiction – courtesy of The Reader.

title: Min Jin Lee on "American Hagwon" and writing "social novels"
summary: The Korean-American novelist and bestselling author of "Pachinko" talks about her latest book, "American Hagwon," part of her series chronicling the migration of Koreans around the world.
story: It's been nearly a decade since Min Jin Lee's last book made her a literary phenomenon. "Pachinko," a sweeping historical epic chronicling four generations of a Korean family living in Japan, sold more than two million copies in the United States. It was adapted into a popular series on Apple TV.

But all that success didn't come easily. "When 'Pachinko' first came out as a hardcover, it was never on the bestseller lists," said Lee. "If you look at my hardcover sales, they're abysmal. So, if you start out with failure, it's really easy."
Did she consider "Pachinko" at its beginning a failure? "Oh, I think you can ask my publishers!" she laughed. "They would just say, this didn't sell!"
It wasn't until The New York Times named it one of the best books of the year, and it was selected as a National Book Award finalist, that "Pachinko" took off.
Lee's latest novel, "American Hagwon" (published by Cardinal), is the third in a series she calls "The Diaspora Quartet," chronicling the migration of Koreans around the world.

"Every industrial revolution had people leaving the farm to go to the city," Lee said. "And now we have environmental diaspora, where people don't have water in their communities anymore. You have economic diaspora, where certain jobs don't exist anymore, like manufacturing. I'm focusing on Koreans, because those are the people that I know about. But I'm really writing about this modern condition."

It's a deeply personal story for Lee. She came to America in 1976, when she was seven years old. The middle of three girls, her family moved to Elmhurst, Queens, where she grew up in a very blue-collar neighborhood. Her parents, a marketing executive and piano teacher in Korea, opened a newspaper stand and, later, a jewelry shop.
"As a little kid, I was so unbearably shy," Lee said. "I didn't really speak or interact with my peers very well."
But she tested into a highly-competitive public high school, where she found friends – and her footing.

From there it was on to the Ivy League, where she discovered something important was missing: Yale did not offer Korean language or Korean history courses – which, Lee says, was ignoring the full story.

"I think because of the Cold War and because of the Korean War in American history, I do think this is a rational thing to ask for," she said. So, Lee organized a letter-writing campaign, and convinced the university to start a Korean Studies program. "I think that it really helped the school," she said. "My mom has this whole theory that wherever you go, you should make it better than when you found it."

While at Yale, Lee was also struggling with a serious liver condition. "I learned that I would get liver cancer in my 20s or 30s; that's what the doctor said to me," she said. "I was like, 'Oh, if I have until 35, what do I want to do?' So, it gave me this sort of courage that I don't think normally I would have had."

Lee went to law school, then to a big firm. But before long, the hours and the stress caused her liver disease to flare up, and she decided to take a leap. "I thought, if I walk away from money and status and power, at least I'll find tremendous enrichment for me," she said.

Lee found that by writing what she describes as "social novels": "I think it's to write realistic fiction that reflects on society today, saying, this is what I think and this is the way things should be," she said.
Lee conducted thousands of interviews with people of Korean descent. In her conversations, one topic came up more than any other. And so, in "American Hagwon," she takes on education.

"A hagwon is a for-profit learning center," Lee said. "In Korea, you can go to a hagwon to become a police officer. You can go a hagwon to become a K-pop idol. And you can go to a hagwon to learn English. So, starting at the age of four or five, 80% of Koreans in South Korea send their children to hagwons."

Much of the book takes place in hagwons in Korea and the U.S., centering on a family whose life is upended when they come to America. Lee said of the father, John Koh, "John goes to the most elite school in Korea; and yet, he ends up working frying fish for somebody else."

The family's experience raises big questions about the value of education: "Sometimes someone will tell you, you go to college to get a job," said Lee. "But other people will say education should be a form of transformation and liberation. Gradually, as I worked on the book, the more I was interested in wisdom. Like, how do you obtain wisdom? How do you live a wise life?"

While "American Hagwon" is set in the 1990s, Lee says what's happening in the world today makes these questions essential. She opens her book with the line: "The rules of engagement have changed already."

"I think this is the condition of the modern person in the 21st century, and 2026 for certain, especially in the era of AI," she said. "The rules of engagement have changed already, and you didn't know. Like, we didn't get the memo. Everybody is changing the game, the paradigm, the rules. Now that we know that, what are you supposed to do? How do you educate your children? How do you retool yourself?"

Thanks to an experimental treatment in her 30s, Lee's liver disease was cured. In Harlem, where she lives with her husband and raised her son, she's already researching her fourth book, the final in her Diaspora Quartet.

Lee said, "What I would really love is if readers could feel that they have the internal resources to manage the change that feels alarming and threatening to them, and then have the internal resources and the fortitude to care for others. There's no way we're going to be able to make it through this era unless we have each other."

title: U2 on 50 years and their duet with Dolly Parton
summary: The Irish quartet celebrates its 50th birthday with "Carnaval de Luz," their first album of new music in nearly nine years. Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. talk about their song "Torn," a duet with Dolly Parton that would prove to be her last recording.
story: When U2 came knocking, Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. didn't just arrive with new music; the band came bearing gifts, which they proceeded to place over a photo of Bruce Springsteen.
"We just wanna get Bruce Springsteen off your wall," Bono said. "There's some new blood coming through! But honestly Bruce, give the young people a break."
The up-and-coming Irish quartet is celebrating its 50th birthday this year – that's half a century of hits.

In September, U2 went back to the Dublin school where they first came together. Playing Mount Temple Comprehensive was "kind of amazing," said The Edge. "We used the music room in Mount Temple as our rehearsal space."
Bono said he didn't know what to expect from the students there: "I was nervous going out there."
"There were a couple of cheeky signs, like, 'When is Oasis playing?'" said The Edge. "But for the most part they really seem to get into it."
It was at Mount Temple in 1976 where Mullen pinned a note to the school bulletin board looking for bandmates. "I'd no expectations that anyone would show up, bizarrely," Mullen said.

The four got together via word of mouth. "Yeah, it's one of those funny things that the note is legendary," said Clayton. "And then when we started to talk about it, we realized none of us had seen it, and we'd been told about it by a friend or whatever."
The band has just released "Carnaval de Luz," their first album of new music in nearly nine years, created through a process that Bono called "chaotic."
The Edge reframed that as "nicely chaotic."
"Very functionally dysfunctional," Bono continued. "You would be shocked at just how raw it is and how just about to collapse."
"We're not precious in any way," The Edge said. "Until almost the record is in the store, we will try and improve and change and develop."
Won't you drive yourself nuts doing that? "Yeah. We do!" The Edge laughed.

The new album marks the return of drummer Larry Mullen, Jr., who had to sit out the band's 2024 residency at Sphere in Las Vegas with a neck injury that threatened his career. He said he wasn't terribly confident that he would be able to come back: "I had a congenital fusion, from moving like that for over 50 years, it basically had had enough," he said. "Yeah, a lot of people were very much on the page of, you've had a great life, you know, this is not worth it."
He risked paralysis if the surgery went wrong. "But you know what? I really wanted to get back and play in any capacity," Mullen said.

Asked if they were worried that he might not play again, The Edge said, "At some point, if Larry had had to retire, we would have had to have made a very difficult call about whether U2 can go on at all."
"Maybe we could have got a better looking, more fun drummer," Bono added.
The band calls "Carnaval de Luz" an album of "defiant joy." It includes the song "Torn," a duet with Dolly Parton that would prove to be her last recording
Bono said he approached singing with her on the track "With great trepidation."
Parton had shared the song with Bono: "She was like, 'You can take this wherever you want to go, and I might like where you want to take it,'" he said. "But you didn't know until it came back."
How generous an act is that for a songwriter? "Oh, no, not just a songwriter; one of the great songwriters who ever lived," Bono said.

U2 will be back out on the road next year, aiming for another groundbreaking live show. "That's our promise to our audience, is to try and have a shot at the best night of anybody's life," said Bono. "That's what we want out of our show."
Half a century on, U2 is still striving to be heard. "Whether it's relevant or not is really not up to us," said The Edge. "But whether we want to try and be relevant is up to us."

Asked what it means to be relevant, The Edge replied, "To be relevant is to speak of the moment. That's why we write songs. We all believe that we could next week write the best U2 song we've ever written. So, there's a lot to fight for, really."
"We think we are at our best," said Bono. "And if anyone out there thinks they're better … come and take it!"
