title: Richard Sterban of The Oak Ridge Boys dead at 83
summary: Richard Sterban's iconic bass voice powered The Oak Ridge Boys' "Elvira" to No. 1. His family revealed he battled pancreatic cancer since March.
story: Richard Sterban of Oak Ridge Boys has died. He was 83. (Getty Images)
Richard Sterban, whose unmistakable voice helped make The Oak Ridge Boys’ "Elvira" a country music classic, has died. He was 83.

The singer died Saturday, Nov. 14, in Hendersonville, Tennessee, from complications of bronchitis and pneumonia following a long battle with cancer, according to an announcement from his family and The Oak Ridge Boys.

"We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers. Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time, we find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus," his family said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

Sterban publicly announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis in September 2025, revealing that doctors had diagnosed him that March. Despite his health struggles, the country music veteran expressed hope that his faith and medical care would help him recover and return to performing.
JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71
Sterban announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis last year.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"With the help of the Good Lord above, I believe I will be able to get through this," he said at the time. He also thanked fans for their prayers and said he hoped to return to the road within several months.
NEW PANCREATIC CANCER PILL COULD RESHAPE TREATMENT AS EARLY TRIAL RESULTS STUN RESEARCHERS

After stepping away from touring in May 2025, Sterban returned to the Grand Ole Opry on Jan. 30 and 31, 2026, joining his bandmates for performances of "Elvira" that brought audiences to their feet, according to the announcement.
"Having Richard on stage with us again was one of God’s greatest blessings," fellow Oak Ridge Boys singer Duane Allen said.

Richard Sterban, Tanya Tucker and William Lee Golden attend the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum Class of 2026 Medallion Ceremony in Nashville, Tenn., on Oct. 18, 2026. (Getty Images for Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum)
GEORGE STRAIT PULLS OFF INCREDIBLE CAREER ACCOMPLISHMENT WITH STUNNING CONCERT

Born April 24, 1943, in Camden, New Jersey, Sterban began singing in Sunday school at age 6. His voice transitioned from soprano to bass by eighth grade, setting him on a path that would eventually take him from gospel quartets to some of music’s biggest stages.

Before joining The Oak Ridge Boys, Sterban performed behind Elvis Presley as a member of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet. He toured and recorded with Presley and appeared in the 1972 concert film, "Elvis on Tour."
Later that year, he left the job to become The Oak Ridge Boys’ bass singer.
"I wanted to be in the best vocal group in the world," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Alongside lead singer Allen, baritone William Lee Golden and tenor Joe Bonsall, Sterban helped transform the Southern gospel quartet into a country and pop crossover act. Their hits included "Y’all Come Back Saloon," "Bobbie Sue," and "American Made."
The Oak Ridge Boys said it was a "blessing" to share the stage with their bandmate earlier this year.  (Omar Vega/WireImage)

But it was Sterban’s booming bass refrain on the group’s 1981 recording of "Elvira" that became his musical calling card. The song reached No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on the pop chart and earned a Grammy Award.
OUTLAW COUNTRY SINGER DAVID ALLAN COE DEAD AT 86
"It’s the song everyone hopes to hear at our concerts," Sterban said on its 40th anniversary, according to the announcement.
The group became Grand Ole Opry members in 2011 and entered the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80
Their decades together also forged deep personal bonds.
In January 2021, Allen reflected on his relationship with Sterban, Golden and Bonsall.

LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY - AUGUST 22: Joe Bonsall, Duane Allen, William Lee Golden, and Richard Sterban of the Oak Ridge Boys performs during the Kentucky State Fair on August 22, 2021 in Louisville, Kentucky. (Photo by Stephen J. Cohen/Getty Images) (Stephen J. Cohen/Getty Images)
"I think the four of us have grown closer than we’ve ever been in our whole career," Allen told Fox News Digital at the time.
RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

The Oak Ridge Boys also developed a lasting friendship with former President George H.W. Bush. At his request, they performed "Amazing Grace" at his funeral in Houston in December 2018, taking an overnight flight after a concert in Washington state to attend.
"There’s no way we wouldn’t do it," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Away from the stage, Sterban was a devoted baseball fan and a part owner of the Nashville Sounds minor league team for 30 years. He continued recording late in life, contributing to several tracks on The Oak Ridge Boys’ October 2026 album, "Buried Treasures."

Sterban is survived by his wife, Donna; daughters Lauren and Tori; sons Rich, Doug and Chris; eight grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.

title: Johnny Depp fled Hollywood spotlight for quiet Bahamas life where 'nobody’s pointing a camera at me'
summary: Johnny Depp opens up about how his 1940s Bahamas wood house with a yurt and painting studio became his sanctuary away from cameras and fame.
story: Johnny Depp says that living in the Bahamas has given him "total peace and quiet." (Getty Images)
Johnny Depp turns to the Bahamas to experience a private life.
During an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Depp opened up about craving privacy and not being able to have it in the United States.

"Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody’s pointing a camera at me or staring. I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me," Depp told the outlet.
‘GREASE’ STAR STOCKARD CHANNING SAYS SHE’S ‘HAPPY BEING A RECLUSE’ AFTER LEAVING AMERICA
Johnny Depp lives in the Bahamas most of the time these days, he said. (Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for The Red Sea International Film Festival)

Depp famously purchased his own island in the Bahamas in 2004. In 2009, he told Vanity Fair that "escapism is survival to me," and that, after playing a difficult role, "my head was done in. I needed to escape. So being able to get on the boat and move allowed my head freedom again."

He continued, "Somehow, the mathematics led me here to my island. I don’t think I’d ever seen any place so pure and beautiful. You can feel your pulse rate drop about 20 beats. It’s instant freedom. And that rare beast—simplicity—can be had. And a little morsel of anonymity."
The actor added, "Whenever I was getting frustrated about being ‘novelty boy’ and making movies, I told myself, Calm down. I can come down here and disappear."

Depp told SCMP Style in 2023, "Where I feel the most myself in this world, and where I go to feel absolutely normal, I suppose, is my place in the Bahamas, because it’s an island and nobody’s looking at me. You’ve got to have some sanctuary, a safe place where you can escape the scrutiny and the interest of others, a place where you can just sit on a beach, read, paint, meditate or whatever, that’s freedom to me. That’s the only real freedom."
Johnny Depp has said in the past how much his home in the Bahamas means to him. (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images)

Making music is also something Depp likes to do on his island. Telling WSJ about how he passes his time there, he said, "I like to grab about four or five books and flop on the couch and read. Or I play guitar in my music studio."
In the 80s, Depp was in a band – music was what originally brought him to Los Angeles in 1983, not acting.

"Soon after, I met actor Nicolas Cage at a friend’s house. Nic came to see my band several times, and we became friends," Depp said. "Six months later, he suggested I try acting. I was up for anything that would help pay the bills."

Johnny Depp performed with Alice Cooper during a concert at The O2 Arena on July 25, 2025, in London, England. (Jim Dyson/Getty Images)

Johnny Depp transformed into Scrooge for the newly released movie "Ebenezer." (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)

"There was a great veil lifted when my first child was born. And suddenly, I understood exactly what everything had been for," Depp said. "There were years of that, that I thought, ‘What am I doing? Why am I doing these movies?’ This is what it's all about."

title: Sammy Kershaw accepts CMA apology after country stars speak out over red carpet access
summary: Sammy Kershaw's CMA Awards red carpet denial ignited a firestorm among country music artists who say the industry sidelines legends for influencers.
story: 'Outnumbered' panelists discuss country star Rodney Atkins' advice for young people to avoid social media fads and the impact of social media on America's youth.

Sammy Kershaw and Rodney Atkins spoke out about being denied permission to walk the red carpet at this year’s Country Music Association Awards, prompting criticism over how the organization treats veteran country artists.

Last week, Kershaw, 68, shared a statement on Instagram in which he revealed that the organization rejected his request to walk the carpet at the upcoming ceremony with his wife, Mendy, a decision that he called "extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing."

Following Kershaw's post, Atkins, 57, announced that he and his wife, Rose Falcon, were also denied red carpet access and would no longer be attending the ceremony, which will be held on Nov. 18 and marks the CMAs' milestone 60th anniversary.
COUNTRY STAR CODY JOHNSON SAYS NASHVILLE WANTED TO CHANGE HIM BEFORE SUCCESS
Country musician Sammy Kershaw spoke out after being denied access to the 2026 CMAs red carpet. (Getty Images)

After facing backlash from other country musicians and fans, the CMA issued a response in which the organization explained that its red carpet criteria helps manage limited space and security needs and apologized to those who "felt excluded by those decisions." The CMA also added that it was speaking with Kershaw's team.
On Tuesday, Kershaw shared a post in which he said that he had accepted an apology from the CMA as well as an invitation for himself and Mendy to walk the red carpet and attend the ceremony.

The controversy sparked an uproar among country artists, who argued that the CMA has welcomed influencers, actors and crossover celebrities onto the red carpet while sidelining veteran performers. In addition, other country musicians raised broader concerns about how the industry as a whole recognizes artists who helped shape the genre.

In his initial post on Nov. 5, Kershaw wrote that the denial of his request to walk the CMAs carpet "really hurts me." He explained that he learned of the rejection just two weeks ahead of the awards show after he and Mendy had already rearranged his touring schedule and booked flights and hotels.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Kershaw said he and his wife, Mendy, pictured at the 2016 CMAs, had already booked flights and hotels.  (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"My wife, Mendy, and I don't get to attend these events very often, due to touring and schedule conflicts," Kershaw wrote at the time. "She was really looking forward to us sharing a special evening together celebrating country music. Then, to find out I was denied the red carpet two weeks before the show, after being strung along for several months and expecting we would be attending, WTF?"

Kershaw pointed to his decades-long career and longstanding relationship with the CMA to question why he was excluded. He cited his more than 50 years in the music business, millions of records sold, over two dozen Billboard hits, a past CMA Horizon Award nomination and his status as a "lifetime CMA member" since 1992.
The musician also noted that he previously "donated" his time to perform at CMA Fest, and that he hoped he had earned the right to walk the carpet alongside his wife just as they had in the past.

"I’m blessed to still be out on tour every year, performing for the greatest fans in the world doing what I love," Kershaw wrote. "I believe there should be room to recognize the artists who have spent their lives contributing to this organization’s success.

"I love country music, but never in a million years would I think that a successful country music entertainer (and I’m not the only one) would not be able to walk the red carpet. It’s extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing. I guess the next time I attend the CMA’s, it will be in tribute after I’m gone, if I’m lucky," he concluded.

Two days after Kershaw's post, Atkins shared a video in which he revealed that he and his wife, who is also a longtime CMA member, had also been excluded from the CMAs red carpet and decided to skip the event.
"Well, I found out that Sammy Kershaw and I have something in common this year. Neither one of us got approved to walk the CMA awards red carpet," he began.

"When I heard about Sammy, I thought, 'What a shame. He's a great guy, sweetheart of a dude. Spent his life representing country music.' Then I found out the same thing happened to me," Atkins continued. "And in a way, I get it. I've always been kind of an outsider, maybe a shrub in the landscape of country music."
Rodney Atkins said he and his wife, Rose Falcon, were also denied red carpet access. (Getty Images)
NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS

Atkins went on to emphasize that he was having his strongest touring year, that his album "True South" reached the second round of CMA voting for album of the year and that his latest single could extend his chart presence into a third decade.
In a statement the musician shared alongside the video, Atkins expressed his gratitude to his fans "who made this career possible."
"You've always made me feel welcome in country music, and that's what matters most," he wrote.

"After more than 20 years as a CMA member and countless CMA Fests I’ve played for free, Rose and I were denied red carpet clearance, just like Sammy Kershaw. So we’ve decided not to attend this year’s CMA Awards," Atkins shared. "I also believe the artists who helped build the foundation of country music, like Sammy Kershaw, deserve a place in its celebrations."

The ""She Don’t Know She’s Beautiful" singer‘s post was met with supportive comments from other country stars, including some from the younger generation that paid tribute to Kershaw for his foundational contributions to the industry.
"If you haven’t earned the right to be there then nobody has… disappointing to say the least," Riley Green wrote.
Carly Pearce commented, "Many of us wouldn’t be here without artists like you…"
Jake Owen declared himself "Team Sammy," while Granger Smith added, "So sad for country music. I grieve for the old CMA."
"This is wild! I’ll give you my spot!!," Drew Bainbridge offered. "You paved the way for all of us on that carpet."
Other artists questioned why influencers were invited to walk the carpet while Kershaw was denied.
"Ugh this makes me sad for country music. Can we please bring back the legends and not influencers?" Kylie Morgan wrote.
"They’ll let zero talent influencers walk the red carpet but not Sammy Kershaw? I hate it here," Meghan Patrick commented.
Riley Green was among the country stars who rallied behind Kershaw. (John Nacion/WireImage)

Veteran country star Mark Chesnutt reacted to Kershaw's snub by the CMA in a lengthy statement on Facebook in which he criticized the organization, arguing that it prioritizes celebrities from outside the genre over longtime country artists.
"So Sammy Kershaw won’t be allowed to walk the red carpet at the big CMA Awards," he wrote. "Well that’s about right. The CMA doesn’t care about us old 90s guys any more."

"It’s a shame they don’t respect the stars that dominated the charts in the past thirty years or before that but they sure roll out the welcome mat for pop stars and Hollywood movie stars and even hip hop artists," he continued. "Anything but country music gets the performance spots on the show."
Chesnutt also contrasted the country music industry's treatment of the genre’s history with the recognition received by rock icons.

"Rock n Roll honors its history and respects its legends while country music industry executives seem to ignore its rich history and its legends," he wrote. "Thank God there’s still a lot of people that love traditional country music. They keep coming to our shows and showing their love and respect for the music we’ve made for nearly forty years now and we’ll keep working for them and not for those who don’t matter to US!"
Mark Chesnutt said that the CMA "doesn’t care about us old 90s guys any more." (Rick Diamond/Getty Images for Country Thunder)
Country singer Pam Tillis, who also rose to fame in the 1990s, also addressed Kershaw's red carpet denial, though she clarified that her criticism was not solely directed at the CMA.

"So let’s talk about today’s drama in country music: Sammy Kershaw and the CMAs. I’m not going to single out the CMA, because this happens all the time in our business," she wrote in a post on Instagram. "It’s the nature of our industry that the rising stars get the spotlight, just as we did at one point."
Tillis emphasized the importance of preserving a legacy, pointing to her own experience growing up as the daughter of country icon Mel Tillis.
"I learned early that a legacy doesn’t keep itself," she wrote. "Somebody has to stand up and say, ‘This artist mattered. They made a contribution.’ I’ve done that for Daddy most of my life."
She acknowledged that rising stars naturally receive attention, but argued that established performers still connect with generations of fans.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"And I’ll tell you what I’ve seen: the country audience is a multigenerational audience, and ‘90s country is still very viable, even if it isn’t always visible," she wrote. "A lot of us have three generations of fans showing up to our shows, singing, whooping and hollering for our songs. Many of today’s artists are making it big with their own spin on the ‘90s sound."

"I dare say many of us have felt the sting of being passed over for this, that and the other, in order to create an image that’s only part of the picture," Tillis continued. "I know today’s new artists need all the support they can get in such a crazy, competitive market. But legacy artists who want to show up can be the bridge between where this music came from and where it’s going."
"Many of us never say anything about these slights," she added. "We just keep on doing our thing. As an artist who is a lifetime CMA member, Sammy just spoke out."
Pam Tillis said she had learned early that a "legacy doesn’t keep itself."  (Getty Images for Stagecoach)
On Monday, the CMA released a statement responding to the backlash and citing space and security criteria for red carpet management.

"In recent days, several artists and their fans have spoken out about this year’s CMA Awards red carpet guidelines," the organization wrote. "Like any major televised event, the red carpet has criteria that exists to help manage limited space and the security needs for both the artists and the media. We are deeply sorry anyone felt excluded by those decisions."

"Our organization’s mission is to honor the history and celebrate the excellence of Country Music," it continued. "With this 60th anniversary year, we are working extra hard to simultaneously spotlight the last six decades, while also celebrating what has been a tremendous year in 2026. It’s not easy to do all of that in just one night, but we are up for the challenge."

"We also know this is about more than a red carpet, and we are committed to keep listening and keep finding ways to make sure all artists feel welcome and at home here," the CMA added. "To that point, we are in touch with Sammy Kershaw’s team and look forward to continuing that conversation."

On Tuesday, Kershaw shared a positive update, revealing that CMA leadership had "extended a sincere, heartfelt apology" which he had accepted following a "sincere and meaningful private conversation."

"The CMA has also extended an invitation for my wife, Mendy, and me to walk the red carpet and attend this year's awards alongside our fellow artists," he wrote. "I am grateful for that invitation and appreciate their willingness to listen, acknowledge our concerns, and work toward a positive outcome."

Patrick Duffy's mother was doing a crossword puzzle when two armed men returned to the bar she and her husband owned in Montana, and one of them shot her husband. Moments later, she rushed toward him and was shot and killed, too.

The "Dallas" star, 77, recalled the final moments of his parents' lives during an appearance on the "Still Here Hollywood" podcast, revealing how the double murder unfolded and how he found the strength to carry on.
The murders took place nearly 40 years ago, on Nov. 18, 1986.

He just threw them out of the bar, and they went somewhere, finished whatever they were drinking, and the anger boiled up and they went back in."

"And then, if that wasn't stupid enough, instead of just running, they jumped over the bar to the cash register, took the money and a couple of bottles of booze and then left."

title: Princess Diana’s legendary White House dance with John Travolta almost didn’t happen
summary: Princess Diana danced with Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck and Ronald Reagan that evening, but it took coaxing to get John Travolta onto the floor.
story: "Princess Diana: Love, Life, Legacy — A Life of Giving," an exhibition at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, reveals the story behind Princess Diana's famous dance with John Travolta and showcases her iconic velvet gown.
John Travolta had all the right moves, but when the chance to dance with Princess Diana came along, even Hollywood's smoothest dancer got cold feet.

The Princess of Wales and the actor lit up the White House ballroom in 1985, creating one of the most unforgettable moments in royal and Hollywood history. Diana was attending a White House dinner hosted by President Ronald Reagan and first lady Nancy Reagan when she took a spin with the heartthrob.

More than four decades later, their legendary dance is being celebrated at "Princess Diana: Love, Life, Legacy — A Life of Giving," an exhibition at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, California. More than 700 artifacts connected to Diana's life are on display.
PRINCESS DIANA, HOT DOGS AND A PRESIDENTIAL MATCHMAKING ATTEMPT: ICONIC ROYAL VISITS TO AMERICA
American actor John Travolta dancing with Princess Diana in Cross Hall of the White House, Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (Glasshouse Images)

The collection, presented through a partnership between the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute (RRPFI) and Renae Plant's Princess Diana Museum, features the velvet gown designed by Victor Edelstein that Diana wore that night.
But the iconic dance nearly didn't happen.

Princess Diana's "Travolta" dress is a highlight of the exhibition dedicated to the late Princess of Wales and her warm friendship with the Reagans. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"In preparation for the state dinner, the Marine Band that was going to perform the music during the dinner was told to rehearse music from 'Saturday Night Fever,'" Melissa Giller, chief marketing and cultural programming officer at RRPFI, told Fox News Digital.
WATCH: PRINCESS DIANA'S ICONIC DANCE WITH TRAVOLTA GETS NEW SPOTLIGHT

"The social secretary, Gahl Burt, she orchestrated it after speaking with Mrs. Reagan that after the dancing began, Gahl would walk up to John Travolta and tap him on the shoulder and encourage him to have a dance with Princess Diana," Giller said. "Now through the whole evening, Princess Diana danced with Ronald Reagan. She danced with Clint Eastwood. She danced with Tom Selleck and many others."
But when it came time for Travolta to step onto the dance floor with Diana, he needed some coaxing.
President Ronald Reagan dances with Princess Diana in Cross Hall of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"When it was time, Gahl Burt walked up to John Travolta and tapped him on the shoulder," Giller said. "He was actually a bit hesitant. He didn't know if it was something he should do. But after some encouragement, he went up and asked the princess to dance."

Prince Charles and Princess Diana met President Ronald Reagan and First Lady Nancy Reagan at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985, during an official visit to the United States. (Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty Images)
Travolta mustered the courage and approached Diana. The two then waltzed across the checkered floor to music from "Saturday Night Fever."
"They ended up dancing for 15 minutes," Giller said with a smile.
President Ronald Reagan and Nancy Reagan welcome Princess Diana and Prince Charles at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (AFP via Getty Images)

"Every presidential library archive has a photo that's the most requested by the public. President Nixon's library is the photo of Elvis meeting President Nixon. And one of our most requested photos is the one of Princess Diana dancing with John Travolta."

Princess Diana is seen here with John Travolta in the Cross Hall of the White House in Washington, D.C., at a dinner for Prince Charles and Princess Diana of the United Kingdom on Nov. 9, 1985. (Alamy Live News.)
Travolta later admitted he was nervous before approaching Diana.

"I didn't think they'd ask me to dance with her," he told Esquire Mexico in 2021. "I had the great privilege and honor of doing so, and I thought, 'There must be a reason for doing this and I better give it my all.’ That meant lead the dance well and make sure we had fun. That was the easy part, but just the fact of greeting Diana appropriately, being confident and asking her to dance was a complicated task."
President and Mrs. Reagan welcome Prince Charles and Princess Diana to the White House on Nov. 9, 1985. (Bettmann Archive)
The "Grease" star also recalled how special it was to dance with Diana.
John Travolta later revealed that dancing with Princess Diana was one of the highlights of his life. (John Shelley Collection/Avalon/Getty Images)

"Think of the setting. We were at the White House. It's midnight. The stage is like a dream. I approach her, touch her elbow, invite her to dance," he said. "She spins around and gives me that captivating smile, just a little sad, and accepts my invitation. And there we were, dancing together as if it were a fairytale."
In the 2021 interview, Travolta also recalled his disbelief over the once-in-a-lifetime encounter.
Princess Diana's childhood keepsakes on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
"Who could imagine that something like this is going to happen to you one day? I was smart enough to register it in my memory as a very special, magical moment."

Travolta also told Dutch television station Één that it was Nancy who told him Diana wanted to dance with him.

"[She] said, 'It is her wish,'" the actor recalled. "At midnight, I had to tap her on her shoulder, and I had to say, 'Would you care to dance?' She turned around and dipped her head in that Lady Diana way, and we were off for 15 minutes dancing."
Princess Diana's Versace dress. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"I'll never forget it," he continued. "I'm so honored that I was able to experience this, and I know for a fact that it was her highlight of being in the United States; it was her favorite moment. So I feel I made her life better, she made my life better, and I'm very sorry that she's not here."

Diana, Princess of Wales, wearing a cream lace gown with a scalloped neckline designed by Murray Arbeid and the Lover's Knot diamond and pearl tiara, smiles as she attends a dinner at the British Ambassador's Residence in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 11, 1985. (Getty Images)
During a 2016 appearance on "Good Morning America," Travolta was asked if there was anything from the 1980s that he'd like to bring back to the 2010s. He said he'd love to dance with Diana again.
"That was one of the highlights of my life, so that's probably the best moment of the '80s."
Princess Diana's honeymoon shoes and hat on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
Giller noted that the Prince and Princess of Wales maintained a close friendship with the Reagans.

The former Prince Charles is seen here attending a dinner with President Ronald Reagan and his wife Nancy at the White House in Washington, D.C. (Jean-Louis Atlan/Sygma)

"When Princess Diana got married to Prince Charles, Ronald Reagan, as President of the United States, could not go because the assassination attempt happened a few months ago and he was [still] recovering," Giller explained. "So, Mrs. Reagan went on behalf of President Reagan, as well as the United States. And I think that sort of bonded her with Princess Diana, although of course, Mrs. Reagan was much older than Princess Diana."
"They shared a kinship, especially once Princess Diana became a mother," Giller said. "You can see that in [their] letters and their relationship."
Princess Diana's "final goodbye" dress was designed for the Princess of Wales but never worn before her tragic death in August 1997. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
The exhibition features letters Nancy and Diana wrote to each other over the years, as well as gifts the Reagans received from the Prince and Princess of Wales.
Princess Diana with Nancy Reagan at the White House in 1985. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Giller said the exhibition aims to show visitors the woman behind the royal title, highlighting Diana's humanitarian work and influence beyond her relationship with the Reagans.
"Diana: Love Life Legacy — A Life of Giving" showcases more than 700 original artifacts from Princess Diana's extraordinary life. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"This isn't just an exhibition about dresses and shoes and jewelry," she said. "This is an exhibition about a woman who truly cared about her family, about her people, about all people, not just those in Europe, but around the world."

title: ‘Below Deck’ star arrested after brawl leaves 17-year-old dead
summary: João Franco, the former "Below Deck Mediterranean" star, and his brother claim self-defense after their arrest in Turkey after a fatal brawl.
story: "Below Deck Mediterranean" star João Franco was arrested after a brawl. (Greg Endries/Bravo/NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images)
Former reality star João Franco and his brother were arrested in Turkey after a fistfight outside a clothing store that left a 17-year-old dead.

In CCTV video obtained by Page Six, the former "Below Deck" star and his brother, Carlos Franco, are seen leaving a store in the Bodrum district of Muğla Nov. 7 with an employee following closely behind them.
Carlos appears to throw the first punch, after which more employees rush out of the store.
At first, João is seemingly trying to de-escalate the situation, often placing himself between his brother and the store employees, before appearing to get involved and throw punches himself.
'BELOW DECK' CAPTAIN SANDY SAYS SHE AND WIFE LOST 'ALL OF OUR MONEY' IN ALLEGED $1.6M CONTRACTOR SCAM
João Franco and his brother were arrested in Turkey after a fight that resulted in the death of a teenager. (Fred Jagueneau/Bravo via Getty Images)
The fight escalated to the point one of the men appeared to grab a nearby stool, seemingly to throw it at Carlos and João.
The Associated Press, citing the Demiroren News Agency, reported that 17-year-old Muhammet Koyabakan fell during the fight and hit his head on the ground. Koyabakan later died in the hospital.
João seemingly tried to de-escalate the situation several times. (Mark Rogers/Bravo via Getty Images)

João and his brother were initially detained and were later arrested. While it is unclear what charges they face, the Demiroren News Agency reported they told police they acted out of self-defense and denied hitting Koyabakan.
According to the news agency, João and his brother were intoxicated and swearing during an argument, which then escalated into a physical fight.

title: Former Miss USA contestant warns aspiring beauty queens she wouldn’t touch Miss Universe ‘with a 10-foot pole’
summary: The TLC documentary "Crown of Deceit" explores pageant scandal allegations, and Taylor Hale details her experience competing as Miss Michigan USA and what followed.
story: Miss Michigan 2021 winner Taylor Hale tells Fox News Digital she'd steer clear of Miss Universe, raising doubts about the international pageant.
The crown may look glamorous, but one former Miss USA contestant is warning aspiring beauty queens what's waiting beyond the national competition may not be worth the risk.
Taylor Hale, who was crowned Miss Michigan USA in 2021, isn't discouraging young women from competing, but she has a stark warning about chasing the Miss Universe dream.

"I hope you win your state pageant. I hope you are highly competitive at Miss USA," she told Fox News Digital ahead of the premiere of TLC's documentary, "Crown of Deceit: Inside the Miss Universe Scandal."
FORMER MISS NORTH CAROLINA USA SAYS CONSERVATIVE CHRISTIAN VALUES PLAYED ROLE IN LOSING CROWN

Taylor Hale, who competed in Miss USA in 2021, called for sweeping changes at Miss Universe, saying the organization should be "burned to the ground and then rebuilt from the ashes." (Matt Winkelmeyer/GA/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)

"And I hope that gets enough eyes on you so that you can achieve whatever it is outside of being Miss USA. Because as Miss USA, you have to go to Miss Universe, and that is a whole other ball game that I wouldn't want to touch with a 10-foot pole."
Hale said she still supports women competing on the national stage.
"I really, really like the new director. I think Thom Brodeur is a really great director. He cares about the women and the well-being of all the girls, teen and miss," she said.
WATCH: FORMER MISS USA CONTESTANT HAS WARNING FOR FUTURE MISS UNIVERSE HOPEFULS
But she cautioned that winning a national title shouldn't mean surrendering control of what comes next.
"So, chase your dream, pursue the dream, but also understand that you have to have some ownership and real directorship of where you're going to go afterwards," Hale said.
"Because I don't know if Miss USA at Miss Universe is going to fulfill the fantasy anymore."
ARREST WARRANT FOR MISS UNIVERSE CO-OWNER ISSUED AFTER COURT NO-SHOW IN FRAUD CASE
Taylor Hale praised changes at Miss USA but questioned whether competing at Miss Universe still offers young women the opportunities they hope to gain from pageantry. (TLC/Taylor Hale)
When Fox News Digital asked whether the organizations could regain contestants' trust, Hale said Miss USA has made strides toward greater transparency.
However, she said Miss Universe requires more sweeping changes.
"Miss Universe has to, I think, be burned to the ground and then rebuilt from the ashes," she said.
WATCH: FORMER MISS USA CONTESTANT SAYS MISS UNIVERSE MUST BE 'BURNED TO THE GROUND' AND REBUILT AFTER SCANDALS
She added that new leadership and management would be necessary to restore her confidence in the global competition.
MISS MEXICO SPEAKS OUT AFTER HEATED CONFRONTATION WITH MISS UNIVERSE EXECUTIVE GOES VIRAL

While competing as Miss Michigan USA in 2021, Hale said she experienced sexual harassment from Max Sebrechts, vice president of Miss USA at the time, the morning after she failed to advance to the finals.

After declining an invitation Sebrechts allegedly sent through a social media direct message to visit his presidential suite, Hale said he approached her at a hotel and twice initiated unwanted, overly intimate embraces. Sebrechts has denied all allegations of sexual harassment and misconduct made against him by former pageant contestants.
Former Miss USA contestant Taylor Hale accused former pageant executive Max Sebrechts of sexual harassment. He denied the allegations. (Justin Baker/Getty Images)
Hale said she wasn't the only contestant to receive his message, calling the experience "so offensive … icky and infuriating."
She added, "You can do every single thing right and still be put in a position where, 'OK, great, now I have to deal with this on the backend.'"
Hale said she immediately reported the incident and was promised a meeting with the general counsel for WME-IMG, the entertainment company then associated with the pageant organization.
However, she said pageant leadership did not provide her with answers before sending a mass email six weeks later announcing Sebrechts' departure.
Alexis Fagan-Williams, a Miss Michigan USA 2023 and a "Big Brother" winner, and Miss Michigan USA 2021 Taylor Hale attend the Jovani NYFW Show. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for Jovani Fashion)

Hale called for more accountability, stronger financial backing and major corporate sponsors willing to invest in contestants' safety rather than simply attaching their names to the pageant's glamour.
"We need more sponsors that are not just charitable, but actually invested in real business practices," Hale said.

Hale pointed to Halle Berry as an example of the opportunities pageants can provide, arguing that young women shouldn't have to choose between pursuing those opportunities and feeling protected.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Miss USA Organization and the Miss Universe Organization for comment.
"Crown of Deceit: Inside the Miss Universe Scandal" is available to stream on TLC and HBO Max. (TLC )

The three-part documentary, "Crown of Deceit: Inside the Miss Universe Scandal," examines allegations of rigged competitions, financial turmoil, lawsuits and a battle over who controls the Miss Universe Organization.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The docuseries also explores the controversy surrounding the 2025 Miss Universe pageant, held in November 2025 in Thailand, according to a news release. The competition faced a series of scandals, including confrontations between contestants and pageant executives, last-minute judge resignations and accusations that the competition was rigged.
Omar Harfouch, a Miss Universe judge who made headlines when he abruptly resigned just before the 2025 pageant, appears in the documentary.

Harfouch resigned after accusing pageant organizers of rigging the competition, alleging that the top 30 finalists had been selected before the event began. The Miss Universe Organization has denied his accusations.

Thai business tycoon Jakkaphong "Anne" Jakrajutatip appears at a Miss Universe event in Bangkok. She was reportedly convicted in a fraud case involving a corporate bond investment worth approximately $951,927. (AP Photo/Sakchai Lalit)

Jakkaphong "Anne" Jakrajutatip, the founder of JKN Global Group, which co-owns the Miss Universe pageant, was sentenced to two years in prison after being convicted in a fraud case involving a corporate bond investment worth approximately $951,927, the Bangkok Post reported.
The Bangkok South Kwaeng Court handed down the sentence Dec. 26, 2025, while Jakrajutatip was absent, according to the outlet. Jakrajutatip reportedly remains at large.

The docuseries also examines Miss Universe President and co-owner Raul Rocha, whose bank accounts were frozen as part of a criminal investigation into alleged drug, weapons and fuel trafficking, according to a December 2025 report by The Associated Press.
Neither Rocha nor the Miss Universe Organization responded to the AP's requests for comment about the allegations or investigation at the time, the outlet reported.
"Crown of Deceit: Inside the Miss Universe Scandal," is available to stream on TLC and HBO Max.

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton get unexpected help enforcing strict rule for George at elite school: experts
summary: Prince George's Eton College smartphone ban aligns with Prince William and Kate Middleton's strict no-internet phone policy for their children.
story: Royal author Hugo Vickers explains why Prince George could find freedom, privacy and a sense of normalcy at Eton College despite his future as Britain's king.
Prince William and Kate Middleton are reportedly giving Eton College's smartphone ban the royal thumbs-up, especially for their eldest son, Prince George.
The 13-year-old began his studies at the prestigious boarding school in September, where first-year Etonians are banned from using smartphones, according to The Telegraph.
Instead, Year 9 students like George are issued basic "brick phones" with no internet access, limiting communication with their parents to calls and texts outside school hours.
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON COULD SEEK 'GENTLEMAN'S AGREEMENT' TO PROTECT PRINCE GEORGE AT ETON: EXPERTS
Eton College said the decision to ban smartphones for first-year students is intended "to balance the benefits and challenges that technology brings to schools."
Eton reportedly tightened restrictions on first-year students' school-issued iPads in September 2026 in response parental concerns about gaming and internet browsing.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, and Prince William, Prince of Wales, walk with their 13-year-old son, Prince George of Wales, as he arrives for his first day at Eton College Sept. 8, 2026, in Berkshire, England. (Adrian Dennis/WPA Pool/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Eton College and Kensington Palace for comment.
In 2025, William told actor Eugene Levy on the Apple TV+ series "The Reluctant Traveler" that "none of our children have any phones, which we’re very strict about."

Prince George arrives for his first day at Eton College in Eton, west of London, on Sept. 8, 2026. Prince William and Catherine accompany him as headmaster Simon Henderson and provost Nicholas Coleridge greet the family. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
That same year, William told Brazilian TV host Luciano Huck during the 2025 Earthshot Prize events in Brazil that it had been "really hard" to protect his children from the harms of social media.
WATCH: PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE AT ETON COLLEGE COULD LOOK VERY DIFFERENT: EXPERT

"Our children don't have phones," he explained at the time. "I think when George moves on to secondary school, then maybe he might have a phone that has no internet access. And, to be honest, it's getting to a point where it's become a little bit of a, like, tense issue.

"But I think he understands why," William continued. "We communicate why we don't think it's right. And, again, I think it's the internet access I have a problem with. I think children can access too much stuff they don't need to see online, and, so, having a phone and text message, the old sort of 'brick phone' as they call them, I think that's fine."
A view of Eton College, Eton, Berkshire, June 1962. (Archive Photos/Getty Images)

"It has been rumored that William and Kate were having battles with George over having a smartphone with internet access," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. "Usage could get him into trouble but also allow him access to views on the royal family, good and bad, which may worry him.
Kate Middleton and Prince George at Eton College. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"It is now becoming more common practice for schools to ban smartphone usage during school days, and parents want age-appropriate locks on internet technology."
British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that Eton's smartphone policy is "music to Prince William and Princess Catherine's ears."
Eton College Chapel is the main site of worship for students at Eton College, a famous English boys' school. (Mark Kerrison/In Pictures via Getty Images)
"Prince William and Princess Catherine restrict smart devices to protect their children from internet safety risks," she explained.

"A healthy rule of accessing only 'brick phones' at Eton only enables essential communication and calls and texts at home. The couple take great comfort in knowing that Prince George will not be wasting his time gaming, 'doom-scrolling,' or accessing inappropriate online content.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The Prince and Princess of Wales, seen here on the Isle of Mull, western Scotland, April 30, 2025, agreed that their eldest, Prince George, would attend Eton College. (Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images)

"Prince George has never owned a smartphone," Chard continued. "He will be more than happy with a brick phone. As Princess Catherine has shared, smartphones can create an emotional disconnection. Prince George has years of smartphone access ahead of him and certainly will not go without."

Eton College, a world-renowned all-boys boarding school, was founded in 1440 by King Henry VI. It serves students between the ages of 13 and 18. About 1,350 students attend Eton, where they live in 25 boarding houses, each housing approximately 55 pupils, according to the school's website. People magazine reported that tuition was about $80,000 for the 2025-26 academic year.
A view of Eton College, founded by King Henry VI (Archive Photos/Getty Images)

William and his younger brother, Prince Harry, attended Eton, making them both "Old Etonians." Princess Diana's father, John Spencer, and brother, Charles Spencer, also attended the school, as did Queen Elizabeth II's cousins, the Duke of Kent, the Duke of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent.
Prince William signs in on his first day at Eton College Sept. 6, 1995. (Anwar Hussein/WireImage)

Hugo Vickers, author of "Behind Closed Doors" and a fellow "Old Etonian," told Fox News Digital that Eton College's use of "brick phones" is "sensible." Vickers has written several books about the British royal family.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Behind Closed Doors: The Tragic, Untold Story of the Duchess of Windsor" by Hugo Vickers is available now. (Pegasus Books)
"In my day, most of our communication was by writing a letter home," he said with a smile.
Prince William stands at Eton College in Eton, United Kingdom, wearing a waistcoat as a member of the elite society group called "Pop." (Tim Graham/Photo Library via Getty Images)

"And there was about, if I remember rightly, about four telephone boxes planted at different places around the school. On a Sunday morning, if you wanted to ring your parents, you had to get there, and then you'd have to queue up while other people were in there. It sounds very archaic now.
"And sometimes you never got into the telephone box because it's time to go to chapel or something.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Students from Eton College in the Mound Stand react to Harrow students during a cricket match between Eton and Harrow at Lord's Cricket Ground in London, England, May 10, 2024. (Philip Brown/Getty Images)

"So, I think the whole thing about communicating with parents is a whole new concept," Vickers continued. "Basic communication with parents is a good thing, but, of course, to get the full advantage of the school, it's probably better not to be linking to things all over the world via internet."
Melanie Sanderson, managing editor of The Good Schools Guide, told People magazine that Eton College's phone decision "was very much welcomed by parents."
A young Prince Harry at Eton College (Tim Graham/Getty Images)
"And the boys are so busy, they don't have time to be sat on their beds scrolling TikTok," she said.

title: ‘Saved by the Bell’ star Tiffani Thiessen says she needs hip replacement at 52 after painful diagnosis
summary: Tiffani Thiessen revealed a torn labrum and hip dysplasia diagnosis on a podcast, joking she's "basically a German shepherd" ahead of hip replacement.

"My doctor didn't say it was pickleball, but it probably hasn't helped," she admitted. "I have not been able to play in the last couple weeks because my hip's been so bad."

title: Randy Travis’ wife says doctors gave country legend 1% chance of survival before miraculous comeback
summary: Randy Travis' wife Mary reveals the emotional journey from a 1% survival chance to releasing "Same Old Way" more than a decade after his stroke.
story: Randy Travis' wife Mary reveals the emotional journey from a 1% survival chance to releasing "Same Old Way" more than a decade after his stroke.
Randy Travis' life was turned upside down by a devastating health crisis that doctors gave him just a 1% chance of surviving, according to his wife, Mary.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the country legend — whose new 12-track album, "Same Old Way," is out now — and his wife, Mary, reflected on that life-changing ordeal more than a decade ago, explained how hope and faith played a pivotal role in his recovery, and shared how his determination helped him rebuild his life and reconnect with music.

"They had already told us he had 1% chance of survival. And that was the first couple of days in the hospital," Mary said. "So here we are, five and a half months later, he's still here. He's still improving. We went through the second brain surgery. He came through that with flying colors. The first one is when they said he's not, you know, he doesn't have any chance. But, you know, once you get over those and you start seeing the glimmers of hope and the hand of God on the whole thing."
RANDY TRAVIS' HEALTH CRISIS BEGAN WITH 'CONGESTION' AND ENDED IN A FIVE-MONTH HOSPITAL STAY
Randy Travis' wife, Mary, says the country legend was given a 1% chance of survival in 2013. (Getty Images for the Grand Ole Opry)

The "Forever and Ever, Amen" singer was hospitalized in 2013 for congestive heart failure tied to viral cardiomyopathy. He subsequently suffered a massive stroke that left him with partial paralysis and affected his speech. What began as a trip to seek treatment for congestion became a five-and-a-half-month hospital stay, followed by years of rehabilitation.

"We went through three years of rehab every single day, so we were very quiet and out of the limelight, if you will," she added. "We, you know, we were at home. We went to rehab every day for about three years."
Travis won many awards throughout his 40 years in the music industry, including seven Grammy Awards. (Oscar Abolafia/TPLP/Getty Images)

Eventually, Mary said, Travis "got tired" of the constant rehabilitation and decided to "go live life." Their trips back to Nashville helped renew their hope that he could once again be involved in the music he loved.
WATCH: RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

Travis has since found new ways to share his music and connect with fans. In May 2024, he released "Where That Came From," using AI technology to recreate his signature singing voice. His "More Life" tour continued through 2026, with Travis appearing alongside Mary while guest vocalist James Dupré and his longtime band perform his hits.
VINCE GILL GAVE AMY GRANT A REALITY CHECK DURING RECOVERY FROM BRAIN INJURY
Mary previously told Fox News Digital that Randy's health crisis cemented their relationship. (Amy E. Price/Getty Images)

Now, with the release of his first album of original material in more than 18 years — featuring 12 previously unreleased songs recorded between 1986 and 2013 and restored by his longtime producer, Kyle Lehning — Mary is reflecting on the determination and gratitude that carried her husband through his toughest moments.
CELINE DION BREAKS DOWN ONSTAGE DURING EMOTIONAL RETURN AFTER 6-YEAR HIATUS

"Just being with this guy has been such an inspiration to me because, going through even the tough times in the hospital, the nurses would come in and cut him or stick him or poke him or do whatever, and they'd walk out the door. And if he wasn't in his coma and he was aware, he’d say, ‘Thank you.’ That was Randy Travis," she said. "And they'd turn around and look like, you got to be kidding me, you know. But that was Randy Travis."
Randy Travis, Mary Travis and James Dupré visit the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, Tenn., on March 5, 2025. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
That same spirit, she said, followed him into rehabilitation and remains evident today, even as aphasia continues to affect his ability to communicate.

"I have pictures of him there in the rehab center and he's smiling. He's laughing. He’s giving it all he's got. Randy Travis hasn't changed. And that's still the man that I get to sit beside right now," she said. "He still has that, that love for life, the love for people."

For Mary, the release of "Same Old Way" is especially emotional because it represents an opportunity they once weren't sure would ever come again. Before his stroke, she said, they assumed there would be many more albums and years of making music ahead.
BILLY RAY CYRUS CHEATED DEATH DURING SEPSIS, VOCAL PARALYSIS BATTLE BEFORE STAGING MUSIC COMEBACK
Travis' new album, "Same Old Way," was released Nov. 13. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"It's really an emotional thing, because 18 years ago when he put out his last one, we thought that the world was an oyster and there was gonna be so many more," she said. "But the stroke happened, it was 13 years ago, and everything changed."

"Thirteen years ago, we had no idea, based on where we were then, when we were in the hospital, that we would have this opportunity. So, in a way, it’s a miracle," she added. "I get emotional when I think about it, just because I wanted to hear his voice so bad again."
Randy Travis and James Dupre perform during the Volunteer Jam: A Musical Salute to Charlie Daniels at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, Tenn., on Aug. 18, 2021. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

Hearing those recordings, Mary explained, offers listeners a chance to experience Travis' voice at different stages of his life — and gives the couple another reason to appreciate how far he has come.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Life is so precious and so fragile, but it’s so wonderful also. And to be able to do something like this, it’s pretty monumental," she said. "It doesn't happen often that somebody has the opportunity to do this after a life-changing moment."

title: Jim Caviezel says he’ll ‘always’ be disappointed he isn’t in ‘Passion’ follow-up, hasn’t talked to Mel Gibson
summary: Jim Caviezel reveals his disappointment over not returning as Jesus in Mel Gibson's "Resurrection of the Christ" and why "Ghost Soldier" won out.
story: The "Ghost Soldier" actor told Fox News Digital why he decided to play Jesus in 2004's "Passion of the Christ."
Jim Caviezel said he’ll always be disappointed that he wasn’t able to return as Jesus Christ in Mel Gibson’s upcoming "Resurrection of the Christ."
"Always will be disappointment with that one. Always will be, but I wouldn't have been able to do this film," he told Fox News Digital of his new movie "Ghost Soldier," which was released on Nov. 11.
Caviezel said "there was a moment" before 2004’s "Passion of the Christ" that he might not have done the film.
'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' WRITER REVEALS MEL GIBSON'S DARK SPIRITUAL WARNING ABOUT 'PASSION' FOLLOW-UP
Jim Caviezel is gearing up to star in his next role, "Ghost Soldier." (D Dipasupil/Getty Images)

"A friend of mine said, ‘I think you're going to do well. You have to look at each film as, can you move on? Because you have this one moment,’" he said. "My initials were JC. I was 33 years old, and I couldn't get that out of my head. And I felt like I had been prepared my life to go through this. But if I said ‘No,’ there's no going back."
'THE PASSION OF THE CHRIST' RETURNS TO THEATERS IN 4K WITH A 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' SNEAK PEEK

Caviezel said he "couldn't live with it, so I took the film knowing that it was going to do a lot of detriment. Not much has changed in 2,000 years. Jesus is as controversial now than he's ever been. Always will be this way. And so, but I like to engage in that."
The characters in "Ghost Soldier" taught him the "warrior spirit. And it was the same application when we did ‘The Passion.’"

He added that he hasn’t talked to Gibson about "The Resurrection of the Christ."
Caviezel told Raymond Arroyo on his podcast earlier this week that Gibson "really didn’t need me" for the follow-up.
"The Passion of the Christ" starred Jim Caviezel as Jesus of Nazareth. (Lionsgate/Fathom Entertainment)
MEL GIBSON'S 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' REVEALS FIRST PHOTOS AFTER LONG-AWAITED PASSION SEQUEL

"It’s a smaller role. The first one, it was critical. Every play. And you put that against this action film that has great substance like '[The Count of] Monte Cristo' and I was the main dude in it. So good luck to the new guy ‘cause it will be really hard. As I said earlier, it’s a hell of a lot harder to play Jesus than Superman."
Jim Caviezel stars in "Ghost Soldier." (Vlad Cioplea/Sony Pictures)
He added, "What we did on that movie, they can’t touch it. Nothing. When I’m dead and gone, that’s an annuity. People are going to keep coming back and finding God, and I did my job."
WATCH: JIM CAVIEZEL SAYS HIS NEW FILM ‘GHOST SOLDIER’ DOESN'T HAVE ‘HOLLYWOOD FAKE STUFF’
In "Ghost Soldier," which was released on Veterans Day, Caviezel plays a former Green Beret, and he said he drew on his decades-long relationship with the Navy SEALs for the part.
In Ridley Scott’s "G.I. Jane," Caviezel played a SEAL trainee.

Jim Caviezel attending a screening of "Ghost Soldier" at Naval Air Station North Island in Coronado, California. (Getty Images for Sony Pictures)

"So I kind of knew who they are, and they've helped me over the years in many of the films I've done," he explained. "This one came across my desk and it was authentic. Chris Papasadero, who wrote it, is a Green Beret. He was a real deal. So, it didn't have that Hollywood fake stuff."
Caviezel said he resonates with his character who fights against a powerful corporation threatening his rural Wyoming community.

"I love my country, and it is a country, and a country has to have borders," he said. And I spent a lot of time in ‘Sound of Freedom’ with a lot of the guys that worked on the border and what was coming over. I don't want terrorists in my country. I don't want the government taking our waterway and make the land useless. I know those people because I grew up with those people. And so like James Stewart did in ‘Mr. Smith Goes to Washington,’ this character does it, but he does it in a small town, and he's not going to allow them to do that to people he loves."
During filming, Caviezel spent time in 36-degree water.
The actor is seen in "The Passion of the Christ." (Alamy)
"One thing I don't care for is being cold," he admitted. "We were very, very cold."

The actor used a mindset he learned when "G.I. Jane" when his character was going through "surf torture," in which cadets training to be SEALs are forced to lie on the beach as the freezing Pacific Ocean washes over them.

He said he asked SEALs who served as consultants on the film how they dealt with the cold, which also helped him during "Passion of the Christ" "because I was extremely hypothermic for five and a half months doing that film."
Mel Gibson's "The Passion of the Christ" opened in New York City on Feb. 24, 2004. (Getty Images)

The most important thing, he said, "is that I wanted to make the veterans proud. I wanted them to see that I did my homework, and I don't know from one film to the next whether I'm going to pull it off. And so I lean on them quite a bit. I think that is something that makes me very happy when they're proud of the work that we did on this."

"Every time you do a movie like this, you get a referendum by the public and they kind of determine whether or not you're going to be seen anymore," he said. "And so far, so good 40 years later, one film at a time. I mean, really one film at a time."

title: Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor forced to retire as health battle threatens hearing
summary: Roger Taylor says his tinnitus has been "getting steadily worse," forcing the iconic Duran Duran drummer to step away after decades on stage.
story: Facing the possibility of losing his tongue, Poison drummer Rikki Rockett recorded messages for his kids. Now, he's celebrating 10 years cancer-free. Rockett is the author of a new memoir, "Ghost Notes: My Life in Poison."
Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor announced he is "retiring from playing the drums" and stepping away from the band due to health concerns.
The band released a statement on their official Instagram, noting his retirement comes on the heels of "a worsening of his recently diagnosed tinnitus."

"This is one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever had to make," Taylor said in the statement. "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I’ll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they’ve shown us over the years. But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse, and I’ve reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors."
He went on to say that "figuring out the timing of all of this has not been easy, but I’m going out on a real high."
Roger Taylor, drummer for Duran Duran, announced he is retiring from playing drums. (Virginia Turbett/Redferns)
THE OFFSPRING GUITARIST KEVIN ‘NOODLES’ WASSERMAN STEPS AWAY FROM TOURING OVER ‘SERIOUS HEALTH ISSUE’

He noted that the band "just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour," after which they headlined a show at BST Hyde Park for the second time, returned to record in the studio with guitarist Nile Rodgers and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

"I couldn’t have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I’ll treasure forever," he added. "I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John."
Taylor said it was a difficult decision to leave the band but that it was time to listen to his body. (Chris Walter/WireImage)

The statement highlighted Taylor's contributions to the band's success, noting he "has been at the heart of Duran Duran’s sound across two remarkable chapters," first in its "era-defining early records" and then again when the original line-up reunited in 2001.
After coming back together in 2001, the group released six more chart-topping albums, with Taylor "performing with them to millions of fans around the world."
Taylor made the decision to leave the band "after careful consideration" and by listening to medical advice. (Dave Benett/Getty Images for Xerjoff and Duran Duran)
"After careful consideration and medical advice, he has decided that protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first," the statement read.

Fellow band members Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and John Taylor also shared their thoughts, calling Taylor "our brother," and crediting his drumming for helping "define the sound of Duran Duran from the very beginning."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
The other members of Duran Duran called Taylor their brother. (Dave Benett/Getty Images for Xerjoff and Duran Duran)

"Having him back with us since 2001 has been incredibly important to us all," they said. "We completely support his decision and wish him health and happiness. He will always be part of this family, while we continue exploring new and exciting projects with the band."
The post was accompanied by photos of Taylor on stage performing with the band.
Taylor returned to perform with the band in 2001 following a breakup in the 1980s. (TV Times via Getty Images)

Fans of the band took to the comments section to wish the musician well as he closes this chapter of his life. One of them was his son, Elliot, who wrote, "Not a bad run, Dad! 🤘 loved capturing some of these moments on stage with you 📸 ❤️."

"Your rhythm has been the soundtrack to the best moments of my life and entire generations," another added. "Even though you are choosing silence now to take care of yourself, your beat will echo forever in our lives. Thank you for everything Roger!❤️🥁"

Fans in the comments section thanked Taylor for his contributions to music. (Fin Costello/Redferns)

Another fan wrote, "Very sad news! I’m heartbroken! 💔😢But health comes first! Roger, thank you for everything!!! Decades with amazing music and memories! 🖤🖤🖤 All the best! 🙏🏻" with another simply calling him a "legend."

Duran Duran formed in the late 1970s, releasing their self-titled debut album in 1981 and quickly making a name for themselves as a group ready to push the boundaries. They became household names with the release of their second album, "Rio," in 1982, which featured hits such as "Hungry Like the Wolf."
Duran Duran released their debut album in 1981. (Michael Putland/Getty Images)

Despite their success, the band split in the mid-1980s, with two members, including Taylor, pursuing solo projects. However, they came back together in 2001 and released an album with all five original members from the '80s in 2004.

"I think there was always a sense of unfinished business with the original five," Taylor told The Chronicle in 2022. "I think that was a feeling that there was definitely more gas in the tank when we broke up. I think we all felt that, and we came back together and it was pretty amazing."
As a band, they have won two Grammy Awards, have a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.

title: Common blood pressure drug helps more stroke survivors reach critical health target
summary: The REDUCE trial found spironolactone lowered blood pressure by nearly eight points in stroke survivors, but key questions about prevention remain.
story: Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, discusses a recent study that found stroke incidence has more than doubled among young adults.
A low-cost medication could help stroke survivors whose blood pressure remains elevated despite treatment, a new study suggests.

The research, known as the REDUCE trial, looked at whether adding spironolactone, a medication commonly known as a water pill, could help lower blood pressure after a stroke. The findings were presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions, Nov. 6-9, 2026, in Chicago.
Participants were split into two groups. One added spironolactone to their regular treatment, while the other continued with usual post-stroke care.
SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE
Researchers tracked the participants' blood pressure at home over the following six months to determine whether adding the medication made a difference.

After three months, the top blood pressure number was nearly eight points lower on average among people taking spironolactone compared with those receiving usual care – about 126 versus 133, the study said.
Researchers found that adding spironolactone to regular post-stroke care helped lower blood pressure more than usual treatment alone. (iStock)
More patients taking spironolactone also reached the recommended blood pressure goal of less than 130/80. That included 52% of those taking the medication compared with 30% receiving usual care.

"Lowering blood pressure is the most important step in preventing another stroke, yet many survivors struggle to reach recommended blood pressure targets after a stroke," study co-lead author Dr. Jordana Cohen, an associate professor of medicine and epidemiology at the University of Pennsylvania, said in a news release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"When spironolactone was added to post-stroke care, we saw a meaningful drop in blood pressure that may lower the risk of future strokes and heart attacks," she added.

Dr. Alfred Joshua, a California-based board-certified emergency physician and former chief medical officer who was not involved in the research, said the findings are encouraging, but do not yet show that the medication prevents a subsequent stroke.
Researchers found that 52% of patients taking spironolactone reached the recommended blood pressure goal, compared with 30% receiving usual post-stroke care. (iStock)

"We already know that controlling blood pressure lowers the risk of another stroke," Joshua told Fox News Digital. "This study measured blood pressure, so whether adding spironolactone leads to fewer repeat strokes is still an open question."

Spironolactone works by helping the body get rid of extra salt and water, which can lower blood pressure, according to the U.S. National Library of Medicine. It also causes the body to hold onto potassium, so patients taking it need to have their levels checked, the drug’s prescribing information states.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Joshua warned that high potassium is one of the main safety concerns because it can develop without symptoms. The risk can be higher for people with kidney problems and those taking certain medications or potassium supplements.
The medication can also lower blood pressure enough to cause dizziness, he added.
Spironolactone helps the body eliminate excess salt and water, which can lower blood pressure in patients who need additional treatment. (iStock)
"If your blood pressure is still high after a stroke, bring your home readings to your clinician and ask whether this medication is a good fit," Joshua advised.
Study limitations
The trial ended early with 160 participants instead of the planned 200, and about 15% did not have blood pressure readings available at the three-month mark, the researchers noted.
People taking spironolactone were also taking slightly more blood pressure medications overall than those receiving usual care.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The study was not designed to determine whether spironolactone actually prevents another stroke or heart attack. Larger and longer studies are needed to answer that question, according to the researchers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.
