Fox News Digital reached out to the D.C. Council and Judge Di Toro’s office for comment.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: FAA ground stop timeline: Weekend chaos grounds planes and postpones games
summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said overloaded routers tied to contractor L3Harris maintenance work triggered the longest nationwide FAA ground stop in 25 years.
story: Airlines for America president Chris Sununu joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss how thousands of travelers continue to face flight delays and cancellations nationwide following a recent FAA ground stop. They discuss infrastructure challenges and how to go forward.

A communications failure brought departures across the country to a halt Friday, stranding travelers, disrupting professional sports teams and sending federal officials scrambling to restore flights and determine what went wrong.

The longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years ended after more than four hours, but the fallout stretched through the weekend as airlines worked through cancellations and investigators zeroed in on routers tied to the outage.
Here’s a timeline of the shutdown and the federal response. All times are Eastern.
4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

A view from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) in California as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights across the States due to a telecommunications and air traffic control communication outage affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers on November 13, 2026. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Friday afternoon, Nov. 13: Communications trouble triggers nationwide ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials detected instability in radar data and communications at 3:36 p.m., affecting facilities that guide planes approaching airports and traveling between them.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted departures nationwide at 3:54 p.m. as controllers and pilots followed procedures to bring aircraft already airborne safely to the ground. About 3,500 flights were in the air.
FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
Duffy later emphasized that officials had not lost every radar feed or all telecommunications service. The inconsistent information was enough to trigger the shutdown as a safety precaution.
Friday, 4:16 p.m.: Duffy announces investigation into communications problem

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (Tom Brenner/AP Photo)
Duffy said the ground stop was necessary because of "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers."
FAA technicians were investigating, he said.
The disruption also prompted a broader federal response as officials examined whether the failure could have involved malicious activity.
BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

President Donald Trump brought federal agencies together on a call Friday, including intelligence officials, the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Intelligence partners reported they were not detecting the usual signs of a cyberattack, Duffy said.

Steven Cheung, assistant to the president and White House director of communications, later said on X that the White House and administration had acted within minutes of the FAA notice, crediting Trump for the response.
UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE
"Minutes after the FAA notice posted, the White House and Administration sprang into action. Because of that speed and effectiveness, the ground stop was lifted after just a few hours," Cheung wrote.
"A Herculean effort, only made possible by President Trump's leadership."
NFL OFFICIAL DON WILLARD WILL REFEREE TWO GAMES IN ONE DAY AFTER FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS TRAVEL, LEAGUE SAYS
Friday evening: Officials address security concerns as sports teams are stranded

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday, Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a nefarious attack and reassured Americans with loved ones traveling.
"There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said.
TENNESSEE VOLUNTEERS OVERCOME SLUGGISH OFFENSE, JET LAG TO TAKE DOWN TEXAS A&M AND KEEP CFP HOPES ALIVE

TOPSHOT - Planes wait on the tarmac at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a ground stop at all US airports.  (Kamil Krzacynski/ AFP via Getty Images)

The shutdown also left college football teams scrambling to reach Saturday’s games. Texas had already boarded its plane for Baton Rouge to face LSU when the ground stop prevented departure. Tennessee’s scheduled 4 p.m. flight to College Station was also halted.
Teams including Ole Miss, Tennessee and Baylor returned to their athletic facilities as officials weighed alternate travel plans. Some teams sat aboard charter planes for up to two hours.
PRIVATE PLANES AND ROADTRIPS: AEW GOES ABOVE AND BEYOND TO GET TO PHOENIX FOR FULL GEAR DESPITE TRAVEL CHAOS
Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, DC on November 13, 2026. (Zina Desmazes / AFP via Getty Images))
The shutdown also disrupted travel for professional sports teams ahead of a busy weekend.

The Brooklyn Nets were trying to fly from New Orleans to Memphis when their flight was halted, according to The Associated Press. The Memphis Grizzlies were also in New Orleans for a Friday game against the Pelicans, with plans to depart afterward.

The Cleveland Cavaliers and Chicago Bulls also had planned postgame flights. The San Jose Sharks’ flight to Utah for a Saturday game against the Mammoth did not depart before the shutdown, while the Detroit Pistons had reached Miami earlier Friday.
Friday, 8:15 p.m.: Ground stop lifted, but recovery starts slowly
Travelers check a flight information display board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Nov. 13, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images)
The FAA lifted the nationwide order at 8:15 p.m., allowing departures to resume.

Planes began leaving airports including LaGuardia, Los Angeles International and Reagan National. Some travelers at Reagan National had been waiting since around 3:30 p.m. for flights scheduled to leave around 4 p.m.
Duffy warned that reopening the airspace would not immediately get every flight moving. Departures depended on whether airlines had pilots, flight attendants and other crews available.
"It’s going to be slow," he said.
Late Friday into Saturday: College football games rescheduled

Lifting the ground stop did not immediately solve the travel problems for college teams. By 9:12 p.m. Friday, Washington, Texas, Tennessee and Oregon State were heading back to airports, but other programs faced crew availability problems.
Utah’s charter crew ran out of available hours, forcing the team to plan a Saturday morning departure for its game at Arizona. The Big 12 moved kickoff to 10:30 p.m. ET Saturday.
Just after midnight Saturday, the Ole Miss-Oklahoma game was moved to 1 p.m. ET Sunday after the Rebels were unable to leave Friday evening.
Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny said the school objected to the change but was told it would face a forfeit if it refused to play Sunday.
Saturday, Nov. 14: Maintenance work and overloaded routers emerge as focus
Travelers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (Ryan MurphyAP Photo)
At a Saturday briefing, Duffy said contractor L3Harris had been replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections at a remote FAA location.
The copper line was being discontinued, making the replacement necessary, he said.
During the work, a router began generating more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming other routers and disrupting communications and radar feeds.
Investigators were examining whether installation error or faulty equipment caused the failure.
"Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said.

Bedford distinguished the routine maintenance from the administration’s broader air traffic control modernization program. Duffy also said officials would reevaluate when such work should be performed.
Saturday: Airlines regroup as FAA forecasts Sunday recovery
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said "the worst is behind us," with air travel expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.
The Transportation Department said more than 8,000 flight operations resumed Friday night after the ground stop ended, but passengers continued facing delays and cancellations Saturday.
Airlines still needed to reposition aircraft and crews, leaving travelers scrambling to rebook and check whether their flights would operate.
Officials urged passengers to check directly with their airlines for current flight information.
Sunday, Nov. 15: Router testing continues as Duffy presses for funding

Planes wait on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport, New York on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a ground stop at all US airports due to communications problem.  (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Duffy said Sunday morning that air travel would improve throughout the day but probably would not return fully to normal until Monday, updating officials’ earlier prediction of a recovery by Sunday night.
Two routers from Texas and Arkansas were undergoing testing as investigators worked to determine the cause.

Duffy said work in El Dorado, Arkansas, was followed by problems involving equipment in Amarillo, Texas, where a system had been replaced about three weeks earlier. Engineers were examining the routers at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida.
"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said.
He said there was no indication of a foreign cyberattack, while leaving open further investigation if new evidence emerged.

Duffy also pressed Congress for additional funding. He said the $12.5 billion already allocated covered specific upgrades, including radar, radios and electronic flight strips, but did not fund a replacement telecommunications network.
Sunday, 2 p.m.: Travel headaches drag on
By 2 p.m. ET Sunday, 5,280 flights had been delayed and 1,709 canceled within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware.
Dallas Fort Worth, Atlanta and Chicago O’Hare were among the hardest-hit airports tracked in the update, with hundreds of delays at each.
The disruptions continued Sunday afternoon as airlines worked to restore normal schedules.
FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

Scott Kirby, chief executive officer at United Airlines Holdings Inc., during a Bloomberg Television interview at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) in Newark, New Jersey. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Sunday, Nov. 15: United CEO calls for action

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby praised the FAA’s decision to halt flights and thanked employees and customers for their patience during the disruption. He also called for better technology and full staffing to help prevent future outages.
Kirby said he had spoken directly with Duffy, Bedford and aviation leaders from both parties in Congress about the impact on United’s passengers and employees.
"This moment must be a call to action," Kirby said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.
"It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now."
Kirby said lawmakers from both parties were committed to modernizing the system while holding the FAA accountable.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News' Grady Trimble, Anders Hagstrom, Stephen Sorace, Trey Wallace, and The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Buttigieg takes swipe at Trump administration amid FAA flight chaos
summary: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg joked he'd help travelers rebook flights at a hotel bar after the FAA's nationwide ground stop Friday.
story: At the "What’s Next" gathering in Denver, Democratic leaders weighed the party’s future and whether they could see themselves in the 2028 presidential race.

DENVER — Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg took a swipe at the Trump administration’s handling of Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, joking that he would help stranded travelers rebook flights as delays and cancellations continued.

I’ll begin with a public service announcement," Buttigieg told reporters in Denver. "I will be available in the hotel bar following the concert for anybody who needs to rebook their flights or get a refund per your rights."

He made the remark as the "What’s Next" conference wrapped up in Denver. The two-day gathering, hosted by Majority Democrats, brought leaders together to discuss the party’s direction after its midterm victories.
DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg joked he would help stranded travelers rebook flights as he weighed in on the FAA ground stop. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

The FAA lifted the ground stop shortly after 8 p.m. Friday, more than four hours after it began, but flights remained delayed and canceled over the weekend. The agency cited safety concerns and serious air traffic control communications issues.

Buttigieg, who said he had no inside information about the cause of the ground stop, later questioned why the aviation system’s safeguards had not prevented an outage of that scale. He said he was watching the disruption as a traveler with a flight scheduled for Saturday.

"The system has many redundancies in it, so that normally, if there’s one point of failure, something else can catch it," he said. "It is not clear to me why that redundancy did not prevent an outage of this magnitude."
SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, left, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appear during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Shawn Thew/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Trump administration officials offered a mixed account of the failure. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cause remained under investigation, including whether a contractor made an error or equipment failed.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin later said the stoppage was not caused by artificial intelligence or a cyberattack, but by aging infrastructure that needs to be updated. President Donald Trump told Fox News that the system had broken down because of its age.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
People wait in Terminal B during a nationwide ground stop at Orlando International Airport on November 13, 2026 in Orlando City. Nearly 7,000 flights have been delayed or cancelled. ( )

Friday’s disruption was the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The first came in January 2023, when the FAA paused domestic departures for about 90 minutes because of an outage in its Notice to Air Missions system, which provides pilots with safety information.

The FAA said at the time it found no evidence of a cyberattack. Buttigieg ordered a review of that outage and directed the agency to report on what happened and recommend steps to prevent a recurrence.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: NYC DSA urges AOC to run for president while planning to take over City Council
summary: NYC's Democratic Socialists of America voted to urge AOC to run for president in 2028, but some resolutions sparked an AI-generated controversy.
story: Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas reports on the New York City Democratic Socialists of America's plans to gain control of the City Council, its efforts to expand its political influence across the city and its push for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028 on 'Varney & Co.'
The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America overwhelmingly voted to urge Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., to run for president in 2028 on Saturday.

NYC-DSA approved a resolution making the call in a 291 to 123 vote at the chapter's annual convention. Gustavo Gordillo, co-chair of the local DSA chapter, said the vote was not a formal endorsement, but is instead a "a commitment to encouraging and building the foundation for a presidential campaign."

"AOC and New York City DSA are committed to building a stronger democratic socialist movement and DSA will create the conditions for a presidential campaign capable of advancing a working-class political agenda," Gordillo said at a press conference on Saturday.
DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA LEADER SAYS ‘MANY’ IN GROUP WOULD BE 'THRILLED' AT AOC IN 2028

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., speaks on stage during a campaign rally for New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani at Forest Hills Stadium in the Queens borough of New York City on Oct. 26, 2025. (Photo by ANGELA WEISS / AFP) (Photo by ANGELA WEISS/AFP via Getty Images)

The chapter also laid out its plans to take over New York City's City Council, among other resolutions. Several of the party's resolutions ran into controversy for appearing to be AI-generated, according to a report from Politico.
When run through the AI detection tool Pangram, the 2029 City Council election resolution was rated 100% AI-generated, the outlet reported.
Two other DSA resolutions were reportedly flagged as AI-generated as well, related to expanding DSA membership in community boards and interaction with South Asian communities.
The chapter has a policy against AI usage and voted on Saturday to formally oppose the expansion of AI.
NYC-DSA co-chair Grace Mausser pushed back on the accuracy of the Pangram results in a statement to Politico.
New York City Democratic Socialists hold a rally in Union Square on Nov. 16, 2025, to mark the start of a campaign to tax the rich and win universal childcare. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu)
AOC CAMPAIGN MEMO FRAMES GROWTH FROM PROGRESSIVE FIREBRAND TO NATIONAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY FORCE

"We are highly skeptical of the results coming out of Pangram as resolutions are often authored and edited in consensus by multiple members," she said, adding that Pangram’s tools "are made by the same industry that’s scraped writers’ work without permission and now sells software to accuse people of not writing their own words," Mausser said.
Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside of a Trump owned building during a May Day rally in New York City in 2019. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Pangram claims that its service can correctly identify AI-generated text 9,999 out of 10,000 times. A University of Chicago study also found that Pangram has a near-zero error rate.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Congress' incoming wealthiest member vows to crack down on politicians getting rich in office
summary: Joe Strada said he plans to crack down on congressional insider trading and politicians enriching themselves, drawing on his rise from bowling alley mechanic.
story: Florida congressional hopeful Joe Strada explains how he built a half-billion-dollar business, why he entered politics and what matters more to him than money.

EXCLUSIVE: Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., poised to become the wealthiest member of Congress, told Fox News Digital that he plans to crack down on politicians who enrich themselves while serving in public office when he takes office in January.

Strada, who went from working as a bowling alley mechanic to owning a nationwide HVAC company, is expected to become Congress' richest member, according to Forbes. The incoming Republican argued that public office should be about serving Americans rather than accumulating personal wealth.
"We need to make sure that we hold politicians accountable," Strada told Fox News Digital. "Nobody, and I mean nobody, should get rich in public office. We're there to serve the American people."
Democrats regained majorities in both the House and Senate as a blue wave swept the country. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
"If you want to get rich, stay in the private sector. I went into business to get rich, not Washington, D.C. I'm going to Washington, D.C., to serve the American people," he continued.
The congressman-elect said combating congressional insider trading and political profiteering would be among his priorities as he prepares to leave the private sector for Capitol Hill.

Strada pointed to his own rise from a blue-collar worker to a successful businessman as proof that the American Dream remains achievable, arguing that excessive government intervention has made it harder for others to follow a similar path.

"I started with nothing. I was a handyman at a bowling alley. If I can do it, other everyday Americans can. Government needs to get out of their way and help them succeed," Strada said. "It's so important to give people opportunity to succeed and achieve their version of the American dream, and now it's time to open that up."
"That's what I plan to do in Washington, D.C., give every American the opportunity they need to succeed, prosper, open a small business and start a career," he added.
"I'm living proof of it," Strada said, referring to his own success.
Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., said he plans to crack down on politicians who enrich themselves while in public office. (Fox News Digital)

The incoming Republican also warned that the growing popularity of democratic socialism and proposals for expanding government programs could undermine American entrepreneurship, innovation and small-business growth.

"I think it's important to show people the opportunity. The talking points of ‘free this, free that’ sounds great, but we do not want to suppress the American people. We instead want to show them that their goals and ambitions are achievable," Strada said.
"It was achievable for me. I never went to college, the thought of college was not even in conversation with my parents. Going to college for me was unachievable," he added.
Strada said his early work experience taught him the importance of discipline and perseverance, values he believes should be emphasized to younger generations.

"I knew I had to work, and I worked hard," Strada said, adding that young Americans could benefit from a greater emphasis on work ethic. "I think if we can instill that in young people today, they'd be better off."

The congressman-elect also identified housing affordability as a major obstacle preventing Americans from achieving financial independence, pledging to pursue federal deregulation, lower construction material costs and workforce development initiatives to make homeownership more accessible.

"Housing cost is ridiculous. I have so many examples of ways we can still build a high-quality home for substantially less money, and more Americans could live out their dream of owning a home," Strada said.
The U.S. Capitol is shown in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 7, 2026. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As he prepares to take office in January, Strada said he hopes to secure a seat on the House Appropriations Committee, where he believes his business experience would allow him to "best serve the American people."

title: Trump's top officials retreat behind military gates as ex-FBI deputy points to what's fueling threats
summary: Scott Bessent joins Todd Blanche, Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth at Washington D.C. military bases amid Iranian assassination threats.
story: Former CIA station chief Dan Hoffman examines reported Iranian threats that prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his family to relocate to a military base. He also discusses allegations of Iranian cyberattacks in France and reported cooperation between Iran and Russia to circumvent U.S. military and economic restrictions.

Military bases around Washington, D.C., have become an increasingly common refuge for some of President Donald Trump's most powerful officials, as threats linked to Iran and a surge in threats against public officials raise security concerns across the administration.

"So you have this combination of a permission structure on the left for violence, combine it with the ability to track it and create a long paper trail, and the numbers explode, and these threat matrices go crazy," former Secret Service agent and former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest senior administration official to relocate to a military installation, joining a growing number of top Trump officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats that extend well beyond the White House.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
Scott Bessent, US Treasury secretary, speaks to members of the media outside the White House in Washington, D.C., Nov. 5, 2025. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the Secretary’s Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the Secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety. The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials," a source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital.

Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, but did not elaborate.
The Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials.
Attorney General Todd Blanche also relocated to a military base from his home around March, a different source familiar with the arrangements told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

The Justice Department charged a member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2022 in an alleged murder-for-hire plot targeting former Trump national security adviser John Bolton, while prosecutors disclosed in 2024 that another Iranian operative had allegedly been tasked with developing a plan to assassinate Trump.

Bongino said federal protection decisions are generally driven by threat assessments that account for threatening communications, social media activity and intelligence gathered by security personnel. Agencies responsible for protecting senior officials use those assessments to determine what level of protection is necessary.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran said last month that threats against the agency's full-time protectees had increased more than 40% from the previous year, with roughly 10,000 threat cases recorded in 2026 at the time.
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Secret Service for comment.
"Pretty much, sadly, anyone at the cabinet, or even sub-cabinet level, with any kind of public persona in the Trump administration, needed a detail," Bongino said.
US EVACUATES 13 MILITARY AIRCRAFT FROM SECOND UK BASE AS NEW IRAN THREAT RAISES ALARM

US Second Lady Usha Vance, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bassent, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick arrive for US President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump to greet Britain's King Charles III and Queen Camilla during an arrival ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, on April 28, 2026. (Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)

The assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and multiple attempts on President Donald Trump's life have heightened concerns about political violence, as security officials confront a growing volume of threats against public officials.
Bongino pointed to his own experience as FBI deputy director, saying his security needs were comparable to those of some of the government's highest-ranking law enforcement officials.
"Mine was on par with the attorney general and the FBI director that we had to expand it," Bongino said of his threat assessment and security detail. "It was an independent analysis."

Bongino said social media has made threats against public officials easier to track, but the sheer volume of online activity has also created more work for investigators trying to determine which threats are credible.
SECRET SERVICE CHIEF SAYS THREATS AGAINST PROTECTEES UP 40%, CITES INTERNET AND MENTAL HEALTH

A U.S. Secret Service police officer stands outside of the White House the day after President Donald Trump announced U.S. military strikes on nuclear sites in Iran on June 22, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
Bongino said the disruption to Bessent's personal life underscores the seriousness of the security concerns surrounding his move.

"For him to have to uproot his life. And move on to a military facility where the housing's not terrible in those places, but it's certainly not what he's used to," Bongino said. "This stuff, it's not a convenience issue, I can promise you that. This is definitely serious stuff."

Lawmakers have also raised concerns about security and federal spending. Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., secured House Armed Services Committee approval in June for a proposal seeking a Pentagon report on political appointees living in military housing, including the threats justifying their moves, legal authority for the arrangements and rental costs.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., also questioned whether the reported transfer of $415 million in Secret Service funding to White House construction projects could affect the agency's protective operations, citing federal watchdog concerns about staffing and resource shortages.

Barry Donadio, a former Secret Service agent who served during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, similarly told Fox News Digital that the decision to relocate Bessent to a military installation suggests an extraordinary level of concern among those responsible for his protection.
"My first inkling is that the [threat] is so high that they cannot protect him with certainty, unless he is on a military base which speaks volumes for the situation at hand," Donadio said.
TRUMP ADMIN APPROVES $351 MILLION FOR WHITE HOUSE SECURITY MEASURES AMID QUESTIONS OVER BALLROOM FUNDING
U.S. Secret Service Uniformed Division officers patrol near the White House on March 9, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Donadio said the move could indicate that officials believe Bessent would be safer on a military base than at a private residence.

"They may have foiled an attack already that is not being publicized, and as an extra measure, have moved him to a military base for protective custody," Donadio said, clarifying that he did not mean Bessent was in custody, but rather under heightened government protection.
Bessent is not the only senior Trump administration official whose security concerns have prompted a move to military housing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing.
TRUMP ADMIN APPROVES $351 MILLION FOR WHITE HOUSE SECURITY MEASURES AMID QUESTIONS OVER BALLROOM FUNDING
President Donald Trump attends a Cabinet meeting in the Cabinet Room at the White House in Washington on May 27, 2026. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)
The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence, while Bessent's move comes amid reported threats linked to Iran.

Bongino said threats against high-profile officials can also extend beyond their time in government, describing an incident in which an individual allegedly appeared at a California television studio with a manifesto threatening him and other officials.
"I mean, this stuff is real, it happens every day," Bongino said. "And when you're living through it and you're not accustomed to it, you know, and it follows you after office too."

He said officials including Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Hegseth understood that public service in the administration could make them targets even after leaving office.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fort McNair, a historic Army installation along the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., has emerged as one of the military properties housing senior Trump administration officials. The installation, which dates to the late 1700s, is home to the National Defense University and traditionally provides residential quarters for senior military leaders.

Fort McNair's residential quarters are divided into two housing groups, according to a 2020 National Capital Planning Commission report, while a 2024 Army filing identifies 27 historic homes built before 1919 at the installation.
The Army's housing website lists 88 historic dwelling units across Fort McNair and nearby Fort Myer combined, without specifying how many are at each base.

The growing use of military housing by senior civilian officials also raises questions about who approves the arrangements, whether officials pay for their accommodations and what impact, if any, the moves have on housing traditionally reserved for military personnel.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Inside Senate GOP's tense post-election reckoning as Thune clashes with Republican critics
summary: Senate Republicans kept John Thune as leader by acclamation after a heated closed-door meeting that some lawmakers compared to "Festivus."
story: Incoming Senate Minority Leader John Thune discusses the GOP's 2026 midterm election performance following Senate leadership votes. Thune argues that cost-of-living concerns were a driving factor in the election results.

Senate Republicans huddled for hours on end to define their remaining time in power and determine if the leadership they had backed so far was the right choice moving forward into a new era in Washington, D.C.

Some closed-door meetings over the last nearly two years Republicans have controlled the Senate have been animated, with policy pitches devolving into shouting matches — President Donald Trump and Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., infamously sparred over the Iran war earlier this year.

This confab, their first since Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats roared back into the majority, was different. In part, it was meant to develop a plan that would carry them through the final weeks of this year — that was agreed upon during the meeting, but not without its own drama after the fact on who could lay claim to the GOP’s 54-day blitz.
SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., arrives for Senate Republican leadership elections at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 10, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
It was also a test to see if Republicans wanted to keep Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., as their leader, or delay until a challenger appeared.
But Republicans pushing for a delay acknowledged part of the problem: Who would want the job?
"I got the job because nobody else wants it," Thune told Fox News Digital after the dust settled in the Old Senate Chamber.

And he did, along with much of the same leadership team that Senate Republicans elected when they won the majority two years ago, by acclamation, meaning no lawmaker objected to their leadership slate.

Some told Fox News Digital it was like "Festivus," the holiday etched into Gen-Xers' brains from "Seinfeld" known for its airing of grievances. Others described it as a frank, needed debrief as the GOP picks through the debris of Election Night.
GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS

"It really was, to be honest with you, as profound as the loss was last week. I would have expected more emotions, which I consider to be a good sign," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital. "But I think it's almost — It's self-governing because nobody can dispute that it's a problem."
"Now it's not like you're looking for the silver lining," he continued. "It doesn't exist. It is what it is, and you've got to react."
But there were some "testy" moments, particularly between Thune and Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., the driving force behind the push to delay leadership elections.
For Thune, the main question was what anyone else in the Senate GOP would have done differently in his shoes.

"I just think that you come through an election like this and everybody's looking for scapegoats and there's a lot of blame casting that goes on, and I just wanted to get up and basically defend what we had done and accomplished," Thune said.

"And I think the operative question is, tell me what you would do differently? Both on the political side and the legislative side. So we had a good, we had a robust conversation, and it does. It always gets a little bit testy in the back and forth, but I thought that, by and large, the discussion was very candid, and certainly gave everybody an opportunity to be heard."
CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—'

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., arrives for the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Johnson acknowledged that he was "prone to interrupting, I’m rude that way," and told Fox News Digital that he was sure Thune was "not happy that I did that," but assured that there was no "animus" between the two.
"In politics, everything has to be so black and white, and, unfortunately, for our base, the way to really rev them up is inter-conference fighting, which is not helpful," Johnson said.

"So, again, I didn't really like doing this, but it had to be done," he continued. "I mean, we had to, and in the end, I think, resulted in a very, very good conversation and pretty well revealed we're just lucky to have anybody who wants those jobs."
Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital that Thune showed "moments of exceptional leadership" in the heat of the meeting.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He noted that the top Republican's rebuttal reminded lawmakers of the "ebb and flow of the politics in our country," dating back to 1986, when former President Ronald Reagan, then entering his final midterm election similar to Trump, lost eight seats in the upper chamber.

"Obama lost nine Senate seats in 2014, it looks like we're going to lose eight, depending on what happens in Alaska," Daines said. "So it's within the kind of the historic norms of going back and forth."
"And the leader forcefully laid that out and then talked about what he needed to do going forward to unify and eventually reclaim the majority," he continued.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Small town residents cry for help as immigrant influx fueled by trucking industry has unintended consequences
summary: A Fox News Digital investigation reveals Hamilton Township's freight fraud crackdown yielded 561 traffic stops and 36 arrests in southwest Ohio.
story: An influx of Uzbek immigrants and trucking companies is fueling frustration in southwest Ohio, where residents are raising concerns about alleged fraud, roadway safety and changes in their neighborhoods.
This article is Part 3 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating trucking fraud, public safety, and assimilation concerns in southwest Ohio. You can read Part 1 here and Part 2 here.

OHIO - An influx of Uzbek immigrants and trucking companies, coupled with mounting concerns about roadway safety and alleged fraud, is fueling frustration in southwest Ohio, where residents are speaking out about changes they say have left them feeling unsafe on their roads and increasingly uneasy in their own neighborhoods.

Jane, a resident of southwest Ohio, is one of many who have been affected by the Uzbek influx, which she says ultimately drove her out of a new home she purchased in the area after just 18 months of living there.
"I have literally been screaming about what has been going on for years, and I'm like somebody needs to take notice of this," Jane told Fox News Digital.

Jane recounted repeated problems involving neighbors she identified as Uzbek, describing unsupervised children grabbing moving cars, climbing construction equipment, threatening to punch, kick or choke her dog, and taking her child's bicycle while ignoring demands to return it. She also described children urinating on neighbors’ vehicles, adults slaughtering chickens outdoors in view of her frightened child, and semi-truck cabs obstructing driveways.
WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH

An influx of Uzbek immigrants and trucking companies is fueling frustration in southwest Ohio, where residents are raising concerns about alleged fraud, roadway safety and changes in their neighborhoods. (Fox News Digital/Andrew Mark Miller ; iStock)
Jane described feeling "incredibly uncomfortable" encountering groups of roughly 15 men she identified as Uzbek gathered on the grass between neighboring homes while she was walking her dog.
"They all look at me like I have like 12 freaking heads, like I'm the most disgusting person in the world," she said.

Jane also described a situation where a group of Uzbek men showed up at her neighbor's door late at night carrying large bags before being told by the neighbor they had the wrong address. That neighbor then watched them go across the street into a garage and count cash that came from inside those bags.

She estimated calling police roughly 20 times or more and said she felt authorities were unwilling or unable to intervene, leaving her family feeling they had little recourse but to leave. Jane was granted anonymity and is not using her real name due to fear for her family’s safety and possible retribution.
TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATING 75 TRUCK DRIVER SCHOOLS FOR FRAUD, HELPING NON-CITIZENS GET LICENSES

In nearby Middletown, Fox News Digital visited a site in mid-October that used to be a restaurant where GHOSTOPSUZ, a resident who has been flagging suspicious trucking companies and Uzbek influx to his followers anonymously online, used to frequent every Sunday after Mass with his family as a child.

Today, the building is abandoned and in disarray with smashed-out windows and no sign of life inside, but registered as the active headquarters of a trucking company, UAG Express, with over two dozen violations for infractions including vehicle maintenance, unsafe driving, suspended-CDL and an hours-of-service violation.

"It's devastating, dude, I mean, it really is," GHOSTOPSUZ said as he walked around the dilapidated building that had multiple big rigs parked in the back but no sign of any recent activity. The location was recently highlighted by Border Hawk News.

"My daughter plays competitive volleyball, so we're on these roads that we're sharing with these people that don't speak English, don't understand our laws, can't read our laws and frankly, I don't think they care, it’s quite obvious…and it doesn’t show respect for the community that you're in to do things like this."
OUT OF CONTROL, UNQUALIFIED ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKERS ENDANGERING KIDS ON US ROADS, INSIDER WARNS: ‘JUST MADNESS’
Fox News Digital reached out to UAG Express, owned by Aziz Ishanov, for comment but did not receive a response.

On Nov. 4, Fox News Digital attended a meeting where dozens of Hamilton Township residents expressed their concerns to the local trustees and told stories of first-hand experiences ranging from alleged trucking fraud to the mosque, to crowded schools, to crime concerns related to the Uzbek community in the area.

"It has been a great place to grow up, now I'm very concerned at this point with what we're learning about the fraud from these trucking companies, the Uzbek trucking companies, about the funds that they're using to build the mosque right now. I'm just wondering, how did this get approved in the first place?" One local resident asked.

Residents voiced concerns about a wide variety of issues including Uzbek men leering at women outside gyms, crowded schools, an unsupervised Uzbek child who recently drowned in a local pond, and Uzbek truck drivers offering money to women to get inside their trucks.

One resident said, "Christian values are not compatible with Islamic values; they just simply aren't, and I don't like calling a people group out, especially as a Christian, that's very hard for me to do. But the facts are the facts, and we have to look at the facts. They are not here to assimilate; some are, I'm sure. But I know how they operate."
"We are drowning," one resident said while discussing the crowded schools and students who can't speak English which has stretched resources thin. "We are drowning here, our kids our suffering."

Local law enforcement has taken action on the trucking safety issue, and in the meeting, Hamilton Township Police Chief Quillan Short unveiled the data from a recent freight fraud crackdown that multiple local agencies coordinated between Oct. 19-23.

That operation resulted in 561 traffic stops, 258 truck inspections, 423 citations and 73 vehicles being placed out of service. Authorities also placed 49 drivers out of service and made 36 arrests, including 31 on charges related to immigration-related offenses, according to data presented by Short.
Hamilton Township Trustee Darryl Cordrey, in a statement to Fox News Digital, called the results of the crackdown "staggering" especially considering it only lasted 5 days.

"Hamilton Township residents have every right to be concerned about unsafe commercial vehicles , unqualified drivers on our roads, and other criminal issues that have stemmed from the substantial increase in commercial trucking operations in Hamilton Township," Cordrey said. "Our residents should not have to bear the consequences of failures in immigration policy and commercial trucking oversight."

Cordrey added that the Biden administration's immigration policies have "contributed to the broader problems we are now confronting" and that he is "fully committed" to doing his part to resolve the issues working alongside local, state, and federal agencies.

Ohio Republican state lawmaker Michelle Teska was present at the meeting as well and has taken action on the issue in the form of a bill to strengthen commercial-driver licensing requirements, including a measure requiring driver examinations to be administered in English.

"We have a community that's being inundated with people from a certain area and how they got here is through the trucking industry, and they got here because, again, in the state of Ohio, you can get a CDL and a driver's license in 10 different languages," Teska told Fox News Digital, adding that she and the Hamilton Township trustees share the frustration and are doing what they can to address it despite many of the issues being rooted at the state and federal level.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Islamic Center of Maineville under construction in southwest Ohio. (Fox News Digital)

The federal government has ramped up efforts to crack down on trucking fraud over the past year, and the Department of Transportation and Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration have mounted a sweeping crackdown on fraud and safety violations, placing roughly 34,000 drivers out of service for failing basic English-language proficiency requirements, revoking or canceling more than 31,000 illegally issued commercial driver’s licenses, and shutting down or purging nearly 10,000 noncompliant driving schools from the federal registry.

"This is a safety issue," Teska said. "This is not a partisan issue in any way, shape, or form, but this is a safety issue, and you know we've had a rape conviction, a federal human smuggling indictment, a fatal crash where a driver couldn't communicate with troopers without a translator, and every single one of those things was preventable."

Warren County Prosecutor David Fornshell previously told Fox News Digital that clearly "there’s something going on" within the Uzbek community in southwest Ohio that "warrants at least awareness on the part of law enforcement."
"I would say hardly a week goes by where we don't have some felony case involving an Uzbek, it's pretty frequent at this point," Fornshell said.

On Friday, the Islamic Center of Maineville, the mosque that has drawn the ire of some in the community, posted on its Telegram channel that it acknowledges the concerns and is hoping to work with the community to resolve them.

"On behalf of the Hamkor Uzbek Cincinnati Association, we recognize that some local residents have concerns and questions about our community. We believe that mutual respect, open communication, and understanding are the best ways to address these issues," the message said. "Our Uzbek community is willing to listen to local residents, understand their concerns, clear up any misunderstandings, and work together to find practical solutions. We want to build trust, strengthen relationships, and promote unity between the Uzbek community and our neighbors. We believe that respectful dialogue and cooperation, rather than arguments and division, will help us move forward as one community."

Data from the 2024 Census show that roughly 1,500 people born in Uzbekistan live in Greater Cincinnati, while about 3,800 Uzbekistan-born residents live across Ohio. Uzbek community leaders say the actual population is significantly higher, estimating that roughly 4,000 Uzbek families live in southern Ohio, including U.S.-born children.

"Our community was selected by the Uzbeks because they didn't think we would push back on their foreign influence," online researcher Nodawolf, a local resident who has been at the forefront of reporting on alleged trucking fraud over the past year, said via a statement read by an attendee at the trustees meeting. "Here we are. We are here to say that our community will not be exploited for their monetary gain."
America Up Close is a Fox News Digital Politics series taking the country’s biggest political debates beyond Washington to uncover their real-world costs for the Americans living with the results.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Justice Alito warns America must preserve 3 core principles regardless of country’s ‘atmosphere’
summary: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito outlined three principles he says Americans must always prioritize amid the 2026 midterms and the Iran War.
story: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito discusses retirement rumors on 'Fox News Sunday.'
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recently laid out three principles Americans must cling to to ensure the integrity of the republic: freedom of speech, religious liberty and racial equality.

"I'm not saying we're entering the dark age, but these are things that we have to preserve no matter what the atmosphere is in the country or the world at the time," Alito said during a fireside chat with Mollie Hemingway, editor-in-chief at the Federalist, which followed the Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner at the 2026 National Lawyer's Convention in Washington D.C.

The remarks come on the heels of the blue tsunami of the 2026 midterms, with Republicans losing 42 House seats and eight Senate seats, with the Alaska U.S. Senate race still uncalled. Democrats are set to take control of Congress with eight lawmakers backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Both incoming and returning members have pressed for investigations and subpoenas targeting President Donald Trump and his administration.

United States Supreme Court Associate Justice Samuel Alito poses for an official portrait at the East Conference Room of the Supreme Court building on October 7, 2022 in Washington, DC. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN
Alito's remarks also come amid the ongoing Iran war, which has destabilized oil supply chains across the globe, causing the price of goods and gas to jump.
The 76-year-old jurist said preserving freedom of speech is paramount, warning that "you cannot have Democratic self-fulfillment if you cannot have robust free speech."
"Even speech that is hurtful to some of the people who hear what is being said," Alito said.

He also stressed the importance of freedom of religion, even as the Supreme Court is set to rule on at least two major cases this term centered on religious freedom: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy and Grand v. City of University Heights.

President Donald J. Trump greets Associate Justice of the Supreme Court Samuel Alito as he departs from a ceremony to swear in Secretary of Defense Mark Esper in the Oval Office at the White House on Tuesday, July 23, 2019, in Washington. (Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
SUPREME COURT OFFERS SUPPORT FOR CATHOLIC PRESCHOOLS CHALLENGING STATE FUNDING REQUIREMENTS
"I think that we have placed religious liberty on a sounder footing than it was on 20, 25 years ago," Alito said.

"Religious liberty is central to human dignity, and in a society that is as religiously diverse as this country, we've got people who adhere to practically every religion that exists in the world," Alito continued. "We are not going to be able to get along, I think, amicably, productively, if we don't respect everybody's right to follow whatever religion they want, or for people of faith, they're also free to do that."
"That's essential," Alito said.
He rounded off his trifecta by saying that America must maintain racial equality, declaring it "essential for our pluralistic society."

Supreme Court Associate Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas wait to leave the stage after the inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla/AFP via Getty Images)
FEDERAL JUDGE TOSSES TRUMP ADMIN HARVARD ADMISSIONS LAWSUIT, LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO FUTURE CHALLENGE

"That is the principle that Dr. Martin Luther King famously articulated in his speech at the Lincoln Memorial, where he said he looked forward to the day when children would be judged by the content of their character and not by the color of their skin," Alito said.
"If we don't hold to that principle, then I think the society is going to start to come apart," Alito said.

The Supreme Court agreed in October to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education this term, a challenge brought by parents of Asian American students alleging that a Maryland school district’s admissions policies unlawfully discriminate despite appearing race-neutral.

Alito mentioned the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, which ended affirmative action in college admissions, as among the most consequential rulings from the Supreme Court in the past few decades.
TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME'

Alito's discussion comes as questions swirl about his possible plans to retire. In a Bloomberg article published after the midterms, Alito said that the Democrats' sweep did not change his plans to stay on the Supreme Court.
Alito, nominated by President George W. Bush, has served on the bench since 2006.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"With those, with those 20 years, I jumped to 42nd in the the list of all-time service by Supreme Court justices," Alito said.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: White House lawyer's hardball warning to Dems has legal experts on both sides questioning one key threat
summary: William Scharf's letter warns Democrats that abusive subpoenas could cross into criminality, but Rep. Robert Garcia says Trump has something to hide.
story: Fox News senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich reports on growing tensions between the White House and House Democrats over plans to investigate Trump administration officials and issue subpoenas. Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn explains the legal challenges both sides could face.

White House Counsel William Scharf sent a letter to California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform ranking member, Nov. 9, warning Democrats against running afoul of their allotted powers related to investigations and subpoenas.

The letter put Democratic lawmakers on notice of the "foundational limits that the Constitution imposes on congressional investigations and subpoenas" and suggested their actions could cross the line of criminal misconduct.
Garcia, poised to chair the committee next year when Democrats gain the House majority, responded to the letter by suggesting the president has "something to hide."
AG BLANCHE CLASHES WITH ANCHOR ASKING WHETHER IT'S HIS 'JOB' TO DEFEND THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

Legal experts from across the political spectrum who spoke to Fox News Digital suggested that, while the White House is within its rights to challenge individual subpoenas, it faces significant obstacles if it decides to seek criminal indictments related to Garcia's oversight activities.

"In short, the administration can assert privileges, negotiate over requests and challenge particular subpoenas through the appropriate legal process, but criminal prosecutions are, to mix metaphors, a very different animal that face a higher bar," Ilya Shapiro, director of constitutional studies at the right-of-center Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital.
Will Scharf during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., Aug. 6, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Congressional investigations also enjoy protections under the Constitution's speech or debate clause, which the Supreme Court has held shields lawmakers from judicial interference when their investigative activities fall within the legitimate legislative sphere.

Shapiro explained that Democrats "promising indiscriminate subpoenas are inviting challenges to their demands" because congressional committees "must act within their jurisdiction, respect witnesses’ constitutional rights and connect investigations to a legitimate legislative purpose."
Garcia, however, maintains that his calls for investigation are consistent with his constitutional authority as a lawmaker.

"Let’s be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said in his statement.

"The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse. The Trump administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the president’s lawyers."

Scharf sent the letter a week after Democrats issued statements and social media posts calling for subpoenas and impeachment trials for Trump administration officials after Republicans' major loss during the 2026 midterms. At the time, some pointed out that Republicans used similar language to call for investigations into Democratic officials.

Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom and a constitutional law expert, told Fox News Digital Scharf is correct in his assertion that Garcia's investigations cannot be motivated by simple spite but suggested the White House may run into problems if it tries to get criminal charges to stick.

"Scharf is correct in his citation of Watkins v. U.S. that the Supreme Court has held that congressional investigations not connected to a legitimate legislative purpose and whose only intent is harassment and trying to seize personal, private information are unconstitutional and beyond the power of Congress," von Spakovsky wrote in an email.

"Problem is that I am not sure what criminal statutes, if any, could be applied. There are statutes over harassment of federal officials, 18 U.S.C. 111, 115, but those require physical threats. What the Watkins precedent holds is that the courts cannot enforce subpoenas issued by Congress that are part of an improper, unconstitutional investigation."
TOP DEM ON COMMITTEE FIRES BACK AFTER WHITE HOUSE COUNSEL WARNS AGAINST OVERREACH AMID INVESTIGATION THREATS
Incoming House Oversight Committee leader Rep. Robert Garcia warned that Democrats could investigate President Donald Trump's pardons and allies of the president. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"No statute makes oversight a crime, and Scharf’s letter doesn't say one does. Its point is that a committee's process doesn't shield conduct that would be a crime for anyone else. Conspiring to intimidate federal officers out of doing their jobs falls under 18 U.S.C. 372," Will Chamberlain, senior counsel at the right-of-center Article III Project, told Fox News Digital.

"Congress' oversight authority is broad but not unlimited. There is no congressional power to expose for the sake of exposure and any investigation requires a valid legislative purpose. Congressional investigative activity conducted in an official capacity wouldn't be prosecutable."
He added that what could be prosecutable would be a separate conspiracy to intimidate federal officials "evidenced by threats, press releases, things of that nature."
Molly Nixon, a senior fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute, had broadly similar thoughts.

"White House counsel is correct that courts have required congressional investigations to serve a legitimate legislative purpose, though the constitutional boundaries of that requirement are not as clear as Scharf asserts. I don’t think the letter is on solid ground when it makes the leap to suggesting potential criminality," she told Fox News Digital.
DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to reporters outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House office building on Nov. 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government," Scharf wrote.

"Recent public statements underscore these concerns. You and your congressional colleagues have asserted that they will issue subpoenas to harass, threaten, and deter dedicated members of the Administration from further service.

"Compulsory process is a power Congress has for oversight functions, and only for oversight functions. Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end," the letter added.

"Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality," the letter continued.
"And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation."

Those further investigations, however, are unlikely to result in criminal charges, according to Devon Ombres, senior director for courts and legal policy at the left-of-center Center for American Progress.

"You know, I don't think that there is any reasonable basis for the administration to argue that Congress cannot undertake its constitutional obligations of conducting oversight, and I can't imagine that there's any type of criminal statute that would apply in this context," he said in a phone call.
"That's not to say that this DOJ won't try and shoehorn something in, as they've already done, but I don't think that Scharf has a legal leg to stand on."
While criminal charges would face significant legal obstacles, Ombres says he fully expects the Trump administration to try blocking the subpoenas through lawsuits.

"The White House and the DOJ is going to throw everything, including the kitchen sink, at subpoenas," Ombres said.

title: Dems seize on midterm rout to demand ICE reform, but polls reveal a twist in who prioritized immigration
summary: Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido and Texas Democrats push 2028 candidates to prioritize immigration reform after flipping Republican-leaning districts.
story: Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, claims Trump’s unfulfilled promise to lower prices and backlash over deportations as factors driving Hispanic voters toward Democrats.
Democrats are seizing on their sweeping midterm victories to demand immigration reform, even as polling shows economic concerns far outpaced it as a priority for both Democratic and Hispanic voters.
The push follows Democratic gains nationwide, including wins in Texas congressional districts redrawn to favor Republicans and major upsets in the state’s Senate and gubernatorial races.
Some winners are casting the results as a mandate to challenge President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and putting prospective 2028 Democratic presidential candidates on notice.

"Whoever wants to get our support in ’28 has to prioritize immigration reform, period," Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, D-Texas, who defeated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in South Texas, said last recently at a news conference alongside fellow Texas Democrats pushing for immigration reform.
REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES
But Fox News Digital polling showed 27% of Republican voters ranked immigration as their top issue, compared to just 3% of Democrats.

Pulido flipped a redrawn, Republican-leaning South Texas district, ousting De La Cruz, who won her re-election in 2024 by 14.2 points. Pulido campaigned on affordability while tying Trump's immigration enforcement raids at worksites to workforce shortages that hurt the economy.
Supporters of immigration reform joined Democratic lawmakers for a news conference on Capitol Hill Nov. 11. (Fox News Elaine Mallon)

Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital voters who split their tickets between Trump and down-ballot Democrats in 2024 were responding this year to both affordability pressures and the president’s immigration crackdown.

"He made a promise that he was going to bring prices down on day one. Liberation didn't happen, so people remembered that," Cuellar, whose district encompasses border town Laredo, told Fox News Digital.
"Second thing is he said he was going to focus on criminals. He didn't stop there. He started going after construction workers."

Democrats’ wins came as an estimated 14.5 million Latinos voted across the country in the 2026 midterms, according to UnidosUS. The group’s Texas state director, Eric Holguín, said Democratic support among Latino voters rivaled levels seen in 2008, when Barack Obama won the presidency.
"Cost of living was the No. 1 issue that we saw with Latino voters in Texas and across the country as well," Holguín told Fox News Digital, referring to polling conducted by UnidosUS.

Pre-election polling conducted by the Fox News Voter Poll showed that, for 45% of polled Hispanic voters, the economy was the most important issue the country faced, followed by the state of democracy for 26% of voters and then immigration at 15%.
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE
For Hispanics voting in Texas, polling followed a similar trend with the economy the No. 1 issue for 45% of voters, the state of democracy for 25% of voters and immigration for 15%.

"People right now, they see their pocketbooks, they see the bank accounts, they see the grocery bills, they see their electric bills, they see their gas bills, and they're saying, 'Hey, a lot of promises were made to us in 2024 by President Trump, and he's had almost two years to deliver on those promises. And, not only has he not delivered on those promises, he's made them worse with the war in Iran,'" Holguín said.
Trump said the Iran war hurt Republicans in the midterms as conflict in the Strait of Hormuz has destabilized oil supply chains, causing gas prices to soar.
Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center, told Fox News Digital voters were likely motivated by a rejection of Trump rather than enthusiasm for Democrats' policies.
Supporters of immigration reform gather on Capitol Hill for a news conference held by Democratic lawmakers after the midterm sweep. (Fox News Digital Elaine Mallon)
"It was driven by an anger that the president hasn't delivered on the promises that he made, particularly bringing down the cost of living and decreasing international tensions," Olsen said.

"People see that inflation is higher than when he took office, and America is involved militarily in more places than they were under the Biden administration, and that's not what they thought they were getting."
HISPANIC VOTERS ARE NATURAL CONSERVATIVES. REAGAN KNEW. GOP NEEDS TO PROVE IT AGAIN
During a 60 Minutes interview, Trump said some of his deportation policies were "too tough"and that a deal with Democrats was "doable."

Miguel Valenzuela, a business owner in Texas who joined American Families United for the Nov. 11 news conference, said he had spent years warning Republicans that their approach to immigration risked alienating Hispanic voters who otherwise shared some of the party’s values.
"Hispanic values, family, faith, hardworking," Valenzuela, who does not identify as a Democrat, told Fox News Digital. "That sounds like a Republican, right? "

Valenzuela said he attended local Republican political events and urged the party to address immigration reform before pushing away an entire voting bloc. He argued that children of immigrants were reaching voting age and making their frustrations known at the ballot box.
"Those kids have now become of age, and they are voting. And since they are now voting, this is exactly what I had been warning about for years. And it happened last week," Valenzuela said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Holguín warned Democrats that keeping Latino voters’ support will depend on delivering results.

"They’re put on notice right now. Everyone’s watching what they do," Holguín said. "They’re looking for major change in how our government’s run and how our government delivers for the people."
Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre defended Trump’s immigration policies and applauded the president for keeping affordability at the center of his agenda.

"President Trump is keeping his promise to secure the border and enforce our immigration laws to keep American citizens safe. While Democrats fight among themselves and focus on impeaching President Trump, Republicans remain united and focused on making life more affordable for working American families."
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.
