title: Democrats eye killing Senate filibuster, and lawmaker warns move could be a 'double-edged sword'
summary: Ed Markey says the filibuster must be "on the table" as Democrats take the Senate, while Andy Kim warns the move could be a "double-edged sword."
story: Fox News Digital pressed Democratic lawmakers on eliminating the Senate's 60-vote threshold as the party weighs its legislative priorities while taking control of the chamber.
Democrat senators are leaving the door open to eliminating the Senate filibuster as their party prepares to take control of the chamber.
One lawmaker said the move must be on the table, while another warned it could be a "double-edged sword."
"Obviously, the filibuster is something that has to be on the table," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., told Fox News Digital when asked about Democrats' plans for the chamber.
But Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., warned that changing the rules could carry consequences long after Democrats leave power.
SCHUMER, JEFFRIES SIDESTEP QUESTIONS ON NUKING FILIBUSTER, LAUNCHING ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER BLUE WAVE
Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., speaks during a hearing on Capitol Hill. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

"Some of these things that we see here can be very much a double-edged sword," Kim said. "I'm not saying that's to deter us from doing it if we decide to do it. But I wanna make sure that everyone's clear-eyed about what we're doing."

Scrapping the Senate's 60-vote hurdle would allow Democrats to advance most legislation with a simple majority, weakening Republicans' ability to block their agenda but also giving the GOP the same advantage if it regains control.

Fox News Digital pressed the senators on whether Democrats would consider changing the rules while President Donald Trump remains in office or wait until a potential Democratic presidential victory in 2028.
"We're discussing a progressive agenda right now and amongst the other Democratic senators," Markey said. "So, I'll be listening to everyone's views on what is the best strategy."
SCHUMER'S GRIP ON POWER SLIPS AS DEMS BEGIN TO REVOLT AGAINST HIM, EYE NEW LEADERSHIP
Trump pressed Senate Republicans to abolish the filibuster when trying to pass the SAVE America Act, warning that Democrats would eliminate it if the party took back the majority. And now they have.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., remained silent when asked if he would support Democrats getting rid of the filibuster if they win the White House in 2028. Schumer is under scrutiny from progressives as the party considers who will lead the Senate after winning back the majority.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced Thursday he will run against Schumer for Senate majority leader and is in favor of terminating the filibuster, even going as far as characterizing it as "anti-democratic."

"My personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an anti-democratic … provision. It's not in our Constitution," Van Hollen said. "It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people."
SCHUMER FACES MUTINY FROM NEWLY ELECTED SENATE DEMS AS PARTY PREPARES TO SEIZE POWER
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver Friday as he campaigns to lead Senate Democrats. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

While Van Hollen's personal position is that the filibuster should go, he noted it would need to be a broader discussion among the Democratic caucus on how to proceed with the much-maligned guardrail.
Kim cautioned that changing Senate rules could set a precedent Democrats might later regret.
"When you open the door … you gotta be ready," Kim said. "You don't wanna shoot from the hip when it comes to really big issues that are affecting our country in this way."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He suggested pushing legislation "through other means" before jumping to nuking the filibuster.

"I think we as a caucus would need to think through … what would we want to pass such that that would be an obstacle, you know, and I think we should be pushing as much as we can through other means," Kim said.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Dems descend on Denver to size up 2028; we asked who wants in the race
summary: Josh Shapiro, Elissa Slotkin, Cory Booker and Ruben Gallego tested 2028 messaging at a Denver conference, and Chris Van Hollen bowed out early.
story: At the What’s Next gathering in Denver, Democratic leaders weighed the party’s future and whether they could see themselves in the 2028 presidential race.
DENVER — Democrats are already making their case for 2028.

Fresh off sweeping midterm victories, party leaders and rising stars descended on Denver for the What’s Next conference. Several potential presidential contenders tested their 2028 messaging before a crowd of activists, strategists and operatives.
The conversations offered an early look at who may be considering a run and who is already stepping aside.

Less than 24 hours after announcing a challenge to longtime Senate Democratic leader Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., told reporters he was "no longer pursuing" a presidential bid.
SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED

"I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people," Van Hollen told reporters in Denver, pointing to what will be at least a 55-seat Democratic majority in the chamber.
Van Hollen made the comments as Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., weighed whether to make another run for the White House in 2028.
'A lot of hard thought'
Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., is among the Democratic figures drawing attention as the party begins looking toward 2028. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)
Booker said he is giving "a lot of hard thought" to a potential 2028 presidential campaign, though he said his focus now is pushing for what he called an "American renewal."
"My purpose right now, I want to see America in the next five years have the biggest renewal, the biggest resetting of the economic table so it works for all Americans," Booker told Fox News Digital.
He pointed to the cost of housing, healthcare and childcare as evidence that many Americans are struggling to get ahead.
"The gap I’m concerned about is not the gap between left and right anymore. It’s a gap between the American people and the American dream, and I want to see that gap close," he said.

Asked what he might do differently if he ran again after his unsuccessful 2020 campaign, Booker said candidates should be "their authentic self." He also warned that political divisions are pulling the country apart, saying, "We are not each other’s enemies. We are our fellow patriots. And we all need to start pulling in the same direction."
'Won't have any news to make about that any time soon'

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020, said he would have no news about a potential 2028 bid "anytime soon." (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

While Van Hollen ruled out a presidential bid, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic candidate, told reporters in Denver he would not have "any news to make about that anytime soon."
Even so, Buttigieg has not ruled out another run.
'We'll let you know'

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a potential 2028 contender, said he wants to be "a loud voice" in shaping the Democratic Party’s future during the What's Next conference in Denver, Colo., Nov. 13, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, fresh off of major victories in his home state, said, "I've decided to be a loud voice in this process that we're going through right now as a party to put ourselves in the best position to compete."
When asked about his 2028 timeline, Shapiro said, "That would be a personal decision my wife and my kids and I make.
"When we're ready to say something, we'll let you know."
'I haven't made any decisions'
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., told reporters in Denver she is seriously considering a 2028 presidential run during the What's Next conference Nov. 13, 2026. (Jessica Sonkin/Fox News)
Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan told reporters she was "seriously" considering a 2028 presidential run.

"I haven't made any decisions. Whether it's me or somebody else, I just want to be a part of that next generation of leaders going forward that does things differently and understands who they serve," she added.
Pointing to a new crop of Democrats elected in the midterms, Slotkin said, "We had an amazing election night that elected a whole bunch of new folks who represent that."
'I have to figure out how to still be a good dad and run for office'

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said his young family will weigh heavily in his decision on whether to run for president in 2028. Gallego spoke to reporters on the sidelines of the What's Next conference in Denver. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)
Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona said his young family will be a major consideration in his decision.
"I have three kids — 9, 3 and a 1-year-old. You know, it's hard to manage that schedule, and I have to figure out how to still be a good dad and run for office," he said.
"If I run, I'll probably be the only one that has kids that age that doesn't necessarily come from a lot of money. So, I'm going to have to figure all that out."
THE MISTAKE NEWLY ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN’T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS
Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., who has not said whether he will seek the 2028 nomination, used his speech at What's Next to argue Democrats can build a winning coalition across the country.
"In America, all things are possible," he said, pointing to Democratic victories from New Hampshire to Mississippi.
'We've got a very talented field ... even if I do run'
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., said he is "certainly considering" a 2028 presidential run while speaking at the What’s Next conference in Denver Nov. 13, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)
California Rep. Ro Khanna said he is "certainly considering" a 2028 presidential run but has not made a decision.

Khanna, one of the few leaders on the progressive left attending a conference organized by a centrist Democratic group, added, "I think after the reception here, I'm more likely to consider it. I mean, but I'm going around the country seeing whether the message will resonate."
Asked about his timetable, Khanna told Fox News Digital, "I think, starting next year, people will be running."
"Imagine this: We’ve had three 80-year-old presidents in a row, and suddenly you’re going to have a new generation on both sides. I think that’s fantastic for this country," he said.
"I'm excited about some of the people if I do run who would be competitors. It’s going to be great. It’s going to showcase America’s talent."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
With no clear frontrunner in sight, the Denver conference offered an early look at Democrats testing their messages and weighing whether to seek the party’s nomination.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Dems' California redistricting mastermind flips script after helping party win 5 GOP seats: 'Kill'
summary: Paul Mitchell, architect of California's Prop 50, claims Democrats should establish national standards to end partisan gerrymandering for good.
story: Outgoing Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., says the GOP House delegation from his state is dropping to four or fewer seats out of 52 — less than 10% — despite 40-45% of the state’s voters being Republican, calling it pure gerrymandering.

The architect of California's Democratic-friendly redistricting plan, which helped the party flip five Republican-held House seats in November's midterm elections, is now calling on Democrats to put an end to partisan gerrymandering nationwide.
Paul Mitchell claimed in a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed published Wednesday that lawmakers should "kill partisan gerrymandering for good."

He made the comments after California voters approved Proposition 50 in November 2025, temporarily replacing the state's independently drawn congressional districts with a Democratic-friendly map for elections through 2030.
REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES

Mitchell acknowledged in his op-ed that Proposition 50 was designed to benefit Democrats but defended it as a temporary response to Republican-led redistricting efforts before calling for an end to partisan map making altogether.
"I wasn’t trying to do this [op-ed] to time with anyone’s efforts to do further gerrymandering," Mitchell told Fox News Digital Thursday evening.

"I always planned on doing this as soon as the election was over, and I even did a CNN interview with Elex Michaelson during the election coverage, where I said that the answer needs to be to stop this redistricting war and actually fix the problem.

Gov. Gavin Newsom spoke with supporters during a rally with the United Domestic Workers of America about the urgency of voting Nov. 1, 2025, in San Diego. (Nelvin C. Cepeda/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty)

"Prop 50 was the right response to what Republicans in Texas were doing, but recall that when Texas started doing this, our approach wasn’t to just start redistricting ourselves. We did a lot of work trying to get Texas to not start the redistricting wars," Mitchell told Fox News Digital.

"If then someone had said, "Congress will be banning mid-decade redistricting," we would have been all for it. And I supported the legislation by Zoe Lofgren that would have [set up] national redistricting standards."
Mitchell argued that Republicans' midterm losses could make them more receptive to redistricting reform after years of opposing it.

"What makes now really important is that Republicans, who have opposed redistricting reform, should now realize that they lost in this war, so getting out of future wars is something maybe they would take more seriously now," he told Fox News Digital.
As for California, Mitchell believes the Proposition 50 maps will remain in place through 2030 and said the focus should be on restoring a fairer redistricting process in 2031.
He called for Congress to prohibit mid-decade redistricting but argued that such a restriction alone would not prevent partisan gerrymandering when states redraw their maps after each census.
"I think the best solution would be independent commissions in every state," he said.

The California Democratic Party touted Prop 50 as a "direct response to a Republican power grab orchestrated by President [Donald] Trump and state leaders in Texas, who redrew congressional district lines to gain five more seats in the U.S. House of Representatives."
Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom similarly claimed in a Nov. 4, 2025 social media post that Prop 50 "is about standing up to bullies like Donald Trump."
Mitchell's recent op-ed also claims that gerrymandering can erode voters’ ability "to elect the candidates they prefer."
Democrats notably succeeded in flipping all five House seats in California targeted by the party's redistricting push in the November midterm elections, the AP reported Nov. 4.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks at a Yes On Prop 50 volunteer event at the LA Convention Center in Los Angeles. Voters approved the measure, which authorized temporary changes to congressional district maps. (Getty Images)
BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES
"The incoming Congress should make national redistricting a priority, establishing minimum standards for how all states draw their districts," Mitchell wrote in the opinion piece.
A voter marks a ballot in the Kern County Elections Office Nov. 3, 2026, in Bakersfield, Calif. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)
Mitchell serves as the vice president of Political Data Inc., a California-based bipartisan voter data firm. He is also the owner of Redistricting Partners, a Sacramento-based data consulting firm.

Mitchell, across his career, has conducted more than 100 redistrictings for states, cities, school boards and community college districts, including the State of New York Independent Redistricting Commission, the Los Angeles City Council Redistricting Commission and the Long Beach Independent Redistricting Commission, according to Redistricting Partners' website.

When asked about whether California's gerrymandered maps were necessary during a Nov. 8 interview on "California Politics 360," Mitchell said it would have been "a huge mistake" for Democrats to "sit" on their "laurels."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
After Democrats' sweeping victories in November's midterm elections, some states have floated redrawing their congressional maps ahead of the 2028 election cycle, Roll Call reported Nov. 9.

Outgoing Republican Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp said Nov. 4 he would not call a special legislative session to redraw congressional maps or limit the powers of the incoming governor before his term ends in January 2027, WABE reported.

"As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible and fair elections and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state," Kemp said in a statement.

title: Anti-Trump Republican courts other defectors as House weighs another vote against Iran war
summary: Thomas Massie says he's offering Republicans a "life boat from MAGA" as he prepares to push a new Iran War Powers resolution to the House floor.
story: Friction over foreign policy led President Donald Trump to remove JD Vance from negotiating with the Iranian regime. Marc Thiessen tells Stuart Varney that Vance's failure to support key decisions led to his swift dismissal as chief negotiator.

EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans and Democrats are preparing another effort to challenge President Donald Trump's military operations in Iran, with lawmakers signaling that additional Republicans could break with the president and support a War Powers resolution.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital that another Iran War Powers resolution could come to the House floor "in the next few legislative days" or around Christmas.
This would mark the fourth attempt this year to restrict Trump's military actions against Iran.
"I'm offering Republicans a lifeboat from MAGA," Massie told Fox News Digital, expressing optimism that more members of his party could join the effort.
7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS
Three more House Republicans joined Democrats in backing a resolution aimed at reining in President Donald Trump’s war powers during the conflict with Iran. (Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)

House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers, R-Ala., told Fox News Digital that he would oppose the resolution but acknowledged that "Massie has been having conversations with members" in an effort to secure additional Republican support.
Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., echoed Rogers' assessment, suggesting that "one or two" additional Republicans could join Massie and the Democrats who previously supported the measure.
SWING-DISTRICT REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP, PUSHES LIMITS ON IRAN WAR
Reps. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., previously voted in favor of an Iran War Powers resolution.
Barrett told Fox News Digital Thursday he would maintain his support if the new resolution mirrors the previous legislation.
"My position would be consistent for it," Barrett said.
However, Barrett expressed skepticism that additional Republicans would join the effort, noting that few members appeared willing to shift their positions during the previous vote.
GOP HOLDS WITH TRUMP ON IRAN WAR, BUT CRACKS EMERGE AS DEADLINE NEARS
Rep. Thomas Massie speaks with supporters after his concession speech on May 19, 2026, in Hebron, Ky. (Jon Cherry/Getty Images)
Massie also acknowledged uncertainty over whether he could secure more Republican votes, criticizing his party's continued support for Trump's military operations.
"Congress is paralyzed," Massie told Fox News Digital, accusing Republicans of remaining "still in the suicide pact with this administration."
TRUMP SUFFERS RARE HOUSE DEFEAT AS BIPARTISAN VOTE MOVES TO WITHDRAW TROOPS FROM IRAN CONFLICT
House Democrats, meanwhile, expressed optimism that Republicans' losses in the 2026 midterm elections could encourage more GOP lawmakers to break with Trump's foreign policy agenda.

"If they're listening to the people that sent them here, yes," Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., told Fox News Digital when asked whether additional Republicans could support the effort. "That's what they should do."
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., also expressed confidence that more Republicans could join the effort, saying she "thinks they would."

Meanwhile, Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., suggested Republicans may feel less pressure to remain aligned with Trump after the midterm elections, especially as many prepare to leave Congress and others hunker down to serve in the minority.

"The threat of Trump dumping a lot of money into Republican districts is over. Perhaps more members of Congress we think represent their communities will listen to what constituents are saying about the war," Grijalva told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES
U.S. Navy E/A 18G electronic-warfare aircraft patrol the skies over the Middle East as the U.S. military enforces a blockade of Iranian ports, according to CENTCOM. (CENTCOM)

The renewed effort comes as lawmakers continue debating Congress' constitutional authority over military operations and the president's ability to conduct sustained hostilities without congressional authorization.

Under the Constitution, Congress holds the power to declare war, while the president serves as commander in chief of the armed forces. The War Powers Resolution of 1973 establishes procedures and limits for military operations conducted without congressional authorization.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Despite growing discussions among lawmakers, no vote on an Iran War Powers resolution has been scheduled or confirmed.

title: Florida Republican on Democrats' strategy: 'That's the choice they have to make ... persecution or policy'
summary: Controversial Florida congressman says Democrats will choose to pursue persecution over policy but also signals a willingness to compromise, given the right conditions.
story: Florida Republicans warn Democrats are likely to focus on investigating Trump administration officials instead of addressing voters’ concerns.

Florida's Rep. Randy Fine has a blunt prescription for a House Republican conference staring down a steep Democratic majority in January: stop worrying about compromise, hand the minority gavel to Rep. Jim Jordan and start fighting, suggesting Democrats will likely pursue political persecution as the main focus in the next Congress.

In a wide-ranging interview with Fox News Digital, Fine, who expanded his own victory margin to 19 points even as Republicans lost control of the chamber, argued that voters punished the GOP not for its policies, but because they didn't see lawmakers willing to go to the mat for them.
For Fine, the message sent by Jordan's election is unambiguous.
Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., outside the U.s. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Dec. 18, 2025. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"Well, it says to me that we're ready to fight back. I mean, Jim Jordan has two unique qualifications for the job," Fine said.
‘HE BLAMED THE JEWS’: GOP CONGRESSMAN LEVELS EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATION AGAINST JD VANCE OVER ELECTION POSTMORTEM

"One, he's our best fighter. He protected and fought for President Trump during the ridiculous impeachments of President Trump's first term. He's just somebody who knows how to go into the arena and fight back.

"But the second thing is he's an extraordinary communicator. And over the next two years, we are in a very diminished minority. That's going to be our greatest strength is to point out why the Democratic policies won't actually improve anyone's lives, and to point out the policies that we would propose that will.
"So, as a fighter and a communicator, I think he's very well positioned to lead us for the next two years."
Fine downplayed policy as the primary driver of the disastrous 2026 blue tsunami.

"I don't know that we need to change our policies. And I don't even know how much of our messaging we need to change," he said. "What we need to do is we need to fight. I believe that we lost the election because voters thought we didn't care about their problems, because they didn't see us fighting to solve them.

"Voters will vote for you if they see you fighting, even if you fail. But they won't vote for you if they don't see you fighting. Now, I'm a guy who defied the odds. I increased my margin in the election. I may be the only Republican in the country to do that. I won my last election by 14. I won this one by 19."

With House Republicans shifting from passing bills to playing defense after electing Rep. Jim Jordan to succeed outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson as minority leader, Fine drew a sharp line between the two leadership roles.

"Well, it's a very different job. Look, I think if we kept the majority, I think Mike Johnson would still be the speaker. The speaker's job and the minority leader's job are completely different. So, Mike Johnson's job for the next 50-plus days is to try to get as many good things passed through the House as he can.
FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

"Jim Jordan's not going to be able to pass anything. The Democrats could have a 90- to 100-vote majority. His job is going to be to fight back when they're impeaching and they're interrogating and they are being vindictive, but also again to communicate why their policies will not make people's lives better.
Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, arrives for a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club June 10, 2025.  (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"They're going to come out and say Medicare-for-all. We're going to have to say, 'No, no there's no such thing. It's going to be Medicaid-for-all. When you give it to everyone, everyone will suffer. We'll end up like Canada, where there are death panels, or the UK, where you can wait a year or two to get to a doctor.'
"That's what we're going to have to do: fight back and communicate. That's a very different job than what Mike Johnson had to do the last two years."
Gridlock may be the persistent feature of the next Congress, but Fine does not completely discard the potential for compromise.

"Well, first off, compromise isn't inevitable," he said. "We may not do very much for the next two years. And I think that's the most likely outcome. Democrats pass ridiculous things, President Trump vetoes them and then we uphold the veto in the House and the Senate. I think that's the most likely outcome for the next two years.

"If it relates to compromise, you have to see what we're offered. So, for example, if Democrats would agree to voter ID, which is a huge thing the American people want, they might be able to extract a concession from us. If they're willing to stop so much of the ridiculous immigration into this country, they might be able to get concessions from us on other things. So, the problem is this: To Democrats, compromise means we give them what they want. It's always a one-way street.

"It's funny, when Democrats win, they say elections have consequences. When we win, they say we need to be bipartisan. And that's how their viewpoint is. They never come to our side of the world. So, I'll see if they want to compromise. I'll be open to it. But it will truly require us getting some of the things that we want that they have fought us on for the time I've been in Congress."
On foreign policy objectives, Fine points to several Democrats he's prepared to work with, while clarifying his position on Israel.

"Sure. I mean, look, in the Senate, you've got John Fetterman, who I think is an incredibly strong advocate for Western civilization. I don't think it's fair to say I'm an advocate for Israel. That makes it sound like I'm just an advocate for a country. It's more than that.
Sen. John Fetterman participates in a debate June 2, 2025, in Boston. (AP Photo/Steven Senne, File)
"The United States and Israel are the only two countries in the world that are unambiguously standing up to Muslim terror, which seeks to fundamentally redefine life for all of us around the world.

"So, I'm on the side of Western civilization, and John Fetterman embodies that in the Senate. I think you've got guys like Jared Moskowitz and Josh Gottheimer on the House side, on the Democratic side, who do as well. … Unfortunately, I think they're pretty outnumbered at this point, but if they want to fight with me, I'm happy to fight alongside them."
Finally, Fine contends that the Democrats face a clear dichotomy in how they want to proceed to govern, but argues they will likely make the wrong choice:
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The American people elected Democrats not because they wanted investigations and persecution. They elected Democrats because they didn't think we were solving their problems. If they make the mistake of going down the vengeance and persecution path, they'll end up in two years just the same way we did. If they try to solve the problems of the American people, they'll do well.

"The problem is their ideas don't work. Remember, the Affordable Care Act didn't make health care affordable. But if they try to do things that will help the American people, at least they'll be listening to them. But that's the choice they have to make. Persecution or policy. I think they're going to choose persecution, but we'll find out in a couple of months."
David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: GOP midterm bloodbath exposes cracks in Vance's 2028 White House ambitions
summary: Rep. Randy Fine compared JD Vance's post-midterm remarks on the Iran war to 1932 Germany, vowing he will not support a 2028 presidential bid.
story: President Donald Trump said he was fine with Vice President JD Vance's post-midterm critique on the political unpopularity of the Iran conflict, but he would have wanted to hear Vance add that if they had to do it again, they would.

Vice President JD Vance has long been viewed as President Donald Trump's heir apparent, but a string of developments following Republicans' bruising midterm losses is raising new questions about his potential path to the White House in 2028.
Vance is facing criticism from some Republicans over his explanation for the party's election defeats, particularly his decision to blame the Iran war.
Other prominent Republicans are beginning to draw support for potential 2028 bids, complicating the political picture for the vice president.
The political debate follows a devastating election for Republicans, who lost their majorities in both chambers of Congress beginning next year, with at least 30 GOP House members losing their races.
TRUMP SAYS HE DOESN’T DISAGREE WITH VANCE THAT IRAN WAR FUELED GOP LOSSES
The losses have prompted competing explanations from within the party over what went wrong and what Republicans should do differently.
Some of Vance's allies have reportedly urged him to consider sitting out the 2028 race after the midterm losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Nov. 7.
However, others close to the vice president still expect him to run, The Washington Post reported Friday, underscoring the uncertainty surrounding his political future.
Vice President JD Vance speaks during a press briefing at the White House in Washington, D.C., Sept. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

A Vance ally pushed back on suggestions that the midterm losses have diminished his 2028 prospects, saying the vice president will decide whether to run on his own timeline. The ally also argued that Vance would be better served by winning a competitive Republican primary than being handed the nomination, expressing confidence in his ability to prevail if he runs.

In a Nov. 4 post on X, Vance identified several concerns among voters who abandoned Republicans, including inflation, America First priorities and the U.S. relationship with Israel, but he singled out the Iran war as the main reason for the party's defeats.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote, adding that Republicans needed to acknowledge the political cost of the conflict as they consider where to go next.
The post drew sharp criticism from Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., who told Fox' LiveNOW in a Nov. 8 interview he would not support Vance in a potential 2028 presidential primary.
PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE OF VANCE'S IRAN WAR ASSESSMENT, BLAMES TRUMP POLICIES FOR GOP LOSSES
"I definitively will not be supporting the vice president in that nominating contest," Fine said, comparing Vance's remarks to rhetoric from "1932 Germany."

Fine, who is Jewish, accused Vance of blaming Jewish people for the Republican losses, pointing to his criticism of the war and the pollster's finding that some voters wanted a change in America's relationship with Israel.
Vance did not explicitly blame Jewish people in his post, and his office previously declined to respond to Fine's characterization.
Vice President JD Vance walks to board Air Force Two at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)
VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY

"The Vice President did not blame Jews for the Republican Party’s losses in the midterms," a spokesman for Vance told Fox News Digital on Saturday. "The Vice President has forcefully condemned antisemitism on countless occasions, and he will continue to do so."

Some Republicans are already expressing support for possible alternatives to Vance. Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital after the midterms he was "all in" for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, describing him as a potential unifying figure for Republicans after their election losses.
Rubio is among several prominent Republicans whose names have surfaced as possible 2028 presidential contenders, along with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas.
Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida (Alex Brandon/Pool via Reuters; Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Former Vice President Mike Pence also disputed Vance's explanation for Republicans' midterm losses, arguing in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview Thursday that voters had grown frustrated not because Trump launched the Iran war, but because his administration failed to finish it.

"There's no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn't because President Trump started the war or took on Iran. It's because we stopped short and didn't finish it," Pence said.

"As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became ... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump."
Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended Vance's assessment of the midterms, rejecting suggestions that the remarks damaged their relationship.
"No, not at all," Trump told reporters Sunday when asked whether Vance's comments had strained their relationship, according to The Hill.
But the president also stood by his decision to launch the war, arguing that he would make the same choice again despite the political fallout.
Donald Trump Jr. also backed Vance's assessment, writing, "Every word of this is [100 emojis]" in response to his Nov. 4 post on X.

On Thursday, Trump directed Vance to focus his attention on alleged corruption and crime in Democratic-led cities and states rather than pursuing negotiations with Iran, declaring that the United States no longer needed a deal with Tehran.
Vance had played a central role in diplomatic efforts involving Iran, including negotiations over a short-lived truce earlier this year.
Vice President JD Vance praised President Donald Trump's leadership style and work ethic during the interview. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters," Trump wrote in the post. "Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month. Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!
"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"
VANCE ‘PRIVATELY’ BLASTS NETANYAHU AS IRAN WAR DIVIDES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND 2028 AMBITIONS LOOM

Trump has previously signaled support for Vance as his potential successor, telling donors during an Oval Office meeting over the summer that Republicans needed to elect the vice president in 2028, Fox News Digital reported at the time.
But Trump has stopped short of publicly endorsing Vance, and the president has continued to leave open the possibility of other Republicans entering the race.

When asked on Nov. 4 whether he had talked about a prospective 2028 White House run with Vance, Trump replied that the two discuss "a lot of things," Axios reported. "Maybe he [Vance] won't run. I don't know who's going to run."
Still, Vance told Mark Halperin in an October interview that he believes Trump would back him if he jumps into the presidential race, ABC 7 reported.

"I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven't focused on it. We, you, and I have talked about that. Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me," Vance said during the interview.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital's Ashley DiMella and Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this story.

title: One industry increased DC lobbying 337% under Trump; here’s what’s driving the push
summary: Lobbying spending on tariff-related filings surged 337% in 2026 as businesses scrambled to navigate trade shifts, Advancing American Freedom found.
story: Trump’s escalating trade war with Canada could raise costs for businesses and consumers in key battleground states before voters head to the polls.
FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his trade agenda, and businesses are spending more on D.C. bureaucrats to help navigate those rules.

Rachel Greszler, who authored a new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF), said companies are paying lobbyists to seek exemptions from tariffs instead of using that money to expand their businesses, hire workers or raise wages.
A new report from former Vice President Mike Pence's group found that lobbying disclosures mention tariffs rising 239% in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2024.
The total spending reported on those filings jumped 337%, though it may include lobbying on issues beyond tariffs.
A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR

Businesses are increasingly turning to Washington lobbyists to navigate President Donald Trump’s shifting trade policies, with tariff-related lobbying disclosures surging 239% in the third quarter. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
"Affordability is top of mind for many Americans," Greszler told Fox News Digital, arguing that changing tariffs are raising costs, threatening jobs and squeezing paychecks.

Businesses are responding by stepping up their lobbying efforts. Fourteen organizations spent more than $1 million on lobbying in the third quarter, up from two in the same quarter of 2024. Another 105 spent more than $100,000, compared with 26 two years earlier.
Tariffs may also be affecting prices consumers pay.
TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS; NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK
FLOURISH NY FED TARIFFS CHART: 30552508
Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers estimated they added 2.9 percentage points to prices across the consumer goods they studied, including imported and U.S.-made products.
Greszler warned that small businesses unable to afford lobbyists to seek tariff exclusions could be forced to scale back or close.

Trump has defended tariffs as a central part of his trade agenda, arguing they will strengthen U.S. manufacturing and bring jobs and investment back to the country. The White House has also said foreign exporters will ultimately bear the cost.
FLOURISH TARIFF REVENUES CHART: 30871804

A separate analysis from Advancing American Freedom estimated tariffs resulted in about 75,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in their first year and up to 1 million fewer jobs nationwide than would have been expected under pre-tariff trends.
The group said manufacturing was among the hardest-hit sectors despite being a central target of the administration’s effort to bring factory work back.
Trade has been a central focus of the Trump administration, which has used tariffs to reshape U.S. trade relationships and encourage more manufacturing at home. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

The group also said U.S. trade with Canada fell by $50 billion, or 6.5%, before the latest round of Section 338 tariffs took effect. During that period, imports from other countries rose instead of U.S. manufacturing expanding.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As the administration continues to reshape trade policy, businesses will have to decide whether to keep spending on lobbyists and tariff planning or delay investments, hiring and expansion until the rules become clearer.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: GOP newcomer who toppled Cory Mills sets sights on fraud, inflation as he heads to Capitol Hill
summary: Rep.-elect Ryan Elijah, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital he wants to crack down on fraud and congressional insider trading after his midterm victory.
story: Reps. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio; Max Miller, R-Ohio; and Joe Wilson, R-S.C., reflect on GOP losses in the midterm elections and the Democratic flip in Ohio and South Carolina. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

EXCLUSIVE: Florida Republican Congressman-elect Ryan Elijah told Fox News Digital he is heading to Washington with an "appetite" to crack down on fraud and protect consumers and tackle inflation, while calling for bipartisan cooperation in the incoming Congress.
Elijah, a former Central Florida sports broadcaster, made his remarks amid heightened scrutiny of fraud involving taxpayer-funded federal programs across the country.
"I'm going to lean into consumer protection — that's something I fought for my whole life — and lean into fraud," Elijah told Fox News Digital.

"There is so much more Washington could do against fraud. I hope there is a bipartisan appetite on both sides to not only protect consumers but also target some of this fraud that is wasting so much of our tax dollars."
FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'
Former local TV news anchor Ryan Elijah unseated Rep. Cory Mills in a high-stakes Florida GOP primary race. (Mike McClain/Ryan Elijah for Congress)

The incoming Republican, who beat embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., in the Republican primary in August, expressed optimism that lawmakers from both parties could find common ground on addressing fraud and rising costs, arguing that voters sent a clear message during Tuesday's midterm elections.

Elijah said voters "made it loud and clear to both parties" that they "want change, they want inflation to come down and they want life to become a little easier. So, I think both parties need to look at that."
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS BY STATE

Elijah also emphasized that members of Congress represent "100% of the people in their district, not just 50%," arguing that bipartisan solutions are necessary to restore public trust and accountability in Washington.
Beyond fighting fraud, Elijah pledged to restore a spirit of public service to Congress, criticizing lawmakers who use their positions to enrich themselves.
"What you do see is the people that enhance themselves, and people don't want to see that. None of that should be taking place," Elijah said while discussing congressional insider trading.
A view of the east side of the U.S. Capitol Building Aug. 25, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"Members of Congress should not sit on a committee and be able to trade stocks, and that is something that I would support if it moves forward in the next Congress," he continued. "We all have to be on the same playing field, the person back home and the person on Capitol Hill."

Elijah outlined his preferred committee assignments, telling Fox News Digital he would like to serve on the House Energy and Commerce Committee or the House Financial Services Committee, where he could focus on consumer protection and financial oversight.
He also expressed interest in serving on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, describing it as "a great way to bring projects back to my district."
Elijah said his district has "so much growth ahead of us," arguing that a seat on the committee could help address its infrastructure needs.
The incoming lawmaker addressed the challenges Republicans face after losing control of Congress in the midterm elections, urging his party to remain united.
Republican House candidate Ryan Elijah, left, attends a UFL event. (Ryan Elijah campaign)
Elijah said Republicans must "hold the line" on the "progress we've made so far" while working to advance their priorities in a divided Washington.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Elijah is expected to be sworn into the 120th Congress in January.

title: Inside the House GOP strategy to capitalize on Democrats' warring factions in the new Congress
summary: Tom Emmer says House Republicans will use committee hearings and floor votes to hold Democrats accountable as the GOP shifts to minority status.
story: Incoming House Minority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., joins ‘The Ingraham Angle’ to discuss the GOP’s legislative priorities, efforts to support American manufacturing and whether Democrats will work with Republicans to advance their agenda.
EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans are heading into the next Congress ready to brawl.

Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., who will rise from the No. 3 most powerful House Republican to No. 2 next year, told Fox News Digital the GOP will hold the new Democrat majority "accountable" for the far-left faction's ideas over the next two years, even if it cannot control what bills get a vote.

Emmer, who has served as House majority whip the past four years, was elected Tuesday to serve as minority whip alongside incoming House Minority Leader Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. The speaker of the House position turns over to Democrats and will likely be won by current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.
And despite Jeffries being poised to take control of what legislation gets to the House floor, Emmer signaled House Republicans would find ways to push their agenda as well.
JIM JORDAN BECOMES NEW HOUSE GOP LEADER AFTER CLOSED-DOOR VOTE, DEFEATING STEVE SCALISE
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer speaks during a news conference after the House GOP elected new leadership on Capitol Hill Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"What's their answer to dealing with costs and wages? We're going to investigate Trump," Emmer said in reference to Democrats. "That's not going to solve the problems that they created. So, that's going to be the job of the whip, is to make sure that we have a coordinated process — committee hearings, floor votes — to expose and define exactly who these people really are."
PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES
Emmer, in his first print interview since winning the House minority whip job, would not go into detail about how Republicans would utilize floor votes, however.
"There's a toolbox with a bunch of different tools, and you're going to have to build that strategy as you go from week to week," he said.
The Minnesota Republican also signaled there would be little appetite for bipartisanship over the next two years, a sentiment he suggested would come from the other side of the aisle.
"Well, look, they're not going to work with us. That's pretty clear, and I don't even know if they're going to be able to work with each other," Emmer said.
HAKEEM JEFFRIES FACES PROGRESSIVE HOLDOUTS BUT NO RIVAL AS HOUSE SPEAKER RACE TAKES SHAPE

Congressman Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., address a news conference during the congressional delegation's visit to Denmark in Copenhagen April 25, 2025 (Emil Nicolai Helms/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)

"I see nowhere where they're going to work with Republicans. And Republicans who think they are should think again, because they will tell you nice things, and then they will just go do what they do."
Other House Republicans are already coming up with ideas on how to put Democrats on the spot on the House floor in the new Congress.
"We'll file amendments," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "And I think that'll be where having good debaters and communicators would be important."

Holding amendment votes is commonplace before large pieces of legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which Congress has enacted annually for decades to update and reauthorize critical national security policies.

Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., suggested an emphasis on a parliamentary procedure called the "motion to recommit," which allows the minority party to get a vote on altering or even killing a bill in its tracks.

"I expect we'll use that smartly," LaLota said. "But, as well, a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will be wise to work these problems backwards, to know that anything he puts on the floor that he wants to become law or budget needs President Trump's signature and probably 60 votes in the Senate."
Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., said "there's been a lot of conversation about going on offense."
"We want to make sure that they know when they come to the floor, they're gonna dread it, I hope," Harris said.
DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY
But there's another mechanism for forcing a House vote that's been used more and more often in recent years, often by their fellow Republicans.

Privileged resolutions allow lawmakers on either side to get a vote on a given bill within two days of its introduction. It generally begins with a procedural vote on whether to "table" the bill or refer it to committee to stop it before a vote on the measure itself.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., most recently invoked it to force the House to consider impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. But that was defeated when the rest of the House GOP banded together to refer the bill to committee.
The GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital, however, signaled little appetite for using it.

U.S. Rep. Jim Jordan speaks during a news conference after House Republicans elected new leadership for the upcoming session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"I think either party would be wise to build consensus around things that help actually deliver for the American people," LaLota said. "The privileged resolutions have been abused in my time here, and there's a better way to do business."
And Emmer said his main goal for the next two years would be winning back the House majority in 2028, which he insisted was a realistic goal.
He said at least 38 seats flipped by Democrats would be "ready to return to Republican hands" and could see some old faces return.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Asked whether he wanted to see some of those losing GOP incumbents run for their seats again, Emmer said, "I absolutely hope so. I've talked to several already."
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Trump keeps signaling an end to Iran war, but expert warns a crucial piece of his strategy is missing
summary: President Donald Trump declared on Truth Social the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran, one day after proclaiming victory at Arlington.
story: During a speech at Arlington National Cemetery Wednesday, President Donald Trump thanked U.S. service members for their ongoing sacrifices and argued that the U.S. has been pitted against Iran since 1979, when the Islamic Revolution happened.

President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, abruptly shifting his diplomatic message just three days after expressing optimism about negotiations and directing Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues instead.
"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

Trump's latest declaration came just one day after he proclaimed victory over Iran during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, while acknowledging that the conflict had not yet formally ended.
"We won," Trump said Wednesday. "It’s just a question of when we end it. I want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."
TRUMP DEFENDS IRAN WAR DURING VETERANS DAY ADDRESS, SAYS HE IS MAKING THE WORLD 'SAFER'

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a ceremony at Memorial Amphitheater at Arlington National Cemetery to mark Veterans Day Nov. 11, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
The president also thanked veterans "working to ensure the world’s No. 1 sponsor of state terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never have a nuclear weapon."

An administration official defended Trump's strategy, arguing the United States has substantial leverage over Iran through its naval blockade and continued military pressure, even as questions remain about how the conflict will end.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The president has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue with full effect," a U.S. official told Fox News Digital.
"President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States and will make sure that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."
Trump's latest words follow months of predictions that an agreement could be reached soon, including comments earlier this week that Tehran "would love to make a deal."

Trump's declaration raises questions about the future of U.S.-Iran negotiations, including whether diplomatic efforts will continue through other administration officials as Washington maintains its military and economic pressure on Tehran.
AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?
An Iranian flag is displayed at Iran's Bushehr nuclear power plant during an official ceremony on Nov. 10, 2019, to kick-start work on a second reactor at the facility.   (AFP via Getty Images)
Trump has suggested on at least a dozen occasions since February that Iran wanted to negotiate or that an agreement could be reached soon, according to a preliminary review of his public remarks.

Ludovic Hood, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said the administration's combination of economic coercion, military force and regional partnerships is sensible but warned that a crucial diplomatic component remains underdeveloped.

"What’s lacking is disciplined diplomacy to complement the economic squeeze and possible airstrikes," Hood told Fox News Digital. "Our Gulf partners are singing from different hymn sheets, and we need to draw European partners in more meaningfully."

Trump's optimistic assessments began before U.S. military operations against Iran commenced. On Feb. 13, he suggested Tehran could avoid an attack by accepting Washington's terms. After military operations began, he increasingly emphasized Iran's weakened capabilities and the prospect of ending the conflict.
IRANIAN NEGOTIATORS KICKED OUT OF US AS TALKS STALL, TRUMP LAYS OUT 'POSSIBLE' TIMELINE FOR MORE STRIKES
President Donald Trump arrives to deliver remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., Nov. 2, 2026. (Umit Bektas/Reuters)
On March 20, Trump said the United States was "getting very close" to achieving its military objectives.

The administration agreed to a ceasefire in April and continued pursuing a diplomatic settlement, but subsequent military actions and disagreements over Iran's nuclear program and regional shipping have left the broader conflict unresolved.
Trump continued expressing confidence that Iran wanted an agreement, including in May, when he suggested Tehran was eager to negotiate because of the damage inflicted on its military.

During an unscheduled appearance in the White House briefing room Monday, Trump said, "Iran, militarily, is effectively over," while warning that U.S. forces remained "locked and loaded" should circumstances change.
Hood said Trump's seemingly contradictory messages could be part of a deliberate negotiating strategy.
"The administration is pursuing a sensible hybrid strategy of economic coercion, selective use of force and reliance on capable regional allies," Hood said.
TRUMP SAYS IRAN IS 'NEGOTIATING ON FUMES,' BELIEVES REGIME THOUGHT THEY COULD OUTWAIT HIM
Senior military leaders listen as U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks at Marine Corps Base Quantico Sept. 30, 2025, in Quantico, Va. (robynmac)
"Trump’s messaging seems designed to both signal his preference for a diplomatic solution while preserving the option of force."
Hood defended the president's willingness to maintain military pressure.
"Bluster, bluffing and brinkmanship are inherent in the public dimension of negotiations like this; Trump does it, Rubio does it and senior figures in Tehran do it," he said.
"Strategic patience is essential in this standoff, which has essentially been 40 years in the making."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
But Hood also suggested that securing meaningful nuclear concessions or a more cooperative government in Tehran would require coordination with regional partners.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Socialist LA mayor's bold homelessness promise ahead of 2028 Olympics hit with reality check: 'Not optimistic'
summary: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman pledges to halve homeless encampments before the 2028 Olympics, but a local activist warns it won't work.
story: John Alle, co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition, spoke to Fox News Digital about potential gaps in incoming Mayor Nithya Raman's plan to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least 50% before the 2028 Olympics.

Incoming Los Angeles Mayor Nithya Raman has promised to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and homeless encampments by at least 50% before the 2028 Summer Olympics, but one local activist believes her vision may not be realistic.

The blue city’s growing homeless population became a major focus of Raman’s mayoral campaign. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), she plans to expand shelter and housing options while stretching "every dollar as far as possible."

John Alle, a business owner and co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition, told Fox News Digital Raman won’t be able to "hide" the city’s homelessness problem from tourists arriving for the Games and raised concerns about potential gaps in her plan to deliver lasting results.
"I don't think we're going to be able to hide that before the crowds," Alle said, adding that the city has become a "Third World country."
4 OF NATION'S LARGEST CITIES NOW LED BY SOCIALIST MAYORS AFTER TUESDAY'S ELECTION, AFFECTING TENS OF MILLIONS

John Alle, co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition, told Fox News Digital he has concerns that incoming Mayor Nithya Raman's homelessness plan could be a temporary fix ahead of the 2028 Olympics. (Mario Tama/Getty Images; Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

"We're not hiding it now. We're seeing tourists being attacked in Santa Monica. We're seeing tourists being attacked in LA. Our tourism, everything that funds our general fund, our retail sales taxes are all down. The morale of the police, which we need, is down."
Alle warned that Raman’s plan will be a temporary solution that will move homeless people off the streets ahead of the Olympics, and they'll return once the Games are over.
"When the Olympics come, they'll be picked up, they'll be bussed, they’ll be sent elsewhere, and they'll wander right back after the three-week Olympic and Paralympic events."

Former Mayor Karen Bass accepted the Olympic flag during the closing ceremony in Paris two years ago, marking the handoff of hosting duties. This will be the first time LA has hosted the Games since 1984.
According to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority’s 2026 annual count, homelessness rose 3.4% in LA and 1.2% across the broader LA area, undoing two consecutive years of declines under Bass.
But how does Raman plan to follow through on that promise?

Raman has pledged to expand housing, shelter capacity and rental assistance to eliminate long-term encampments by the end of her first term. Raman has previously called the city's "desensitization to homelessness" a "moral failing." Her plan calls for sending medical teams directly into encampments to provide mental health and addiction treatment and help with transitions into long-term housing or care within 90 days.

Raman has also criticized Bass' Inside Safe program, which often places homeless people in costly hotels and motels. Instead, Raman wants to shift funding toward less expensive alternatives, like rental vouchers.
SEATTLE MAYOR KATIE WILSON'S SOCIALIST AGENDA STALLS AMID HOMELESSNESS AND PUBLIC SAFETY CONCERNS
A woman pushes a stroller past a homeless encampment on Cesar E. Chavez Avenue in downtown Los Angeles Aug. 21, 2026. (Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Other parts of Raman’s proposal include sending unarmed crisis response teams rather than police officers to certain emergencies, auditing stalled housing projects and increasing oversight of homelessness spending.
Despite Raman’s ambitious vision, Alle said he isn't convinced her plan will bring meaningful change and argued that city leadership has gone "from bad to worse."
"It's not that much different than Mayor Karen Bass's plan," Alle said.

Alle, who manages roughly 1 million square feet of commercial property across Los Angeles, said he sees the homelessness crisis firsthand and raised concerns about its impact on local businesses and workers.
He warned that treating homeless people on the streets will only prolong the crisis, saying that many Angelenos avoid parts of the city that have been left untouched.
"Pick up the individuals and take them to their facilities away from the parks, away from kids, away from seniors," he said.
Alle said there must be more transparency over how the city has handled more than $1 billion in homelessness funding before allocating more taxpayer dollars.
"She’s got a billion-dollar problem on her hands right now, and she knows," he said.
FURIOUS RESIDENTS CONFRONT HOMELESS HOUSING LEADERS AS POPULAR BEACH COMMUNITY HITS BREAKING POINT
Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman, left, talks with Mayor Karen Bass, right, at Hazeltine Park in Sherman Oaks on Feb. 10, 2024. (Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Raman chaired the City Council's Housing and Homelessness Committee from 2023 until her removal this year amid her mayoral campaign. Alle said Raman will have to explain where the money went but acknowledged her push to investigate the spending.
"To her credit, she wants to audit every single nonprofit and every single agency that spent money, including the nonprofits that are supported by the city with taxpayer funds for programs," he said.
One of the biggest red flags in Raman’s plan is the proximity of supportive housing to families and children, according to Alle. He added that some facilities don't require residents to remain sober.
"There is no commitment for anyone not to use drugs while they're there," he said.
Pointing to her past opposition to restrictions on camping in public spaces and near schools, Alle argued Raman's approach isn’t "aggressive enough."
"I don't see the solutions that have been put forth that could work being used, and, so, I'm not optimistic," he said.
Alle described LA as having a drug and mental health problem, not a homelessness problem. He said the city needs to stop making life on the streets more comfortable for those who refuse help.
"Until those two issues are addressed, we're not gonna solve homelessness," he said.
He urged Raman to find a more practical solution by moving outreach services off the streets and ending LA's sanctuary city status for good.
"Of course, I want her to succeed," he said. "If Nithya succeeds, we all succeed."
Raman ousted Bass in the midterm elections and will take office in December as mayor of Los Angeles, a city of roughly 4 million residents.
