title: Instagram's AI may catch teens lying about their age
summary: Meta's AI age-estimation technology now scans Instagram accounts worldwide, placing millions of teens into stricter safety settings automatically.
story: Bipartisan state coalition secures a historic agreement as Meta agrees to a landmark $16B+ social media addiction settlement. Claudia Cowan reports on the sweeping safety changes mandated the federal court. The social media giant must implement strict daily time limits, overnight blocks and robust age verification tools for teen users on Instagram and Facebook.

My own niece has told me for years that she and her friends could get around age restrictions on Facebook and Instagram when they were younger. They knew how easy it was to make themselves appear older online. And I suspect plenty of parents have heard similar stories. So when I heard that Meta was expanding its AI technology to identify teens who lie about their age, my first thought was, it's about time.

On November 9, Meta announced a worldwide expansion of its AI age-estimation technology. The system looks for accounts that may belong to teenagers, even when someone has entered an adult birthday. Meta says the expansion will place millions more young users into Instagram's built-in Teen Account protections.

The move comes as lawsuits and growing public pressure push Meta to take greater responsibility for protecting young users. After years of concerns about children getting around social media age restrictions, this could be one of the company's most significant attempts yet to address the problem. But how does Instagram's AI figure out someone's age? And can parents trust it to get things right?

FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15
Meta is expanding AI age checks on Instagram to identify teens who may have entered an adult birthday to bypass safety restrictions. (Javier Zayaz/iStock)
How Instagram AI age checks work

For years, entering a birthday was one of the easiest ways to tell Instagram how old you were. The problem was that the app had to rely heavily on what someone told it. Now Meta is using artificial intelligence to look for clues that suggest an account belongs to someone under 18. Instead of relying solely on the birthday listed on a profile, the company's age-estimation technology analyzes account activity and other signals to estimate whether someone may be a teenager.

Meta has previously explained that its age-detection technology can look for clues such as birthday celebrations, references to school grades and information shared in posts or comments. The company has also described separate technology that analyzes photos and videos to help identify accounts belonging to children under 13. According to the company, that technology examines general visual clues without using facial recognition or identifying specific people.

The important thing to understand is that these systems estimate age. They don't establish someone's exact birthday. If Instagram's AI determines that an account likely belongs to someone between 13 and 17, the company can automatically apply Teen Account protections. That means a teenager who entered an adult birthday could suddenly find their account operating under stricter safety settings.
What happens when Instagram identifies a teen?

Instagram's Teen Accounts have been around since 2024. However, those protections depend on the platform correctly identifying younger users. The new worldwide expansion is designed to close that gap. When Meta identifies an account that likely belongs to a teenager, it can apply safeguards that include:

Stronger privacy: Teen Accounts generally start with private settings that restrict who can see posts and interact with an account.Messaging restrictions: Instagram limits direct messages to people a teen follows or already has a connection with.Content filtering: The platform reduces exposure to sensitive material and places teens into age-appropriate content settings.Limits on unwanted interactions: Instagram restricts who can tag or mention teens and filters potentially offensive comments.Time management tools: Teen Accounts include usage reminders and overnight notification restrictions, with additional limits available through parental supervision.
Stronger privacy: Teen Accounts generally start with private settings that restrict who can see posts and interact with an account.
Messaging restrictions: Instagram limits direct messages to people a teen follows or already has a connection with.
Content filtering: The platform reduces exposure to sensitive material and places teens into age-appropriate content settings.
Limits on unwanted interactions: Instagram restricts who can tag or mention teens and filters potentially offensive comments.
Time management tools: Teen Accounts include usage reminders and overnight notification restrictions, with additional limits available through parental supervision.

Teens under 16 generally need parental permission to make built-in safety settings less restrictive. Instagram has also introduced 13+ content settings inspired by PG-13 movie ratings. Those filters are designed to reduce the amount of mature material younger users encounter.

We previously covered how Instagram's PG-13 restrictions give parents more control over what teens see. Of course, no content filter catches everything. And these protections can only help if Instagram correctly identifies the accounts that need them.
ROBLOX SHARES AI CHILD-SAFETY TOOLS PARENTS SHOULD KNOW
Instagram's Teen Account protections include stricter privacy settings and controls over who can interact with younger people on the platform. (Getty Images)
Instagram's AI age checks are going worldwide

Meta began testing AI technology to identify teens using adult birthdays in the United States in April 2025. The company later expanded the system to additional countries, including Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom. In May 2026, Meta announced further expansion into the European Union and Brazil. Now the technology is going global.

According to Meta, millions more teens will receive additional safety protections, even if they originally claimed to be adults. The company is also expanding age-detection technology on Facebook, with a similar rollout planned for Threads later in 2026.

Meanwhile, Meta says it has started using Apple's age-range signal in Australia. With the right permissions, Apple's system can share someone's age range with participating apps. That gives Meta another way to check whether someone meets an app's age requirements. The big question is whether all this technology will finally make it harder for kids to get around the rules.
Why Meta is finally getting serious about teen safety

The timing of this announcement is worth paying attention to. For years, parents and child safety advocates have raised concerns about social media platforms and their effects on young users. Meanwhile, Meta has faced lawsuits alleging that its platforms contribute to harmful experiences for children and teenagers. Meta reportedly reached settlements worth up to approximately $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August 2026. The agreements address lawsuits brought by attorneys general over alleged harm to teens. Under those agreements, Meta committed to strengthening how it identifies teenagers and children younger than 13.

The settlement also includes stronger controls for teens in participating U.S. jurisdictions, including a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram that requires parental permission to disable. Additional provisions address nighttime access and parental oversight. Those commitments are separate from the new worldwide AI expansion, although they reflect the broader pressure Meta faces.

And there's an important point here. Meta has known for years that younger users sometimes enter false birthdays. The challenge has been figuring out how to identify them reliably. The company has introduced safety features over time. But public criticism and legal action have increased the pressure to show that those features actually work. Meta's latest announcement suggests the company is putting more resources behind age detection. The results will determine whether this becomes a meaningful turning point. We reached out to Meta for comment on its expanded AI age checks, but did not hear back before our deadline.
Could Instagram's AI get someone's age wrong?

That's another concern worth examining. AI can make mistakes, particularly when it tries to draw conclusions from someone's online activity. An adult might regularly post photos of younger relatives. Someone could also share old school pictures or birthday celebrations from years ago. That doesn't mean one post will automatically convince Instagram that an adult is a teenager. Meta uses multiple signals when making age estimates. However, mistakes remain possible.

Meta says people who are incorrectly placed into Teen Account settings can take steps to verify their age and restore the appropriate settings. Depending on the situation, Instagram may require proof of age through identification or an age-estimation service. And there's another side to the problem. The technology could miss teenagers who successfully make their accounts appear to belong to adults.

That's why parents should still review their children's account settings rather than assuming Instagram has correctly identified their age. Meta's November 9 announcement did not provide a new accuracy figure for the worldwide expansion. I'd like to see more information about how often the system gets these decisions right and how quickly people can correct mistakes.
CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS
Meta's AI age-estimation technology will not predict an exact birthday, but it will determine whether a user is likely within the teenage age range. (Getty Images)
What parents can expect from Meta

Starting in November 2026, Meta says parents in the United States will begin seeing an informational video in their Instagram feeds. The video will explain how Meta identifies teenagers and places them into age-appropriate protections. It will also link to guidance from internet safety advocate Larry Magid, president and CEO of ConnectSafely.

The guidance explains Meta's approach to identifying younger users and how parents can help ensure their children's ages are accurate. Parents worldwide can also access age-assurance resources through Meta's Family Center. For families, this creates an opportunity to have a conversation about why social media platforms ask for someone's age in the first place.
Tips to help keep your teen safer on Instagram
Even with stronger AI protections, I wouldn't leave everything up to Instagram. There are several practical steps parents can take right now.

Ask your teen to open Instagram and go to their profile. Tap the menu, open Accounts Center, then look for Personal details and Birthday. Make sure the birthday is accurate. Instagram may require verification if someone attempts to change an account's age from under 18 to an adult age.

Open Instagram's settings and look for the account privacy controls. Check whether the account is private and review who can follow your teen. Also review who can send messages. You may find that some protections are already enabled through Teen Accounts.

Instagram's Family Center gives parents additional tools for managing a teen's experience. Parental supervision requires both the parent and teen to agree to the connection. Once connected, parents can review available safety controls and manage certain account restrictions.

Instagram offers daily usage reminders and additional restrictions for teens. Parents can also use supervision settings to manage screen time. On an iPhone, open Settings, then Screen Time to review available app limits. For Android devices, Google Family Link offers parental controls and device management options.

Instagram's 13+ content setting is designed to limit material that may be inappropriate for teenagers. Parents can review these protections and choose stricter settings where available. Remember that filters may still miss content, so it's worth asking your teen what regularly appears in their feed.

This may be the most useful step. Ask your teen whether they have ever felt tempted to enter an older birthday to unlock features or avoid restrictions. Explain that providing the correct age helps Instagram apply protections intended for younger users. And make sure they know they can talk to you if they encounter something uncomfortable online.
Kurt's key takeaways

It's about time. My own niece told me years ago how easily she and her friends could get around the age restrictions on Facebook and Instagram. And I remember wondering why these platforms weren't doing more about it. Now, with lawsuits mounting and public pressure growing, Meta is finally taking a bigger step to address the problem. I'm glad to see it, but I want to know how well this AI actually works. Will it catch teens who lie about their age? And what happens when it gets someone's age wrong? Parents have been asking for better protections for years. It's time for Meta to show that these changes are making kids safer online.

Do you think Meta would be taking these steps without years of public pressure and lawsuits, or has the company finally realized it needs to do more to protect children online? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Health insurance scams to watch for during open enrollment
summary: The FTC sent warning letters to 25 companies over misleading health insurance ads as open enrollment brings a surge of deceptive offers online.
story: CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz discusses his efforts to crack down on health and senior care fraud on ‘Hannity.’

If you've been shopping for health insurance lately, you've probably noticed the ads popping up everywhere. Some promise surprisingly low monthly payments. Others claim you'll qualify for generous benefits or even receive cash rewards for signing up. And with open enrollment underway, those offers can be awfully tempting. But here's what worries me. You could enroll in what looks like a great health insurance plan, only to discover that it barely covers your medical bills when you actually need care.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is now warning about misleading health insurance advertising, including plans that promise comprehensive coverage but deliver far less. Some offers promote medical discount programs rather than traditional insurance. Others may come from scammers impersonating government agencies or familiar insurance companies. With Americans reviewing their coverage for 2027, knowing how to recognize health insurance scams could save you from a very expensive mistake.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
TRUMP ADMIN CRACKS DOWN ON ESTIMATED $10 BILLION IN OBAMACARE FRAUD, BOOTS MILLIONS FROM ROLLS
Before signing up for health insurance, make sure you understand exactly what your plan covers so you don't face unexpected medical bills. (Nansan Houn/Getty Images)
FTC warns 25 companies about misleading health insurance ads

Recently, the FTC announced it was sending warning letters to 25 companies that market healthcare plans or generate sales leads for insurance-related products. The agency identified several advertising practices that could violate federal law. These include misrepresenting a plan's benefits, hiding important costs or falsely suggesting that a limited-benefit product provides comprehensive medical coverage. The FTC also raised concerns about advertisements promising free offers, cash rewards or rebates that people may never receive.

Now, there's an important detail here. The FTC says the warning letters do not accuse any of the 25 companies of wrongdoing. Instead, the agency is reminding businesses about advertising laws and warning that it continues to monitor the market. Officials also indicated that additional letters could follow.

Still, the timing deserves attention. Open enrollment brings a surge of legitimate advertising from insurance providers. Unfortunately, it also gives dishonest marketers and scammers another opportunity to reach people looking for affordable healthcare.
How fake health insurance ads can fool you

Let's say you're searching online for a more affordable health insurance plan. You type a few words into Google and see a sponsored result offering excellent coverage at a price that seems almost impossible to beat. The website looks professional. It might display a familiar logo or suggest a connection to a government program. You click through and enter your phone number to learn more. Before long, someone calls with an offer. They tell you that you qualify for special coverage and encourage you to sign up immediately. You may even hear that the deal expires today.

Here's where things can get tricky. The website might belong to a lead-generation business collecting information for insurance sellers. Lead generation itself is a legitimate practice, but misleading advertisements can send people toward products they never intended to buy. The FTC warns that scammers sometimes purchase search advertisements that imitate official websites. Some use addresses resembling HealthCare.gov or Medicare.gov. Others copy recognizable branding to create the appearance of legitimacy.

We've seen similar tactics with financial scams. CyberGuy previously reported on criminals buying Google ads to steal bank logins. In those cases, sponsored search results directed people to convincing fake banking websites. The same underlying trick can work with health insurance. When an advertisement appears near the top of your search results, it's easy to assume the company behind it has already been checked out. But a paid placement offers no guarantee that the seller or its claims are trustworthy.
The cheap health insurance plan that could cost you thousands

One of the FTC's biggest concerns involves products that look like comprehensive health insurance but offer limited protection. For example, some advertisements promote medical discount programs. You pay a fee and receive access to discounts from participating healthcare providers. While legitimate discount programs exist, they don't provide the same financial protection as comprehensive insurance.

Other products, such as fixed indemnity plans, may pay a predetermined amount when you receive certain medical services. Depending on the policy, that payment could fall far short of your actual bill. Think about what happens if you suddenly need emergency surgery. You might expect your insurance to help cover the expense. Instead, you discover that your plan pays only a limited benefit, leaving you responsible for a substantial portion of the charges.

That possibility makes understanding your coverage so important. Plans sold through the official Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace must cover essential health benefits, including emergency services and hospitalization. They also provide coverage for preexisting conditions. However, deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs can still apply.

You can review those protections directly through HealthCare.gov's explanation of Marketplace benefits at healthcare.gov/coverage/what-marketplace-plans-cover. Before purchasing any plan, ask exactly what type of coverage you're getting. A low monthly premium means very little if the policy leaves you exposed to major medical expenses.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
Scammers use misleading online ads and fake health insurance websites to trick people into sharing personal information or purchasing inadequate coverage. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why health insurance robocalls should raise suspicion

Have you ever answered your phone and heard a recorded message claiming you've been approved for an affordable health insurance plan? Maybe the recording tells you that you qualify for special benefits. It might even suggest that you're running out of time to claim them. Be skeptical.

The FTC's October 29 consumer warning specifically highlights illegal prerecorded telemarketing calls promoting health insurance. Unsolicited recorded insurance sales calls deserve particular caution. They may come from scammers or businesses using questionable marketing practices.

And don't assume a familiar name on your caller ID proves anything. Scammers can manipulate caller ID information to make calls appear to come from legitimate organizations. If you receive an unexpected insurance sales call, hang up. Then contact the insurer through a phone number you've independently verified.
Tips to protect yourself from health insurance scams
You don't need to become an insurance expert to avoid misleading offers. However, a few simple precautions can help you make a more informed decision before committing to a plan.

The safest starting point for comparing ACA Marketplace coverage is HealthCare.gov. You can also call the Marketplace directly at 1-800-318-2596. If your state operates its own Marketplace, the federal website can direct you there. Avoid starting your search through an unfamiliar advertisement or a link someone sends you unexpectedly. Typing the official website address into your browser gives you greater control over where your information goes.

A sponsored result means an advertiser paid for placement. It doesn't mean the government has approved the company or verified every claim in the advertisement. Check the website address before entering personal information. Watch for misspelled domains or websites that imitate official government branding. If something looks suspicious, close the page and navigate directly to the organization you're trying to reach.

Before enrolling, request the plan's Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC) when applicable. This document explains important costs and coverage details in a standardized format. Pay particular attention to deductibles and out-of-pocket limits. Check whether your doctors participate in the plan's network. Also, make sure the policy covers the medications or treatments you need. You can learn more about these documents through HealthCare.gov's Summary of Benefits and Coverage guide at healthcare.gov/health-care-law-protections/summary-of-benefits-and-coverage/.

The FTC specifically warns about misleading offers that promise cash rewards or other incentives for enrolling in healthcare plans. Now, legitimate Marketplace financial assistance does exist. Depending on your eligibility, premium tax credits can reduce what you pay for coverage. However, that assistance follows established eligibility rules. If someone promises guaranteed cash simply for signing up or refuses to explain the terms, take a closer look before providing personal information.

If you're considering a plan sold outside the official Marketplace, contact your state's insurance department. Ask whether the company and agent are properly licensed and whether the product provides the coverage being advertised. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners provides resources to help you find your state insurance regulator. Also, be cautious about anyone pressuring you to enroll immediately. Legitimate insurers should provide the information you need to review a policy before purchasing it.
FAKE SOCIAL SECURITY STATEMENT EMAIL HIDES A SCAM
Reviewing health insurance benefits and costs carefully during open enrollment can help you avoid misleading offers and expensive surprises. (iStock)

Health insurance applications can require sensitive information. That makes fake enrollment websites particularly dangerous. Never provide your Social Security number or banking details to someone who contacts you unexpectedly unless you've independently verified their identity and the reason they need the information. If you're unsure about an offer, contact the insurance company directly. You can also find trained Marketplace enrollment assistance through HealthCare.gov's official help page at healthcare.gov/find-assistance/.

Scammers may use fake health insurance websites, phishing emails or text messages to trick you into clicking malicious links. Strong antivirus software can help detect dangerous websites and block malware that could steal your passwords or personal information. Some security tools can also warn you about suspicious links before you open them. While antivirus protection can't tell you whether an insurance policy provides legitimate coverage, it adds another layer of protection when you're shopping online. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.

Health insurance scams can expose some of your most sensitive information, including your Social Security number and financial details. An identity theft protection service can monitor for signs that criminals are misusing your information and alert you to suspicious activity. Some services also provide assistance if your identity is stolen. Keep in mind that these services can't prevent every type of fraud. If you've already shared sensitive information with a scammer, visit IdentityTheft.gov to learn what steps to take. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com.

If you create an account to compare or manage health insurance coverage, protect it with a strong, unique password. A password manager can help you create and store passwords without reusing them across multiple websites. Also, enable two-factor authentication (2FA) whenever it's available. That extra security step can make it harder for someone to access your account if your password gets stolen.
Important health insurance enrollment dates for 2027

If you're reviewing health insurance for next year, knowing the enrollment deadlines can also protect you from misleading sales pitches. According to the current HealthCare.gov enrollment calendar, federal Marketplace open enrollment for 2027 coverage began November 1, 2026, and ends January 15, 2027. However, there's another important deadline. To have your Marketplace coverage begin January 1, 2027, you generally need to enroll by December 15, 2026, and pay your first premium. Enrollments completed from December 16 through January 15 generally begin February 1, provided the first premium is paid.

Some state-operated Marketplaces may have different dates, so check your state's official website. Medicare operates on a separate schedule. Its annual open enrollment period runs from October 15 through December 7, 2026, for coverage changes taking effect January 1, 2027. If you're comparing Medicare plans, visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). Knowing these dates makes it easier to question someone who calls with a supposedly urgent deadline that doesn't match the official schedule.
What to do if you've already responded to a suspicious insurance offer

Maybe you've already clicked an advertisement or spoken with someone about a plan that now seems questionable. Perhaps you've even paid an enrollment fee. The first thing I recommend is verifying whether you actually have insurance coverage. Contact the insurance company directly using its official phone number. Ask for confirmation of your policy and request written information explaining your benefits.

If you shared financial information with a suspicious seller, contact your bank or credit card company. Explain what happened and ask about protecting your account or disputing unauthorized charges. And if you provided sensitive identifying information to someone you suspect was a scammer, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance on protecting yourself.

You can also report misleading health insurance advertisements and illegal robocalls to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The sooner you investigate a suspicious transaction or possible identity theft, the more options you may have to limit the damage.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about these health insurance offers is how easily someone could believe they're protected when they're actually facing an enormous financial risk. Think about it. You pay your monthly bill, receive something that looks like an insurance card and assume you're covered. Then a medical emergency happens, and suddenly you discover your plan has serious limitations. That's a frightening position to be in, especially when medical expenses can add up so quickly. I also think this FTC warning says something important about how we shop online. We've become accustomed to seeing sponsored results at the top of our searches. But the company willing to pay for that placement may have little to do with the organization we're actually trying to reach. When it comes to health insurance, I would always start with the official Marketplace or a company I've independently verified. And before signing anything, I want to know exactly what happens if I end up in the emergency room. That's the question that can reveal whether a seemingly affordable plan will actually protect you.

title: Is AI deciding who's dangerous in Michigan prisons?
summary: Michigan's new prison scoring system claims 30% better violence prediction, but Recidiviz says it doesn't actually use AI to classify inmates.
story: Incarcerated men participate in employment counseling at a Michigan prison, where security classifications can affect access to job training and educational opportunities. (Michigan Department of Corrections)

What if a computer-generated score could influence whether someone lives in a low-security prison dorm or a tightly controlled cell? Michigan is preparing to test new technology that could affect exactly that.

State officials say the system could improve predictions of future prison violence by approximately 30%. That's a big claim, especially when the safety of correctional officers and incarcerated people could depend on getting those assessments right.

But there's something important missing from early reports about Michigan prison AI. Despite headlines suggesting artificial intelligence will determine how dangerous someone might be, the nonprofit developing the software says AI plays no role in calculating security scores.

Instead, the technology follows predetermined rules, and corrections staff make the final decisions. So, how does the system work? And can Michigan really predict prison violence more accurately without putting too much trust in a computer-generated score?
FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH

No technical experience is needed.

Why security levels can change life behind bars

The Michigan Department of Corrections oversees approximately 32,000 incarcerated people statewide. Currently, corrections employees use a manual scoring process to determine the appropriate security level for each person. Those classifications influence where someone lives and how closely they're supervised. They can also affect access to educational programs and job training opportunities. For someone serving a lengthy sentence, a change in security level can make a significant difference in daily life.

Michigan has four general population security levels: I, II, IV and V. Level I generally allows greater freedom of movement, while Level V involves much tighter supervision. People at lower security levels may have access to more vocational training and higher education opportunities. However, Michigan says programs such as Violence Prevention Programming remain available at every general population security level. There is no general population Level III. Now, the state wants a better way to determine which security level fits each person's current behavior and needs.
What Michigan's new scoring system will change

The Michigan Department of Corrections plans to begin testing the new system on Dec. 1 at selected men's prisons. If the pilot performs well, officials could eventually expand the technology to additional facilities. One significant change involves how often corrections staff can reassess someone's security level. Instead of relying on information collected at scheduled intervals, the new system will allow ongoing reviews using updated prison records. That could help staff recognize changes in behavior sooner.

The software comes from Recidiviz, a nonprofit technology organization that supports criminal justice agencies in 19 states. Its team analyzed 10 years of Michigan prison classification data to help redesign the state's scoring process. Here's how it works. The software examines information already in prison records and calculates a score using factors selected by Michigan corrections experts. Recent disciplinary incidents may carry more weight than incidents from years ago. Meanwhile, someone who maintains good behavior over time may have an opportunity to qualify for a lower security level.

Completing certain rehabilitation programs can also help someone qualify for a less restrictive classification. Additionally, the software can flag a person's record when new information warrants another review. Michigan Department of Corrections Director Heidi E. Washington believes the changes could help improve safety.

"Classifying prisoners at the security level that fits their current behaviors and needs keeps everyone safer," Washington said in the state's announcement. She also expressed optimism that the combination of historical information and research-based scoring could strengthen security throughout Michigan's prison system. The idea sounds promising. But how much confidence should officials place in those computer-generated scores?
GRANDMOTHER SUES AFTER ALLEGED AI FACIAL RECOGNITION ERROR LED TO MONTHS IN JAIL, EXPERTS SOUND ALARM
Michigan uses four general population security levels, from Level I with the fewest restrictions to Level V with the tightest supervision. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
Is Michigan actually using AI to predict prison violence?

This is where the story takes an unexpected turn. On Nov. 2, Recidiviz published an explanation titled, Why We Don't Use AI to Classify People in Prisons. The nonprofit confirmed that Michigan's new classification system does not use artificial intelligence to calculate security scores. The system relies on a points-based formula that corrections employees can examine.

You may hear this type of formula called an algorithm. That's simply a set of instructions a computer follows to complete a task. Think of it like a digital scorecard. The computer reviews specific information and adds up the points according to established rules. Give it the same information, and it produces the same score.

Recidiviz says Michigan corrections experts helped determine which factors belong in the scoring process. Staff can review the calculations and override a score when circumstances require it. For example, someone might have medical needs or personal safety concerns that call for a different housing assignment. Corrections employees can consider that information before making the final decision.

Now, Recidiviz does use AI in other parts of its technology platform. Some tools help corrections employees prepare case notes and organize information from meetings. However, the organization says AI does not determine someone's security level or release. And here's what I find interesting. We're hearing about AI being used in nearly every industry. Yet this particular system relies on a more traditional approach to computer software.

That clarification is important because people deserve to understand how technology influences decisions affecting someone's daily life. Still, using a rules-based system doesn't guarantee perfect results. Even straightforward software can produce questionable scores when the information behind its calculations contains errors.
Can Michigan really predict prison violence 30% better?

This is the number that really caught my attention. In its Oct. 28 announcement, the Michigan Department of Corrections said the redesigned system is expected to improve its ability to predict future violence by approximately 30%. That's a substantial improvement if the technology delivers it. However, the announcement doesn't explain how officials calculated that figure or provide the underlying performance results.

For example, will the system identify more people who might become violent? Could it also incorrectly classify someone as dangerous? And how will officials know whether it's performing better than the current process? Those questions deserve answers because someone's security classification can affect their daily life throughout their sentence.

There's another issue worth considering. The software depends on prison records. If a disciplinary report contains inaccurate information, that mistake could influence someone's score. Even when the information is correct, a risk assessment cannot predict with certainty what someone will do in the future.
NORTHEASTERN CITY VOTES TO END SHOTSPOTTER CONTRACT FOR GUNFIRE-DETECTION TECH DESIGNED TO FIGHT CRIME

An MDOC employment counselor reaches for materials inside a Michigan correctional facility's resource center, where educational and employment resources help incarcerated individuals prepare for life after prison. (Michigan Department of Corrections)
Why better prison technology may not solve Michigan's biggest problem

Even if Michigan's new software delivers more accurate security scores, officials still face a challenge that technology cannot solve on its own. What happens when someone needs higher-security housing but there's no appropriate bed available? Byron Osborn, president of the union representing Michigan corrections officers, raised that concern in recent reporting.

According to Osborn, the department faces a shortage of higher-security beds. He argues that the bigger problem involves a lack of appropriate housing for people already classified as higher risk. Consider what happens if the software identifies someone who needs tighter supervision. Corrections staff agree with the assessment, but the prison lacks space in the appropriate security unit.

Now what? The computer may have helped identify a potential safety concern. However, officials still need somewhere appropriate to house that person. Michigan has announced plans to add 870 high-security beds as part of its Safe Prisons Initiative. Some facility conversions are already underway, while larger construction projects will take longer to complete.

More than 400 of those beds will come from two new high-security units at Oaks Correctional Facility and St. Louis Correctional Facility. The state expects those construction projects to take approximately two and a half years. Osborn has warned that corrections officers and incarcerated people need solutions sooner.

Meanwhile, the state has experienced serious violence inside its prisons, including several recent incidents in which incarcerated people were suspected of killing their cellmates. Better classification could help officials recognize potentially dangerous situations sooner. But the department still needs sufficient staffing and appropriate housing to respond. And that raises another question. How much safer can a prison become if officials identify a problem but lack the resources to address it?
Kurt's key takeaways

I can see why Michigan wants to try something new. Nobody wants to see more violence inside prisons, and if technology can help prevent it, I'm all for giving it a chance. But I was surprised to learn that despite all the talk about AI, this new system actually uses a fairly straightforward scoring process. Corrections staff still make the final decisions, which I think is important when you're dealing with people's safety.

Now, that 30% improvement Michigan is talking about sounds impressive. But I'd really like to know how they arrived at that number. And what happens when the computer gets someone's risk level wrong? Maybe a person has turned their life around, but an old disciplinary record still works against them. That's the kind of situation I'd want someone to take a closer look at before making a decision.

There's also the bigger issue of whether Michigan has enough high-security beds and corrections officers to act on these assessments. You can have the best scoring system in the world, but what good does it do if there's nowhere appropriate to house someone who needs closer supervision? I'll be interested to see what happens when the pilot begins Dec. 1. If it leads to safer prisons and gives people a fairer way to demonstrate they've changed, that would be something worth talking about. But Michigan needs to show us the results.

Would you trust a computer-generated score to help determine how dangerous someone might be, or should decisions affecting someone's safety remain entirely in human hands? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI phishing scams turn your social posts against you
summary: University of Texas at Arlington researchers reveal how AI analyzes public Instagram posts to craft spear phishing emails that feel personal.
story: Kurt Knutsson, the 'CyberGuy', weighs in on warnings of rising AI cyber threats after Bill Gates sounds the alarm. Gates warns of negative surprises within a year and cautions that the world is not prepared for AI upheavals.

You post a few photos from a concert on Instagram. The next day, an email arrives that appears to be from the venue, offering you access to exclusive photos from the show. It mentions the artist you saw and even references the night you attended. Sounds legitimate, right? You might be tempted to click without giving it a second thought. But what if that email came from a scammer who used artificial intelligence to study your social media posts?

That's the alarming possibility researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington have uncovered. Their study shows how widely available AI tools can gather personal details from public social media accounts and turn them into highly convincing phishing emails. Even more concerning, the technology can generate these personalized messages at a scale that once required far more time and effort. Think about the photos and updates you've shared recently. Could someone use those details to convince you an email is legitimate? According to this research, the answer could be yes.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
Public social media profiles can reveal personal details that scammers use to create convincing AI-generated phishing emails. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
How AI phishing scams use your social media posts

You've probably seen your share of phishing emails. Maybe someone claims there's a problem with your bank account or a package couldn't be delivered. Many of these scams follow familiar patterns, and we've become pretty good at spotting the obvious ones. But AI is giving scammers a much more personal approach. Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington studied a technique known as context-aware spear phishing. In plain English, it means using details about someone's everyday life to create a scam that feels like it was written specifically for them.

Let's say you recently returned from a vacation in Brazil. You posted photos of the hotel and tagged a few places you visited. A scammer could use AI to analyze those posts and generate an email that appears to come from your hotel. The message might thank you for staying and offer a discount on your next visit. Everything seems to line up with your actual trip. However, the link could lead to a fake website designed to steal your password or credit card information.

Shirin Nilizadeh, an associate professor in UTA's Department of Computer Science and Engineering who led the study, explained why this is so concerning. "Anyone can be the attacker, and that makes it scarier," Nilizadeh said. And she's right. Someone using these tools may need very little personal knowledge about you. Your public posts can provide much of the information needed to create a believable message.
Researchers show how AI turns personal details into convincing scams

The research team, which included graduate student Elham Pourabbas Vafa and researcher Sayak Saha Roy, examined how AI could analyze public social media activity and generate personalized phishing emails. According to the research paper, the team studied 200 public Instagram accounts. They found that as few as 10 posts from an individual could provide enough information to create highly targeted messages.

The researchers evaluated more than 18,000 AI-generated emails and compared them with thousands of real-world phishing messages. The AI tools pulled information from travel photos and public updates about upcoming events. They also examined personal concerns people had shared online. From there, the technology created emails that appeared relevant to each person's recent experiences. The researchers even tested how AI could customize subject lines, sender names and links to make the messages more believable.

Consider something as simple as posting that you're excited about an upcoming concert. A scammer could use that information to send a fake ticket confirmation or an offer for upgraded seats. If you had recently complained about a delayed flight, an email offering compensation might arrive at just the right moment. These examples show how easily familiar details could be turned against someone. In a user study, participants generally rated the AI-generated emails as more convincing and less suspicious than the real-world phishing examples used for comparison.

However, the researchers evaluated people's reactions to the messages in a controlled setting. They did not measure how many people would actually click the malicious links during a real attack. Even with that limitation, the results raise serious concerns about how easily personal information can be used to manipulate someone's trust.
Why personalized phishing emails are getting harder to spot

One of the most unsettling parts of this research is that scammers may never need to hack your social media account. If your profile is public, they can potentially collect details you've already shared with the world. And those details can make an otherwise suspicious message feel familiar.

An email mentioning a restaurant you visited yesterday might seem harmless. So could a message referencing a concert you attended over the weekend. When the timing and details are accurate, people may be less likely to question where the message came from. That's the advantage scammers are hoping to exploit.

This research adds another concern because AI can automate much of the work involved in creating personalized messages. There's also the problem of how polished these emails can sound. We're used to looking for spelling mistakes and awkward wording. AI can produce professional-sounding messages, so those traditional warning signs may be missing. You could receive an email that looks perfectly normal, references something you actually did and still comes from someone trying to steal your information.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Scammers can use AI to analyze your online activity and send personalized messages designed to trick you into clicking malicious links. (NickyLloyd via Getty Images)
AI safety filters missed most phishing requests

Now, you might assume AI companies already have safeguards that prevent people from using their tools to create phishing scams. They do. But the researchers found that those protections had significant weaknesses. The team tested three widely used AI safety tools: Llama Guard, ShieldGemma and WildGuard. These systems attempt to recognize harmful requests before an AI model responds.

With their default settings, the tools detected only 0% to 19% of the requests to create personalized phishing attacks. That's a pretty troubling result, especially considering how quickly AI can generate these messages.

The researchers then explored whether more specific instructions could help the safety systems recognize these attacks. The improvement was substantial. After researchers adjusted the safeguards to identify context-aware phishing attempts, detection rates reached as high as 99% in their tests. That's encouraging because it suggests stronger safeguards are possible. However, those results came from a research setting. They don't guarantee that every malicious request would be blocked in the real world.

The researchers also left the exact instructions used to generate their phishing emails out of the public paper. They wanted to avoid providing criminals with a ready-made guide. Nilizadeh is urging AI companies to take these threats seriously and improve their protections against targeted social engineering attacks.
How to protect yourself from AI phishing scams

These findings show how easily scammers could turn everyday social media posts into convincing emails. You don't need to stop sharing your life online, but it's worth being more thoughtful about what strangers can see. And there are several practical ways to protect yourself if a suspicious message reaches your inbox.

Start by checking who can see your posts on Instagram, Facebook and other social media platforms. If your accounts are public, strangers may be able to view your photos and personal updates. Consider limiting access to approved followers and reviewing older posts that reveal more than you'd like. You can follow our guide on how to change your Instagram privacy settings. Keep in mind that people can still share or screenshot content from private accounts.

Posting vacation photos while you're still away can reveal where you are. The same goes for announcing upcoming travel plans or tagging yourself at an event. Consider waiting until you're home to share certain experiences. Also, check location tags and other details in your photos before posting them publicly. You don't need to stop sharing the things you enjoy, but a little discretion can make it harder for strangers to follow your activities.

If an email arrives from a hotel or another business referencing something you recently did, don't assume it's legitimate. Open the company's official app or type its website address into your browser instead of clicking the email link. You can also contact the business through a phone number you've independently verified. Be especially suspicious when a message asks you to sign in, provide payment information or respond urgently. Even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed.

Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices if you encounter a phishing attack. Some security tools can warn you about known dangerous websites and detect malware hidden in suspicious attachments or downloads. That's valuable protection if you accidentally click something malicious. However, antivirus software cannot guarantee that every phishing website will be blocked, especially if you voluntarily enter your information. Keep your security software updated and turn on its available protection features. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
Even a simple photo shared online could give scammers clues to make a phishing email seem legitimate. (iStock)

Scammers can learn more about you than you might realize. Data brokers and people-search websites may expose your home address, phone number and other personal details that criminals could use to make phishing emails more convincing. A personal data removal service can help find that information and request its removal from covered websites. While no service can erase everything about you online or remove your public social media posts, it can help reduce the personal information available to scammers. You can also request removals yourself for free, although doing so across multiple websites can take time. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

A scammer who steals one password may try using it to access other accounts. That's why every important account should have a unique, strong password. A trusted password manager can help you create and store them. Enable multifactor authentication wherever possible, preferably with an authenticator app or security key. Passkeys can offer even stronger phishing resistance on supported services. And never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly.

Security updates help close vulnerabilities that criminals can exploit. Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer and browser whenever possible. It's also worth checking that your email provider's spam and phishing filters are active. Gmail, Outlook and other major email services already block many suspicious messages, although some attacks can still get through. If you receive a suspicious email, use the built-in option to report it as phishing.
Know what to do if you click a suspicious link
Accidentally clicking a phishing link doesn't automatically mean your device has been compromised. However, if you think you've encountered a scam, here's what to do next.

Stop interacting immediately: Close the suspicious page. Don't enter personal information or download anything from the website.Scan your device: If you downloaded a file or suspect malware, run a security scan using strong antivirus software.Change compromised passwords: If you entered a password, change it immediately through the legitimate website using a trusted device.Review account activity: Check for unfamiliar logins or suspicious transactions. Sign out of unrecognized sessions and enable multifactor authentication.Contact your bank: If you shared financial information, notify your bank or credit card company immediately. Ask them to help secure your accounts.Report the scam: Report suspicious emails through your email provider and file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/.
Stop interacting immediately: Close the suspicious page. Don't enter personal information or download anything from the website.
Scan your device: If you downloaded a file or suspect malware, run a security scan using strong antivirus software.
Change compromised passwords: If you entered a password, change it immediately through the legitimate website using a trusted device.
Review account activity: Check for unfamiliar logins or suspicious transactions. Sign out of unrecognized sessions and enable multifactor authentication.
Contact your bank: If you shared financial information, notify your bank or credit card company immediately. Ask them to help secure your accounts.
Report the scam: Report suspicious emails through your email provider and file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/.
One final suggestion. When an email seems unusually well-timed or knows something personal about you, give it a second look. That little bit of hesitation could prevent a very expensive mistake.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think most of us understand that sharing personal information online comes with some risk. But this research takes that concern in a direction many people probably haven't considered. You could share a perfectly innocent photo from dinner or a weekend getaway and later receive an email that seems to know exactly where you've been. I can see how someone might trust that message, especially if it arrives at the right time and looks like it came from a familiar business. That's what worries me. AI is making it easier for criminals to use our own experiences to earn our trust. And they may be able to do it without spending much time researching us individually. I'm encouraged that the researchers found ways to improve AI safety filters. I'd like to see companies put those findings to work. In the meantime, I think we all need to be a little more careful about what we post publicly and a lot more skeptical of unexpected emails, even when the details seem right.
Should AI companies be held responsible when their technology helps criminals create convincing scams? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Young paraglider dies after reported emergency sends him crashing into field during Illinois flight
summary: Officials are investigating a fatal paragliding incident involving a 21-year-old man from a Chicago suburb who shared his aerial adventures and daring stunts online.
story: Giovanni Lopez’s death remains under investigation as officials await an autopsy to determine the cause and manner of death.(Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)
An Illinois paraglider died in a weekend crash after reportedly experiencing an emergency mid-flight.
Officials on Saturday identified the victim as Giovanni Lopez, 21, of Woodridge, a southwest suburb of Chicago.
Lopez frequently documented his paragliding adventures and daring aerial maneuvers on social media.
The Kendall County Coroner’s Office said it was notified around 3:40 p.m. Saturday of a possible fatality in Plainfield, an area dotted with farm fields southwest of Chicago.
CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER
Giovanni Lopez, 21, died in a paragliding incident in Plainfield, Illinois, after a reported midair emergency. (Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)
"The Kendall County Coroner’s Office was notified of a possible fatality related to a paragliding incident in the area of Ridge Road and 127th Street in Plainfield, Illinois," the office said.
Officials did not disclose the exact circumstances that led to Lopez’s death.
NBC Chicago reported that Lopez encountered an emergency while paragliding.
HIKER IDENTIFIED, POPULAR TRAIL CLOSED AFTER DEADLY FALL AT UTAH'S ZION NATIONAL PARK
Giovanni Lopez frequently shared videos of his paragliding adventures and daring aerial stunts on social media. (Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)
Witnesses reportedly rushed to Lopez's aid and attempted to help him until paramedics arrived and continued lifesaving efforts, the outlet said.
Upon arrival, coroner’s deputies pronounced Lopez dead at the scene.
Officials said the cause and manner of death will be determined following a forensic autopsy.
The incident remains under investigation by the Plainfield Police Department and the Kendall County Coroner's Office.
Giovanni Lopez wears a motorized propeller unit on his back as part of his paragliding equipment. (Giovanni Lopez/Facebook)

title: NTSB details warning whistles and emergency orders before tanker collision capsized New Orleans riverboat
summary: NTSB investigators detail warning whistles and emergency orders captured on the tanker's voyage recorder before the New Orleans riverboat collision.
story: NTSB investigators detail a steering problem, warning whistles and emergency anchor orders in the minutes before the Atlantic Asphalt struck the docked American Heritage in New Orleans. (Credit: WVUE)

A tanker suffered a steering problem about two minutes before slamming into a docked New Orleans riverboat Friday, federal investigators said Sunday, detailing warning whistles, calls for help and emergency orders before the collision.

The Atlantic Asphalt was heading upriver near the Crescent City Connection Bridge at about 12:26 p.m. when its rudder remained turned to the right, sending the ship toward the Mississippi River’s east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum said.
The tanker struck American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage at about 12:28 p.m. The riverboat capsized in about 22 minutes, according to preliminary information presented by the NTSB.
NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY
NTSB team surveying the wreckage. (NTSB)
Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of data from the tanker’s voyage data recorder, including bridge audio, rudder angle, engine RPM, course and speed.

The recordings captured sounds consistent with the ship’s whistle, warnings and requests for assistance over its marine radio, commands to deploy anchors and emergency shiphandling orders, Barnum said.
11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP
Officials described the steering problem as a "steering casualty," but cautioned that the term does not establish what went wrong.
"It could be many different things. That is something that we are investigating very closely," Barnum said.
AT LEAST 6 PEOPLE INJURED AFTER BOSTON DUCK BOAT OVERTURNS NEAR ENTRANCE TO POPULAR TOURIST ATTRACTION
Tugboats surround the Atlantic Asphalt tanker in New Orleans following its collision with the docked American Heritage river cruiser on Nov. 13, 2026. (Kat Ramirez for Fox News Digital)

NTSB board member John DeLeeuw said investigators have data on the tanker’s speed but are still analyzing it before releasing it publicly. Video showed anchors were down, but investigators are still determining which ones were deployed and how far, he said.

The findings follow a frantic rescue effort that officials said left everyone aboard the American Heritage alive. Roughly 100 people were pulled from the Mississippi River, while responders evacuated more than 80 before the vessel overturned, Port of New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said Saturday.
TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED
"This is a miracle. It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said Friday.
Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday, including two in serious condition. The other six were stable, officials said.
FBI INVESTIGATES SUSPECTED HOMICIDE ABOARD MSC SEASCAPE CRUISE SHIP AFTER SUDDEN RETURN TO TEXAS
The NTSB said Sunday that 140 passengers and 50 crew members were aboard the riverboat, a total of 190.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno also said the American Heritage’s captain was injured but stayed aboard until passengers and crew were accounted for, becoming the last person to leave.
MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING
"Every moment of the critical time [Friday], he did not want to leave his ship," Moreno said Saturday.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Saturday that crews were preparing to remove 16,000 gallons of fuel before salvage operations, warning that removing the capsized vessel could take weeks. DeLeeuw said Sunday that divers had been in the water, with salvage work overseen by the Coast Guard and salvage companies.
UNLICENSED NYC BOAT OPERATOR ALLEGEDLY IGNORED SAFETY WARNINGS BEFORE MOTHER, BABY DIED IN CAPSIZING: FEDS
Port of New Orleans collision map. (Google Maps)
Interviews with American Heritage crew members were underway Sunday. Interviews with the Atlantic Asphalt’s crew were scheduled to begin Monday and continue through the week, Barnum said.

The NTSB expects to release a preliminary report within about 30 days. Sunday’s briefing was its last planned on-site news conference, DeLeeuw said, with further updates to be posted online.

title: Duffy: Investigators examining 2 routers after nationwide FAA ground stop, no signs of foreign cyberattack
summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing deep diagnostics after the ground stop.
story: Fox News correspondent Alex Hogan reports from the White House on the travel chaos resulting from a massive nationwide ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also joins 'Fox News Sunday' to detail the latest on the investigation as he asks Congress for additional funding to modernize the agency's telecommunications network.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing extensive testing as investigators examine whether faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the nation's longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.

Appearing on "Fox News Sunday," Duffy said that investigators have found no indication of a foreign cyberattack, although the FBI and other federal law enforcement partners remain involved in the probe.

"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said. "But we're open, if we see something else, we're gonna continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement."
FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner)

In an update posted on X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris had secured the two routers from remote FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting "deep diagnostics testing" at its headquarters in Florida, with engineers from the FAA, Juniper and Cisco assisting.
The investigation follows Friday's nationwide ground stop, which halted air traffic for more than four hours and contributed to disruptions affecting roughly 15,000 flights Friday and Saturday.

The fallout continued Sunday, with 3,798 flights delayed and another 1,638 canceled within, into or out of the United States as of noon ET, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. Among the hardest-hit airports according to the provided data were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, with 376 delays, and Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, with 363 delays and 195 cancellations.

The shutdown occurred as L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic technology in the FAA's communications system. The work led to intermittent communications and radar gaps, prompting officials to halt flights nationwide.
Duffy said President Donald Trump convened federal officials on Friday as the administration investigated whether the disruption could have involved malicious interference.
"President Trump actually had the whole of government on the phone on Friday," Duffy said. "Was anyone seeing footprints? Was anyone hearing chatter? Was this a cyber attack from a foreign nation?"
"We have no indication that that was at play here," he added.
4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
Duffy defended the decision to issue the nationwide ground stop, emphasizing that passenger safety takes precedence when problems emerge in the FAA's communications network.
"When we have inconsistencies in our network we're going to shut it down," Duffy said.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, D.C. on Nov. 13, 2026, after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop at all airports due to a communications problem. (Zina DESMAZES / AFP via Getty Images)
The transportation secretary also warned that the FAA's communications infrastructure remains outdated despite ongoing efforts to replace copper wiring with fiber-optic technology.
"We're still using an old 1980 architecture for telecom," Duffy said. "I need a brand new telecom system."
BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS
Duffy said AT&T, Verizon and Lumen are prepared to help build a replacement network, but additional congressional funding is needed to move forward.

The request has drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, who argue the administration has yet to spend billions already allocated for air traffic control modernization. Duffy countered that the existing funds were designated for specific upgrades, including radar, radios and electronic flight strips, rather than a new communications network.
Travelers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)
Meanwhile, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that "the worst is behind us," with air travel expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023 and only the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

title: Virginia parents charged after house party draws hundreds of teens, fireworks and alleged underage drinking
summary: Fairfax County police charged Lisa and Aubrey Vaughan after their 13-year-old sons' small backyard party spiraled into a massive gathering with fireworks and crowds.
story: Officers were speaking with homeowners in McLean, Virginia, when a loud boom drew their attention to the backyard, where dozens of teenagers were seen streaming out as another boom rang out on Nov. 6. (Fairfax County Police Department/Facebook)

A Virginia couple who say they wanted to give their 13-year-old sons a safe place to hang out with a handful of classmates ended up facing criminal charges after their backyard gathering exploded into a massive party with hundreds of teenagers, fireworks and police descending on their neighborhood.

Lisa Vaughan, 45, and Aubrey Vaughan, 55, were charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance after Fairfax County police responded to their McLean home on Nov. 6. The couple maintains their innocence, with their attorney saying an invitation intended for just 10 to 20 classmates spread to older students.
"There will be no more," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5 DC, referring to the party for their sons. "We're done."
COLLEGE HOMECOMING PARTY TURNS TO CHAOS AS DECK COLLAPSES, LEAVING AT LEAST 28 PEOPLE INJURED

Lisa Vaughan, 45, and Aubrey Vaughan, 55, were charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance in connection with the party. (Fairfax County Police Department)

Police responded to multiple 911 calls around 9:03 p.m. reporting an out-of-control party. Callers estimated between 100 and 300 people had gathered at the home, where responding officers encountered a large crowd and fireworks being discharged, according to police.

Aubrey Vaughan apologized to neighbors, saying he was "embarrassed" by how quickly the gathering spiraled out of control. He and his wife even had their 13-year-old sons go door-to-door to apologize after police dispersed the crowd, according to FOX 5.
Police bodycam video shared to the department's social media shows Lisa Vaughan standing outside her family's home while speaking with responding officers. (Fairfax County Police Department)

The couple had planned a small eighth-grade gathering, but the invitation circulated on Snapchat and eventually reached students at a local high school, attracting uninvited teenagers, according to the family's attorney.
Aubrey Vaughan said he had "zero idea" high schoolers would show up and that he and his wife struggled to keep them out of their backyard and home.

Police described the gathering as an "underage drinking party," but Vaughan disputed suggestions that alcohol was permitted. He told FOX 5 that the invitation explicitly prohibited alcohol and bags, and that he and his wife were home supervising the entire time.
Responding officers encountered a large crowd of teens and fireworks being discharged at the home. (Fairfax County Police Department)
Aubrey Vaughan estimated the incident lasted about 45 minutes, saying he realized things were getting out of hand roughly 10 to 15 minutes before officers arrived.

"They wanted to maintain a safe place, free from alcohol, for kids to have a good time, but they had no control about all the kids that arrived and caused chaos in their neighborhood," the couple's attorney, Alaric Piette, told FOX 5.

Piette said the parents welcomed officers and offered to let them inspect the party area, but police declined. Both parents later turned themselves in and were released on $1,000 unsecured bonds each.
FAMILIES CONFRONT CALIFORNIA 'PARTY MOM' IN COURT, CALLING HER A 'MONSTER' WHO GROOMED THEIR CHILDREN
Fairfax County Police Chief Kevin Davis acknowledged the challenges parents face when deciding whether to host gatherings at home rather than let teenagers socialize elsewhere without supervision.
"I think it's universally a bad idea to host anything at a home," Davis said, warning that large gatherings involving alcohol, drugs or reckless behavior can quickly become dangerous.

The couple maintains their innocence, with their attorney saying an invitation intended for just 10 to 20 classmates spread to older high school students who overran the party. (Fairfax County Police Department)
The police chief emphasized that "parents have to be parents" and "adults have to be adults," warning that good intentions can have unintended consequences.
Aubrey Vaughan, meanwhile, said he was grateful police helped disperse the crowd and harbors no resentment toward the responding officers.
"The lesson is just make sure you're watching Snapchat," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5.

title: FAA says air travel should be back to normal Sunday after nationwide ground stop

story: Fox News correspondent Stephanie Bennett joins 'Fox Report' from London Heathrow Airport to discuss the massive disruptions following the FAA's national ground stop that triggered more than 13,000 flight delays.
The U.S. air travel schedule should return to normal by the end of Sunday, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford declared Saturday that "the worst is behind us" after the U.S. saw its longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years this weekend.

Transportation Sec. Sean Duffy says the situation arose when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing old copper wiring in the air traffic control system with new fiber wiring, causing a system overload.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaks during a press briefing at Department of Transportation headquarters on Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The work led to "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours. Officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause," he said.
